## 1 · Complexity Analysis {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-complexity]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**1. What does $O(n)$ mean, precisely, and how is it different from $\Theta(n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$f = O(n)$ means that beyond some $n_0$, $f(n) \le cn$ for a constant $c$: an upper bound only. $\Theta(n)$ adds the matching lower bound. Binary search is $O(n)$ (true but loose) and $\Theta(\log n)$ (tight). In interviews people say "O" when they mean the tight bound, but you should know the difference.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**2. Is hash-map lookup $O(1)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Expected/average $O(1)$ under a good hash function and a bounded load factor (resizing keeps it bounded, which is amortized $O(1)$ per insert). The worst case is $O(n)$ when many keys collide, which an adversary can force against a fixed, known hash function, as on Codeforces. Defences: randomised hashing, or a balanced tree map with guaranteed $O(\log n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**3. Explain amortized $O(1)$ for `vector::push_back`. Why must the growth be multiplicative?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When full, it reallocates to $2\times$ (or $1.5\times$) and copies. Over $n$ pushes, the copies total $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots < 2n$, so $O(1)$ amortized. With additive growth by $k$, the copies are $k + 2k + 3k + \dots \approx n^2/2k$, which is $\Theta(n)$ amortized. A single push can still be $\Theta(n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**4. Your solution is $O(n^2)$ and $n = 10^5$. Will it pass?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Usually not: $10^{10}$ operations against a budget of about $10^8$–$10^9$ per second. Very simple inner loops in C++ with SIMD can reach a few $10^9$, so $n = 10^5$ with a tiny constant sometimes passes in 2–3 s, but you should look for $O(n\log n)$. In Python, $O(n^2)$ is hopeless beyond $n \approx 5000$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**5. What is the space complexity of recursive merge sort?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(n)$ auxiliary space for the merge buffer plus $O(\log n)$ for the recursion stack: $O(n)$ total. (A naive implementation that allocates new arrays at every level still has only $O(n)$ alive at once, since the arrays along one root-to-leaf path sum to $n + n/2 + \dots < 2n$, but it allocates $O(n\log n)$ in total.)
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**6. Why is quicksort $O(n\log n)$ "on average" but $O(n^2)$ worst case, and how do you avoid the worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Balanced splits give $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = O(n\log n)$; maximally unbalanced splits (always picking the min or max) give $T(n) = T(n-1) + n = O(n^2)$, which a fixed pivot rule hits on sorted input. A random pivot makes the expected cost $O(n\log n)$ for every input. Introsort (used by `std::sort`) switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, which guarantees $O(n\log n)$ worst case.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**7. How do you analyse a recursive function with memoisation?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Time = (number of distinct states that are actually reached) × (work per state, not counting recursive calls that hit the cache). Space = memo table + maximum recursion depth. For example, the edit-distance DP has $nm$ states with $O(1)$ work each: $O(nm)$ time and space.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**8. What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from $n$ elements?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(n)$, not $O(n\log n)$. Bottom-up heapify sifts down each node by at most its height; there are about $n/2^{h+1}$ nodes of height $h$, so the total is $\sum_h \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} h = O(n)$ because $\sum h/2^h$ converges. Inserting the elements one by one is $O(n\log n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**9. Two nested loops, and the inner one is `while j < n and cond: j += 1` with `j` declared outside. Complexity?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(n)$ total. `j` only increases and is bounded by $n$, so the inner body executes at most $n$ times over the whole run. This is the two-pointer and sliding-window argument (aggregate amortization).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**10. What is pseudo-polynomial time? Is the 0/1 knapsack DP polynomial?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Polynomial in the numeric value of the input, but exponential in its length in bits. Knapsack DP is $O(nW)$, and $W$ takes $\log W$ bits, so it is pseudo-polynomial. Knapsack is NP-hard, so no truly polynomial algorithm is known; the DP is fast only when $W$ is small.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**11. Your Python DFS crashes on a tree with $10^5$ nodes. Why, and what do you do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Recursion depth reaches $10^5$ on a path-shaped tree, above CPython's default limit of 1000 (and raising the limit can overflow the C stack and crash the process). Convert to an iterative DFS with an explicit stack, or run the recursion in a thread with a larger stack size. In C++, the same issue appears on judges with small stacks around depth $10^5$–$10^6$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**12. When does an $O(n\log n)$ algorithm lose to an $O(n^2)$ one?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For small $n$, when the constant factors favour the quadratic one. Insertion sort beats merge sort below roughly 16–32 elements (cache-friendly, no allocation, few branches), which is why hybrid sorts (Timsort, introsort) switch to insertion sort for small subarrays. Asymptotics describe growth, not speed at a specific $n$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="1"}
**13. What is the complexity of checking if a number $N \le 10^{12}$ is prime by trial division, and is it polynomial?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(\sqrt N) = 10^6$ steps, which is fast here. But it is exponential in the number of digits ($\sqrt N = 2^{b/2}$ for a $b$-bit $N$), so it is not polynomial. Miller–Rabin runs in $O(k\log^3 N)$ and is used for large $N$.
:::
:::

## 2 · Proof Techniques for Algorithms {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-proofs]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**1. What is a loop invariant? Give one for binary search.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A statement true before every iteration; it plus the exit condition gives the result. For lower-bound binary search on $[lo, hi)$: all elements before $lo$ are $< x$ and all from $hi$ on are $\ge x$. At exit $lo = hi$ is the answer. The variant $hi - lo$ halves, giving $O(\log n)$ and termination.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**2. How do you convince an interviewer that your greedy algorithm is correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Name the greedy choice and give an exchange argument: "take any optimal solution; if its first choice differs from mine, swap it for mine; the result is still valid and no worse; repeat". Or "greedy stays ahead": after every step greedy is at least as good by some measure. Then mention you would also check it against brute force on small inputs.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**3. Your greedy passes all samples. How do you gain more confidence before submitting?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a brute force (try all subsets or permutations), generate many small random inputs (sizes 1–8, small values to force ties), and compare. Small inputs find counterexamples fastest, and once found, the smallest one usually explains why the idea fails. This takes five minutes and catches most wrong greedies.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**4. Why can comparison sorts not beat $O(n\log n)$, and how do counting sort and radix sort get around it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A comparison sort is a binary decision tree with at least $n!$ leaves, so its height is at least $\log_2 n! = \Theta(n\log n)$. Counting and radix sort do not compare elements: they use values as array indices, which gives more than two outcomes per operation, so the decision-tree bound does not apply. They pay instead with a dependence on the value range or the number of digits.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**5. Can you find the minimum and maximum with fewer than $2n - 2$ comparisons? Is your answer optimal?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: compare elements in pairs, then the smaller against the current min and the larger against the current max: $\lceil 3n/2\rceil - 2$ comparisons. An adversary argument shows this is optimal: $2n - 2$ units of information are needed and only comparisons between two fresh elements give two units.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**6. What is the difference between partial and total correctness? How do you prove a loop terminates?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Partial: if it stops, the answer is right. Total: also, it always stops. Termination: exhibit a variant, a non-negative integer that strictly decreases each iteration (such as $hi - lo$, the number of unprocessed elements, or $a + b$ in subtractive gcd).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**7. What is optimal substructure? Give a problem where it fails.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, so a DP or greedy can build it from them. Shortest paths have it (a subpath of a shortest path is shortest). **Longest simple path** does not: the longest simple path from $u$ to $w$ through $v$ need not consist of longest simple paths $u \to v$ and $v \to w$, because those may share vertices. Longest simple path is NP-hard.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**8. Does Boyer–Moore voting work if there is no majority element?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It returns *some* candidate, which may not be a majority (e.g. $[1, 2, 3]$ returns 3). The invariant only guarantees that **if** a majority exists, it is the candidate. Verify with a second counting pass. Space stays $O(1)$, time $O(n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**9. Why does "binary search on the answer" work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It needs a monotone predicate: if $P(x)$ holds then $P(y)$ holds for all $y \ge x$ (e.g. "can we finish with capacity $x$?"). Then the set of good $x$ is a suffix, and binary search finds its first element with the invariant "$P(lo-1)$ false, $P(hi)$ true". Without monotonicity the search can skip over the answer.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**10. What is the extremal principle? Give an algorithmic example.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Consider an object that is maximal or minimal in some sense and show it has the needed property. Examples: the first vertex of a longest path in a DAG has in-degree 0 (so topological sort can start); the global maximum of an array is a peak; the interval that ends first can be in an optimal schedule.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**11. Find the second largest of $n$ numbers. How many comparisons do you need?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A tournament finds the maximum in $n - 1$; the second largest lost only to the champion, so it is among the $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ players the champion beat: $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 1$ more comparisons. Total $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$, which is optimal by an adversary argument. Two passes ($2n - 3$) or sorting are correct but use more comparisons.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**12. What is an adversary argument?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A lower-bound technique: an adversary answers the algorithm's queries on the fly, consistent with at least one input, choosing answers that reveal as little as possible. If the adversary can keep two inputs with different answers alive for $g(n)$ queries, any algorithm needs $g(n)$ queries in the worst case. Used for min-max, second largest, merging, and query limits in interactive problems.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="2"}
**13. Why is Kruskal's algorithm correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cut property (an exchange argument): for any cut, the lightest edge crossing it is in some MST. Kruskal adds the lightest edge that joins two different components, which is the lightest edge across the cut separating one of those components from the rest. If an MST $T$ lacks it, adding it to $T$ creates a cycle that crosses the cut again through some heavier-or-equal edge; swapping gives a spanning tree no heavier. More generally, forests form a matroid, and greedy is optimal on matroids.
:::
:::

## 3 · Python and C++ for DSA {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-lang]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**1. Does a Python `dict` keep insertion order? Can you rely on it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes. Since Python 3.7 it is part of the language specification (CPython 3.6 already did it as an implementation detail). Iteration, `keys()`, `values()` and `popitem()` (which removes the **last** item) follow insertion order. Updating an existing key keeps its position; deleting and reinserting moves it to the end. `set` has no order guarantee.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**2. How is a Python `list` implemented, and what are the costs of `append`, `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A dynamic array of pointers that over-allocates by about 12.5% when it grows. `append` is amortized $O(1)$ (@sec-cx-amortized); `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` shift every element, $O(n)$. For a queue use `collections.deque`, which is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks with $O(1)$ operations at both ends.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**3. How do you get a max-heap in Python? What about a heap of objects?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`heapq` only provides a min-heap. For numbers, push `-x`. For objects, push tuples `(key, counter, obj)` where `counter` is a unique increasing integer (e.g. from `itertools.count()`), so ties never compare `obj`. For a max-heap with a non-numeric key, wrap the key in a class with a reversed `__lt__`. (Python 3.14 adds `heapq.heapify_max`, `heappush_max` and `heappop_max`, but judges usually run older versions.)
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**4. When do you choose `std::map` over `std::unordered_map`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When you need order: iteration in sorted order, `lower_bound`, predecessor/successor, the minimum or maximum key. Also when you need a guaranteed $O(\log n)$ worst case (no hash attacks, no rehash spikes), or when the key has no hash (pairs, vectors) and you do not want to write one. `unordered_map` is faster on average for plain lookups, especially with `reserve` and a good hash.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**5. What is a strict weak ordering, and what happens if a comparator is not one?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A relation that is irreflexive (`!comp(a, a)`), transitive, and whose "neither is less" relation (equivalence) is transitive too. Sorting and ordered containers assume it. Violations are undefined behaviour: `std::sort` can loop out of bounds and crash, `set` can fail to find elements it contains. The common violations are `<=` instead of `<`, comparators with floating-point tolerance (`abs(a - b) < eps` is not transitive), and comparators that depend on mutable state.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**6. When are `vector` iterators invalidated? What about `list` and `map`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`vector`: any insertion that reallocates invalidates all iterators, pointers and references; otherwise insertion invalidates those at or after the insertion point; `erase` invalidates those at or after the erased position. `list`, `set`, `map`: insertion invalidates nothing, erase invalidates only the erased element. `unordered_map`: rehashing invalidates iterators (but not references to elements); erase invalidates only the erased one.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**7. Why is `lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` slow on a `std::set`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The free function performs a binary search using `std::advance` on the iterators. Set iterators are bidirectional, not random-access, so each advance of $k$ steps costs $O(k)$, and the total is $O(n)$ (with $O(\log n)$ comparisons). The member function `s.lower_bound(x)` walks down the tree in $O(\log n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**8. Python integers never overflow. Does that mean you never think about integer size in Python?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Large integers make each operation cost $O(\text{digits})$ or more, so a DP that grows numbers without reducing modulo $p$ can turn $O(n^2)$ operations into $O(n^3)$ work. Memory grows too: each int is an object of 28+ bytes. `str()` of an int beyond 4300 digits raises `ValueError` by default. And `numpy` arrays use fixed-width types (`int64`), which **do** overflow silently.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**9. Why should you not compare floating-point numbers with `==`? What do you do instead?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Most decimal fractions are not representable in binary, and every operation rounds, so mathematically equal values can differ in the last bits (`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`). Options: compare with a tolerance `abs(a - b) < eps` with `eps` chosen from the magnitudes involved; better, avoid floats: cross-multiply fractions, use reduced integer pairs for slopes, `math.isqrt` for roots, `Fraction` for exact rationals, or scale to integers (cents instead of dollars).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**10. How do you compute $(a - b) \bmod m$ correctly in C++?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`((a - b) % m + m) % m`, because C++'s `%` takes the sign of the left operand, so `a - b < 0` gives a negative remainder. If $a, b \in [0, m)$ already, `(a - b + m) % m` suffices. Python's `%` already returns a value in $[0, m)$ for $m > 0$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**11. What is an anti-hash test, and how do you defend against one?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A test whose keys all collide under a known, deterministic hash function, making each hash-table operation $O(n)$ and the whole solution $O(n^2)$. On Codeforces, libstdc++'s identity hash and fixed prime bucket counts make `unordered_map<int, …>` an easy target. Defences: a strong mixing hash with a random seed chosen at run time (`splitmix64` + clock), `reserve`, or a balanced tree (`map`) with guaranteed $O(\log n)$. In Python, XOR integer keys with a random constant, or avoid hashing (sort, or index a list by value).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**12. Your Python DFS on a tree with $2\cdot10^5$ nodes crashes. What are your options?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The recursion depth exceeds the limit (1000 by default). `sys.setrecursionlimit` alone can lead to a segfault when the C stack runs out. Options: rewrite iteratively with an explicit stack (for post-order work, process a preorder in reverse, or push `(node, state)` pairs); use generator-based recursion with a driver loop; or run the recursive code in a thread with `threading.stack_size` set large. Iterative code is the most reliable.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**13. What do `ios::sync_with_stdio(false)` and `cin.tie(nullptr)` do, and why is `endl` slow?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The first stops C++ streams from synchronising with C's `stdio` after every operation, so they can buffer independently (you must then not mix `cin`/`cout` with `scanf`/`printf`). The second stops `cin` from flushing `cout` before each input operation. `endl` writes `'\n'` and flushes the buffer, which is a system call per line; with $10^6$ lines that dominates the running time. Use `'\n'`, except in interactive problems, where you must flush.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**14. Are Python's `sort` and C++'s `std::sort` stable? Why does it matter?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Python's Timsort is stable; `std::sort` (introsort) is not, `std::stable_sort` (merge sort) is. Stability lets you sort by several keys with several passes (least significant first), and keeps the input order among ties when the problem requires it ("if equal, keep the original order"). Without stability you must add the index as a final tie-breaker.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="3"}
**15. When is Python too slow for a problem, and what do you do about it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the intended solution needs more than about $10^7$ Python-level operations in the time limit: $n \log n$ with $n = 10^6$, heavy data structures (segment trees with $10^6$ queries), or deep recursion. Remedies: submit with PyPy (5–20× faster on numeric loops), push loops into C (built-ins, slicing, `numpy`), avoid recursion and object-heavy designs, use fast I/O. If the constant is still too high, switch to C++.
:::
:::

## 4 · Testing and Debugging {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-testing]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**1. How would you test the function you just wrote?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Walk through the edge cases out loud (empty, one element, two elements, all equal, negatives, the maximum size and overflow, boundaries), trace one small normal case by hand, and say that in practice you would compare it against a brute force on many small random inputs. Mention the specific risky line ("the `<=` in the loop condition") and test it.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**2. What is a stress test, and why are its inputs small?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Run the optimised solution and a slow, obviously correct brute force on thousands of random inputs, and stop at the first difference. Inputs are small so that the brute force is fast, so that a failing case is easy to read, and so that small value ranges produce the duplicates and ties where bugs hide. Almost all bugs that exist for large inputs also exist for some small one.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**3. Your solution passes the samples but you are not sure it is correct. You have 10 minutes left. What do you do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a brute force (five lines: all subsets or permutations), a generator with $n \le 8$ and values in 0..5, and a compare loop. Run it for a minute. If it finds a counterexample, shrink it by hand or by deleting elements, and fix. If not, check the edge cases and overflow on the max test, then submit.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**4. Your solution gets TLE. How do you find out why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First compare the intended complexity with the budget from the constraints. Then generate worst-case inputs (max $n$; sorted; all equal; a path graph; many duplicates; many tiny test cases) and time them locally, doubling $n$ to see the growth rate. Look for hidden costs: `x in list`, `list.pop(0)`, string concatenation in a loop, copying vectors by value, clearing a big array per test, slow I/O (`cin` without `sync_with_stdio(false)`, Python `input()` instead of `sys.stdin`), and hash tables under adversarial keys.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**5. A recursive DFS crashes on large inputs in Python. What are your options?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The default recursion limit is 1000 and the interpreter's C stack is limited too. Options: convert to an explicit stack (iterative DFS, or process vertices in BFS order and then in reverse order for bottom-up computations); or raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` and run the code in a `threading.Thread` after `threading.stack_size(...)` to get a bigger stack. The iterative version is the robust choice.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**6. How do you test a function whose output is not unique, for example "return any valid topological order"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a checker that validates the output against the input (a permutation of the vertices; every edge goes forward), instead of comparing with a reference output. For optimisation problems with many optimal solutions, the checker verifies the solution is valid and that its value equals the brute force's optimal value.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**7. What is shrinking, and why does it help?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Repeatedly replacing a failing input with a smaller one that still fails (delete parts, make values smaller) until no smaller variant fails. The minimal input typically has two or three elements and isolates the cause: "two equal values", "one interval inside another", "two elements when $lo = mid$". It is what property-based testing tools (QuickCheck, Hypothesis) do automatically; the systematic version is Zeller's delta debugging.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**8. How do you generate a random tree? Is it uniform?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Simplest: for $i = 2..n$ connect $i$ to a random earlier vertex, then shuffle the labels. That is not uniform over labelled trees, and its height is only $O(\log n)$ on average. For uniform trees, decode a random Prüfer sequence of length $n - 2$ (there are $n^{n-2}$ sequences and as many labelled trees). For testing, add paths, stars and caterpillars explicitly, since they are the extreme cases for depth and degree.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**9. On Codeforces your solution passes test 1 but fails on test 2, which has many test cases. What is the most likely bug?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
State carried between test cases: a global counter, map, visited array, adjacency list or answer variable that is not reset. Or an early `return`/`break` that leaves part of a test's input unread, so the next test reads garbage. Fix by putting per-test state inside the test loop and reading the whole input of each test even when the answer is known early.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**10. What is "Idleness limit exceeded" and how do you avoid it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In an interactive problem, both programs are waiting: usually your query is still in the output buffer, so the judge never receives it. Flush after every query (`endl`, `fflush(stdout)`, `print(..., flush=True)`). It also happens when you read input the judge never sends (wrong protocol), or when you forget to print the final answer.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**11. How do you test an interactive solution locally?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a local judge: it holds the hidden data, validates each query, answers it, counts queries against the limit, and checks the final answer. Structure the solution so that it takes an `ask` function, and run it against the judge for all hidden values (or many random ones and the extremes). To test the real binary, run the judge as a separate process connected through a pipe. An adaptive judge (adversary) checks the worst case of the query count.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**12. How do you detect and prevent integer overflow?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Estimate the largest intermediate value from the constraints (max $n$ × max value, products, squares, $n(n+1)/2$ counts). Use 64-bit types for anything that can exceed about $2\cdot10^9$, cast before multiplying (`1LL * a * b`), compare as `a > LIMIT / b` instead of `a * b > LIMIT`, and use `__int128` for products of 64-bit values. Detect it with `-fsanitize=undefined` (signed overflow) and with a max-value test. In Python, wrap results in a range check to simulate C++ types.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**13. Should asserts stay in submitted code?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cheap asserts that check assumptions (an index range, "this case cannot happen") can stay: a failing assert gives RE instead of a silent WA, which tells you something. Expensive checks (re-verifying an invariant over the whole array each iteration) must go, or be guarded by a debug flag, because they change the complexity. In Python, `python -O` removes asserts, so never put side effects inside them.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="4"}
**14. What do `-fsanitize=address,undefined` and `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` catch?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AddressSanitizer: out-of-bounds reads and writes on heap, stack and global arrays, use-after-free, double free. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: signed integer overflow, invalid shifts, division by zero, misaligned or null pointer use. `_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`: bounds checks on `vector::operator[]`, invalid iterator use, and comparators that are not strict weak orderings in `std::sort`. All slow the program down, so use them on the failing test, not to measure speed.
:::
:::

## 5 · Introduction to Arrays {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-arr]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**1. Why does `a[i]` cost $O(1)$, and what does the CPU actually do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cell $i$ lives at `base + i·s` (@eq-arr-address). The compiler emits a multiply (often a shift), an add and a load: the address is *computed*, never searched for, so the cost does not depend on $i$ or $n$ (@sec-arr-memory).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**2. Two programs are both $O(n)$ over the same data, but one is several times faster. How can that be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Caches. Memory moves in 64-byte lines, so an in-order scan pays one slow fetch per line and then reads the rest of the line almost for free, with hardware prefetching on top. Scattered access (random indices, linked nodes, a column-order walk of a row-major grid) can pay a full memory trip on nearly every read. Big-O hides this constant (@sec-arr-cache, @fig-arr-cache).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**3. Why is `push_back` amortised $O(1)$ when a single call can copy the whole array?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The capacity doubles, so the copies over $n$ pushes form the series $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots < 2n$. The bound is a worst-case guarantee about every *sequence* of operations, not an average over random inputs. Growing by a constant instead would make the total quadratic (@sec-arr-vec).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**4. What is the difference between `reserve` and `resize`, and why can a reference into a vector become invalid?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`reserve(n)` changes the capacity only (the size stays the same, so `v[0]` may still be out of range); `resize(n)` changes the size and creates the cells. A `push_back` into a full buffer moves every element to a new block, so pointers, references and iterators into the old block dangle. Keep indices while a vector can still grow (@sec-arr-vec).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**5. What is a half-open range, and why prefer it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$[\ell, r)$ keeps $\ell$, excludes $r$, holds $r - \ell$ items and is empty when $\ell = r$. Adjacent ranges $[\ell, m)$ and $[m, r)$ meet with no overlap or gap, the loop is the familiar `for (i = l; i < r; i++)`, and it matches Python slices and every STL algorithm (@sec-arr-ranges).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**6. Name the usual sources of off-by-one errors, and one habit that prevents most of them.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Loop bounds (`<=` instead of `<`), closed versus half-open lengths ($r - \ell + 1$ versus $r - \ell$), neighbour access at the last index, `size() - 1` on an empty vector, and mixing 0- and 1-based positions. Writing the loop invariant ("the state describes $[0, i)$") forces the start and end values to be right (@sec-arr-ranges, @sec-arr-invariant).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**7. The constraints say $n \le 2\cdot10^5$ and a one-second limit. What complexity is safe, and what else do you read off the statement?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(n)$ or $O(n\log n)$; $n^2 = 4\cdot10^{10}$ is far beyond the roughly $10^8$ simple steps per second. Also read the value range (does every sum and product fit in `int`?), whether there are many test cases with a bound on $\sum n$, and the memory limit (@sec-arr-cost, @sec-cx-budget).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**8. When must you switch from `int` to `long long`, and where exactly does `int * int` go wrong?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Whenever a sum, product, count or answer can pass $2^{31} - 1 \approx 2.1\cdot10^9$: a sum of $2\cdot10^5$ values up to $10^9$, a product of two $10^5$s, the number of pairs for $n = 2\cdot10^5$. `long long x = a * b` multiplies in `int` first and only then widens the wrapped result; write `(long long)a * b` (@sec-arr-cost).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**9. Which running states can a single pass maintain, and which cannot? Give an example of each.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Any summary whose new value depends only on the old summary and the new element: a sum, the maximum and its index, the top $k$ for a small $k$, the best pair with an earlier element (via the prefix minimum), the current streak. The median cannot: after $1, 5, 3$ the median $3$ forgets that a $5$ was seen, and that $5$ becomes the median after $9, 8$ arrive (@sec-arr-scan, @sec-arr-p1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**10. In place or a second array: how do you choose, and what makes an in-place loop safe?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Use a second array when it is allowed and clarity matters. Work in place when the statement demands $O(1)$ extra space. Safety means never overwriting a value that a later step still needs: keep the write pointer at or behind the read pointer ($w \le r$), pick the loop direction (data moving right means scanning from the right), swap, or encode both values in one cell (@sec-arr-inplace).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**11. What does "stable" mean for a rearrangement, and which of your in-place tools are stable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Elements the rule does not distinguish keep their relative order. Read/write compaction is stable for the kept elements (Move Zeroes relies on it); swapping from both ends (partition) is not, as the "evens first" example shows; `std::stable_partition` and Python's `sorted` are stable at the price of a buffer (@sec-arr-inplace).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**12. Remove Duplicates II: why compare with `a[w - 2]` and not `a[r - 2]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The written prefix $a[0, w)$ is final and correct by the invariant, so `a[w - 2]` really is the value two places back in the output. The cell `a[r - 2]` lies in the free zone $[w, r)$ and may already have been overwritten: on $[1,1,1,2,2,3]$ the read-side test drops the second 2 (@sec-arr-p2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**13. Rotate an array right by $k$ in $O(1)$ extra space, and prove it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`k %= n`; reverse all, reverse $[0, k)$, reverse $[k, n)$. With $A$ the first $n - k$ and $B$ the last $k$ elements, $(AB)^R = B^R A^R$, and reversing each block back gives $BA$ (@eq-arr-rev). The alternative is the cycle method, $\gcd(n, k)$ cycles of $i \to (i + k) \bmod n$, which writes each element once but jumps around memory (@sec-arr-p3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**14. How do you check whether $b$ is a rotation of $a$, and whether $a$ is a sorted array rotated?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every rotation of $a$ is a length-$n$ window of $aa$, so check that the lengths match and $b$ occurs in $aa$ (index it as $a[j \bmod n]$; $O(n^2)$ naively, $O(n)$ with string matching). For "sorted and rotated", count the circular drops $a_i > a_{(i+1) \bmod n}$: at most one means yes (@sec-arr-p3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**15. Build Array from Permutation in $O(1)$ extra space: what is the trick, and what can go wrong?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Store both values in each cell: `a[i] += n * (a[a[i]] % n)`, then divide every cell by $n$. The `% n` recovers the original value of a cell that is already encoded; forgetting it reads a half-written value. The encoded values reach about $n^2$, which overflows a 32-bit `int` once $n$ passes about $46\,000$ (@eq-arr-encode, @sec-arr-p4-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**16. Values lie in $[0, 100]$ and you need "how many are smaller than each element". Sort, hash, or count?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Count: a 101-cell frequency array plus one running-sum pass over the values gives every answer in $O(n + 101)$ time and constant extra space, beating the $O(n\log n)$ sort and a hash map's constants. For values up to $10^9$ the array would not fit; then sort, or use a hash map when only equality matters (@sec-arr-p5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**17. Does Python overflow? Why should a Python programmer still care about integer ranges?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Python integers are unbounded, so they never overflow, but big ones are slower, and an interview or contest answer in C++ or Java must widen to 64 bits. The reasoning also matters for encodings: packing two values in one cell multiplies magnitudes to about $n^2$ (@sec-arr-cost, @eq-arr-encode).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="5"}
**18. How many subarrays, subsequences and subsets does a length-$n$ array have, and what does that tell you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ non-empty subarrays, so enumerating them is fine up to $n \approx 5000$ with $O(1)$ work each; $2^n$ subsequences and subsets of positions, so enumeration only works up to $n \approx 20$. The count is the feasibility budget for brute force (@sec-arr-counts).
:::
:::

## 6 · Prefix Sums & Difference Arrays {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-pref]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**1. What is a prefix-sum table, and why is $P[0]=0$ the convention that removes your off-by-one bugs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P[i]=\sum_{k<i}a[k]$ for $i\in[0,n]$: $n+1$ cells, each the sum of everything *strictly below* its index. Then any half-open range is $P[r]-P[\ell]$, and an empty range reads $0$ for free. The alternative — $P[i]=\sum_{k\le i}a[k]$ — forces `if (l == 0)` in every query (@sec-pref-def, @sec-arr-ranges).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**2. Why is the difference array called the inverse of the prefix sum?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`prefix(d)` recovers $a$ and `difference(a)` recovers $d$, so the two passes undo each other. Operationally, a difference array is "a range update written as two point updates": $+v$ where the range starts, $-v$ where it ends. That is why one rebuild pass converts $u$ range adds from $O(nu)$ to $O(n+u)$ (@sec-pref-diff).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**3. $n,q \le 2\cdot10^5$, the array is immutable, each query is a range sum. Derive the complexity you are allowed to write.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(nq) = 4\cdot10^{10}$ is hopeless against a $\sim10^8$ budget, so the answer must be $O(n+q)$: build the table in $O(n)$, answer each query in $O(1)$. The constraint pair ($n$ large *and* $q$ large) is the recognition signal; if $q$ were $1$, no table is needed (@sec-pref-p1, @sec-arr-cost, @sec-cx-budget).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**4. Count subarrays with sum $k$. Why not a sliding window, and what is the invariant of the map solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Negatives break the window: extending can lower the sum, so "shrink while too big" has no justification. The map solution walks the prefix sums and uses $\sum a[i:j) = k \iff P[i] = P[j]-k$; the invariant is that before index $j$, `seen[v]` counts the prefix indices with value $v$, so `seen[p-k]` is exactly the number of legal left ends — one lookup per element, $O(n)$ (@sec-pref-hash, @sec-pref-p2-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**5. Why does "divisible by $k$" shrink a hash map to an array of size $k$, and what is the trap in C++?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$k \mid (P[j]-P[i])$ iff $P[j]\equiv P[i]\pmod k$, so the key is the remainder and there are only $k$ of them — time $O(n+k)$, space $O(k)$. The trap: C++'s `%` returns a negative remainder for a negative left operand, so `cnt[r]` indexes out of bounds; normalise with `((r % k) + k) % k`. Python's `%` never returns a negative (@sec-pref-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**6. Which operations get a prefix table, and what do you do when the operation has no inverse?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Anything associative with an inverse — a group: $+$, $\oplus$, and $\times$ away from zeros. Without an inverse ($\min$, $\max$, $\gcd$, product-with-zeros) you cannot cancel a prefix, so you build a **suffix** table instead and combine a prefix with a suffix, which answers "everything to my left/right" but not "the range in the middle" (@sec-pref-other, @sec-pref-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**7. Derive the 2D rectangle formula. Why is the corner added rather than subtracted?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P[r_2][c_2]$ is the anchored block; removing $P[r_1][c_2]$ deletes the top strip and removing $P[r_2][c_1]$ deletes the left strip — and the top-left rectangle $P[r_1][c_1]$ lies in both strips, so it was deleted twice and must be added back once. Inclusion–exclusion: alternate signs by how many sets you removed (@sec-pref-2d, @sec-pref-p4-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**8. Product of array except self: the interviewer says "no division". Why, and what does it cost you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Division by zero: one zero makes the total product zero, so `total/a[i]` is either undefined or wrong for every cell. The two-pass version — forward left products into the output, backward with one running right product — is $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ auxiliary, and has no case analysis at all (@sec-pref-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**9. Find Pivot Index: why do you test *before* accumulating the current element?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The pivot is excluded from both sides. Testing first means `left` is the sum of $a[0{:}i]$ only, and the right side is `total - left - a[i]`; it also returns the *leftmost* pivot, since you return at the first match. Accumulating first would silently include $a[i]$ on the left (@sec-pref-p1-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**10. When may you binary search or two-pointer over cut positions, and when must you scan them all?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only when the prefix sum is monotone in the cut position, which needs every element non-negative. All-positive problems (CF 1006C, "split into three equal sums") allow $O(n)$ two pointers or $O(n\log n)$ searches. Once negatives are allowed (LC 2270, LC 560) the prefix rises and falls, the predicate is not monotone, and a scan of all $n-1$ cuts is the honest bound (@sec-pref-p6-a, @sec-pref-p6-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**11. Where exactly does 64-bit arithmetic become mandatory in this chapter's problems?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the *table*, not just the answer: $2\cdot10^5$ values up to $10^9$ sum to $2\cdot10^{14}$. Greg and Array multiplies a run count of $10^5$ by a delta of $10^5$ and then sums $10^5$ such terms — $10^{15}$. And in C++ widen before the operation: `(long long)a * b` is fine, `a * b` assigned to a `long long` has already overflowed (@sec-arr-cost, @sec-pref-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**12. Your table is $O(n)$ space, but the interviewer asks for $O(1)$. What can you always give up?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The table, if you only need one prefix at a time. A single left-to-right scan can carry `left` as a scalar plus the total, which turns pivot/split/count-equal-suffix problems into $O(1)$ space (@sec-pref-p1-b). What you cannot give up: queries that revisit arbitrary ranges, or a hash map that must remember every prefix value — those genuinely need their $O(n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**13. Two accepted-looking solutions to "count subarrays divisible by $k$" have the same $O(n)$ idea, but one times out on a judge with many test cases. What are the usual culprits?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Constant factors and hidden per-test costs, not the idea. An ordered `map` costs $O(\log n)$ per operation where a bucket array of size $k$ (or an `unordered_map`) costs $O(1)$. Allocating or clearing a $k$-sized array for every test case costs $t \cdot k$ in total even when the inputs are tiny — re-zero only the buckets you touched, or use a map. Flushing output with `endl` after every answer, or unsynchronised C++ streams, can dominate an otherwise linear program. And rebuilding the prefix table inside the query loop turns $O(n+q)$ back into $O(nq)$ (@sec-pref-p2-b, @sec-arr-p5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**14. You need the *longest* subarray with sum $k$, not the count. What changes in the hash-map walk, and why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The map stores each prefix value's **first** index instead of its count, and is never overwritten. For a right end $j$, every left end $i$ with $P[i] = P[j]-k$ works, and the longest range uses the smallest such $i$ — the first occurrence. For the *shortest* range you would store the latest index and overwrite. The seed becomes `first[0] = 0`, the index of the empty prefix (@sec-pref-hash).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="6"}
**15. How does the maximum-subarray problem fit into the prefix-sum picture?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The best subarray ending at $j$ is $P[j] - \min_{i<j} P[i]$, so one pass that keeps the running prefix and the running minimum of earlier prefixes solves it in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. A prefix *minimum* has no inverse but needs none, because it is anchored at the left end. Kadane's algorithm is the same computation: resetting the running sum when it drops below zero is the moment a new prefix minimum appears (@sec-pref-other).
:::
:::

## 7 · Hashing & Counting {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-hash]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**1. What does "expected $O(1)$" mean for a hash lookup, what is the worst case, and who can force it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A lookup costs one hash computation plus a walk along one bucket's chain (or probe sequence), whose expected length is the load factor $n/m$; the table keeps that below a constant by resizing, so the expected cost is $O(1)$ *if the hash codes spread evenly*. The worst case is every key in one bucket: $\Theta(n)$ per operation and $\Theta(n^2)$ for a pass. Anyone who knows your hash function can force it by choosing colliding keys — on Codeforces, multiples of libstdc++'s bucket-count prime. Defences: a seeded custom hash, a balanced tree (`map`), or sorting (@sec-hash-sets, @sec-hash-anti).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**2. In one sentence each: when do you use a frequency array, `unordered_map`, `map`, and a sorted array with binary search?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A frequency array when keys are small non-negative integers (guaranteed $O(1)$, nothing to attack). `unordered_map` for arbitrary hashable keys when you only ask "present? how many? where?". `map` as soon as you need order between keys — the next larger key, the smallest, a range of keys. A sorted array with binary search when the data is built once and never changes, which is compact and guaranteed $O(\log n)$ (@sec-hash-sets).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**3. How do hash tables resolve collisions, and how do Python's `dict` and C++'s `unordered_map` differ?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Two families. **Separate chaining** keeps a list per bucket; libstdc++'s `unordered_map` works this way and grows when the load factor would pass `max_load_factor()` (default $1.0$). **Open addressing** stores keys in the bucket array itself and probes further slots on a collision; CPython's `dict` and `set` work this way and grow at about two-thirds full. Both give expected $O(1)$ and worst case $O(n)$. Python's `dict` also guarantees insertion-order iteration; `unordered_map` guarantees no order (@sec-hash-sets).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**4. You write C++ for a contest with hacks and $n \le 2\cdot10^5$ integer keys. How do you protect the hash map, and what does each part do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Give the map a custom hash: add a seed taken from `chrono::steady_clock` at run time, then mix with `splitmix64`. The mixing makes keys that are multiples of a prime land in unrelated buckets; the seed means the attacker cannot compute the mapping when writing the test. `reserve(n)` is still useful for speed (no rehashing during the fill), but it is not a defence, because the bucket count it picks is predictable. The safe alternatives are `map` (guaranteed $O(\log n)$) or sorting (@sec-hash-anti).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**5. Two Sum in one pass: why must the complement query come *before* the insert? Give an input that breaks the other order.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The invariant is "the map holds only indices strictly before the cursor", which makes $i \ne j$ automatic. Insert-first breaks it for any element that is its own complement: on $[3, 3]$ with $t = 6$, index $0$ stores `3 -> 0`, then queries $6 - 3 = 3$, finds itself, and reports $(0, 0)$. The correct answer is $(0, 1)$ (@sec-hash-complement, @sec-hash-p1-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**6. In C++, what is the difference between `cnt[x]`, `cnt.find(x)` and `cnt.count(x)`? Which one changes the map?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`cnt[x]` returns a reference to the value for `x`, *inserting* `x` with a default value (`0`) if it was absent — so a mere read can grow the map. `cnt.find(x)` returns an iterator to the entry or `cnt.end()`, and `cnt.count(x)` returns $0$ or $1$; neither inserts. In a lookup-heavy loop, write `auto it = cnt.find(want); if (it != cnt.end()) …` and insert only where you mean to (@sec-hash-complement).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**7. A statement asks for pairs $i < j$ with $a_j - a_i = j - i$. Design the key and justify that it counts exactly the wanted pairs.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Move everything with $j$ to one side: $a_j - j = a_i - i$. So the key is $a_i - i$, a pair qualifies exactly when its two keys are equal, and the answer is $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ over the key groups, or `ans += cnt[key]; cnt[key] += 1` in one streaming pass. The keys can be negative, which is fine for a hash map (CF 1520D, @sec-hash-keys, @sec-hash-p2-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**8. How do you count pairs (row $r$, column $c$) of an $n \times n$ grid that are equal as sequences, in Python and in C++?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Python: `Counter(tuple(row) for row in grid)`, then add the count of each column's tuple — $O(n^2)$ expected, since each tuple is built and hashed in $O(n)$. C++: `std::hash` has no specialisation for `vector<int>`, so either write one or use `map<vector<int>, int>`, which works out of the box because vectors compare lexicographically; that costs $O(n)$ per comparison and $O(n^2 \log n)$ in total, which is fine for $n \le 200$ (LC 2352, @sec-hash-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**9. Prove that Boyer–Moore returns the majority when one exists.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each `count -= 1` removes two *different* elements: the incoming one and one standing copy of the candidate. A value $x$ with more than $n/2$ copies loses at most one copy per removal, and each removal also uses up one of the fewer than $n/2$ other elements, so copies of $x$ can never all be removed. At the end, the standing elements are copies of one value, so that value is $x$ (@sec-hash-vote).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**10. When is the verification pass after voting mandatory? Give an input where skipping it gives a wrong answer.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It can be skipped only when the statement promises that a majority exists (LC 169). It is mandatory whenever existence is not promised, and always for the $n/3$ version (LC 229), because the two survivors may include a value below the threshold. Example: $[1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2]$ ends with candidate $3$, which occurs $3$ times out of $7$ — not a majority. Note what verification *cannot* do: it removes impostors but cannot recover a lost winner; with the tests in the right order no winner is ever lost (@sec-hash-vote, @sec-hash-p4-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**11. Longest Consecutive Sequence is $O(n)$ despite a nested `while`. Explain why, and name the two things the argument depends on.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A walk starts only at a value whose predecessor is missing — the bottom of a run — and steps through that run only. Runs are disjoint, so each value is stepped over by exactly one walk, and the walks total at most $n$ steps. The argument depends on (1) $O(1)$ membership, so a *set* rather than a list, and (2) the start test: without it, every value would walk to the top of its run, which is quadratic for one long run (@sec-hash-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**12. Make Sum Divisible by P: why does the *latest* index per remainder give the *shortest* window, and how is "you may not remove the whole array" enforced?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For a window ending at $i$ that needs left prefix remainder $r$, the window length is $i - j$ for the stored index $j$; the latest $j$ minimises it. The whole array corresponds to $j = -1$ (the empty prefix, seeded as `last[0] = -1`) and $i = n - 1$. When the total is not divisible, that window *is* found: at $i = n - 1$ the prefix remainder equals the total's remainder, so the wanted remainder is $0$, which `last[0] = -1` supplies, giving length $n$. The final `best if best < n else -1` rejects it; and when the total is divisible, the function returned $0$ before the scan (@sec-hash-p5-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**13. Why does C++ need `((x % p) + p) % p` while Python does not?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
C++'s `%` truncates toward zero, so the result takes the sign of the dividend: `-7 % 3 == -1`. Python's `%` takes the sign of the divisor, so `-7 % 3 == 1`. A remainder used as a map key or array index must be in $[0, p)$, so in C++ you normalise it; otherwise `-1` and `2`, which are the same class modulo $3$, become different keys and lookups silently miss (@sec-hash-p5-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**14. Contains Duplicate II: hash map, sliding window set, or sorting? Compare them.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The latest-index map is $O(n)$ expected time and stores one entry per distinct value. A window set of the last $k$ values is also $O(n)$ expected time and stores at most $k$ values, which is better when $k$ is small. Sorting (value, index) pairs and checking neighbours with equal values is $O(n \log n)$ guaranteed and immune to hash attacks. In an interview, give the map and mention the other two; on a judge with hacks in C++, prefer the sorted version or a custom hash (@sec-hash-p3-b, @sec-hash-anti).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="7"}
**15. Why can a hash table not answer "the largest key smaller than $x$"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A good hash function deliberately scatters keys, so neighbouring keys land in unrelated buckets; nothing in the table records which keys are close in value. Finding the predecessor would mean scanning every key, $O(n)$. A balanced search tree (`std::map`, `std::set` with `lower_bound`) or a sorted array with binary search answers it in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-hash-sets).
:::
:::

## 8 · Two Pointers {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-tp]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**1. State the invariant of an opposite-ends walk. Which move is legal after "the test failed", and what must you prove before making it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Everything left of $\mathit{lo}$ and right of $\mathit{hi}$ is *decided* — proven unable to appear in any remaining answer; the answer lives between the fingers. After a failed test you may retire exactly *one* end, and only after proving its best chance failed: for pair sums, $a[\mathit{lo}] + a[\mathit{hi}] < t$ means $\mathit{lo}$'s largest partner was $\mathit{hi}$ and it lost, so all of $\mathit{lo}$'s pairs die (@sec-tp-ends). Moving both ends is the classic rejection — one test, two discards, one of them unproven (@sec-tp-inv).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**2. Two Sum II: walk $[1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 11]$ toward target $11$, then answer "why not binary-search the partner of each element instead?"**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 + 11 = 12 > 11$: drop $\mathit{hi}$. $1 + 8 = 9 < 11$: drop $\mathit{lo}$. $3 + 8 = 11$: answer $(1, 4)$, or $[2, 5]$ in 1-based indices. Three glances, $O(n)$ in general. Binary-searching a partner per element is $O(n\log n)$ and also correct; the walk wins because the partner boundary for successive $\mathit{lo}$s only moves *left*, so $\mathit{hi}$ never rewinds and the $n$ searches share one sweep (@sec-tp-p1-a, @sec-tp-count).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**3. Container With Most Water: prove "move the shorter wall". Why is the asymmetry the whole question?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At $(\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ with $h[\mathit{lo}] \le h[\mathit{hi}]$, any future container using $\mathit{lo}$ is narrower and still capped at height $h[\mathit{lo}]$, so its area is below the one just recorded: $\mathit{lo}$ is dominated, retire it. No such argument covers the taller wall — a taller partner inside could raise the height — so retiring it can lose the optimum: on $[1, 100, 2, 100]$, always moving the taller wall reports $3$ instead of $200$ (@sec-tp-p1-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**4. 3Sum: give the three ingredients, the complexity, and the early exits sortedness buys.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort; for each fix $i$, squeeze the suffix for target $-a[i]$; deduplicate (skip equal fixes, skip equal ends after a hit). $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra beyond the sort and the output. Exits: $a[i] > 0$ — break, since three positives cannot sum to $0$; $a[i] + a[i+1] + a[i+2] > 0$ — break, this and every later fix is too big; $a[i] + a[n-2] + a[n-1] < 0$ — only *continue*, since a larger $a[i]$ may still work (@sec-tp-p2-a, @sec-tp-fix).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**5. Why is $k$-SUM solved in $O(n^{k-1})$, and why does 3SUM matter beyond interviews?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix $k - 2$ elements ($O(n^{k-2})$ choices) and squeeze the last two in $O(n)$: $O(n^{k-1})$. For $k = 3$, the conjecture that no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm exists is a standard hardness assumption: since Gajentaan and Overmars (1995), many geometric problems have been shown 3SUM-hard, so a polynomially faster 3SUM would speed all of them up. It plays the role for quadratic problems that the $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparison bound plays for sorting — except that it is unproved (@sec-tp-fix).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**6. Merge Sorted Array: why is writing from the back safe, in one equation? What changes in the code from the front merge?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The write cursor is always $k = p + q + 1$, so while $\mathit{nums2}$ has values ($q \ge 0$), $k > p$: slot $k$ is past every unread $\mathit{nums1}$ value — either free space or a value already moved. A front merge in the same array writes at index $0$, where an unread value sits. The code change: start the three cursors at the ends, compare the *tails*, write the *larger*, and decrement; stop when $\mathit{nums2}$ is empty (@sec-tp-p3-a, @sec-tp-merge).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**7. Squares of a Sorted Array has one input but merges two sorted sequences. Name them and the invariant the two fingers keep.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The negative part, whose squares *decrease* as you move right toward zero, and the non-negative part, whose squares *increase*. Read from the outside in, both give squares in decreasing order, so the largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends. Invariant: the output, filled from the back, holds the largest squares in sorted order, and every unplaced square lies between the two fingers — the larger-tail rule of the back merge (@sec-tp-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**8. Count pairs with sum $\le x$ in a sorted array: give the batching step and the reason the walk is $O(n)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If $a[\mathit{lo}] + a[\mathit{hi}] \le x$, then every pair $(\mathit{lo}, k)$ with $\mathit{lo} < k \le \mathit{hi}$ qualifies (sortedness), so bank $\mathit{hi} - \mathit{lo}$ and retire $\mathit{lo}$; otherwise retire $\mathit{hi}$. Each step moves one finger toward the other and neither moves back, so there are at most $n - 1$ steps; the $\Theta(n^2)$ pairs are counted, not visited (@sec-tp-p5-b, @fig-tp-p5-staircase).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**9. Boats to Save People: state the greedy, sketch the exchange proof, and say which constraint it uses.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort; the heaviest waiting person boards now — with the lightest waiting person if they fit, else alone. If even the lightest does not fit, the heaviest is alone in every plan. If it fits, any optimal plan can be changed by a swap so that the heaviest shares with the lightest without adding a boat (the three cases of exercise 10; the key inequality is $P + Q \le P + H \le \mathit{limit}$). The proof uses that every person weighs at most $\mathit{limit}$, so a solo boat is always legal (@sec-tp-p4-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**10. Number of Pairs / Fair Pairs: give the band identity, and explain why negative values change nothing.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\{l \le \mathit{sum} \le r\} = \{\mathit{sum} \le r\} \setminus \{\mathit{sum} \le l-1\}$, and the second set is inside the first, so the count is the difference of two `count_le` calls. The batching proof reads only "sorted", never "non-negative", so negatives are harmless; what they threaten is bookkeeping — the accumulator reaches $\binom{10^5}{2} \approx 5\cdot10^9$ (64-bit) and $l - 1$ must be computed in a signed type. A one-sweep alternative keeps two boundary fingers that both move left (@sec-tp-p5-b, @sec-tp-p5-c).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**11. Pair of Topics: fuse two arrays into one, and say precisely why sorting them separately is a different problem.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$a_i + a_j > b_i + b_j \iff (a_i - b_i) + (a_j - b_j) > 0$: key each *index* by $d_i = a_i - b_i$, sort $d$, and count pairs with a positive sum. Sorting $a$ and $b$ separately breaks the link between $a_i$ and $b_i$ — the $k$-th smallest $a$ and the $k$-th smallest $b$ usually belong to different topics — so the counted inequality no longer refers to any real pair (@sec-tp-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**12. Runs: give the group-pointer skeleton, its chain tests, and the amortisation sentence. Which two problems in this chapter share the skeleton with a different chain test?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$i$ starts a block, $j$ advances while `chain(a[j], a[j+1])` holds, one settlement per block $[i, j]$, then $i = j + 1$. Chain tests: equality (dedupe, run-length encoding), $\mathit{next} = \mathit{prev} + 1$ (Summary Ranges), same sign (Alternating Subsequence). Sentence: "$j$ never decreases and $i$ jumps past it, so the inner test runs at most $n$ times in total." The pair: @sec-tp-p6-a and @sec-tp-p6-b — and 3Sum's dedup skips are the equality test inside a squeeze (@sec-tp-runs).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**13. When is two pointers the *wrong* tool for a pair problem? Answer in one sentence, with examples.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Two pointers need a predicate whose true set, for each fixed finger, is a prefix or suffix that moves one way; hashing needs only a key and pays memory instead of order. So: unsorted single-pair search with original indices (LC 1 — a hash map), equality or divisibility conditions (pairs with difference $k$, equal remainders — hash grouping, @sec-hash-p2), and "subarray sum exactly $s$" with negative values (a prefix-sum map, @sec-pref-hash) are hashing problems, not squeezes (@sec-tp-why).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="8"}
**14. Trapping Rain Water (LC 42) with two pointers: each step moves one finger and adds water at that column. Justify it — the invariant is not a pair invariant, so what is it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Water above column $c$ is $\min(\text{tallest wall on its left}, \text{tallest on its right}) - h_c$ (counting $c$ itself in both). Keep $\mathit{leftMax}$ = tallest of $h[0..\mathit{lo}]$ and $\mathit{rightMax}$ = tallest of $h[\mathit{hi}..n-1]$. If $\mathit{leftMax} \le \mathit{rightMax}$, then column $\mathit{lo}$'s true right maximum is at least $\mathit{rightMax} \ge \mathit{leftMax}$, so its water is exactly $\mathit{leftMax} - h[\mathit{lo}]$ whatever the unseen middle holds: settle it and advance $\mathit{lo}$. Otherwise settle $\mathit{hi}$ symmetrically. The invariant is one-sided: "the far finger already guarantees a wall at least as tall as the near side's maximum". $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space — the region idea of @sec-tp-inv applied to columns instead of pairs.
:::
:::

## 9 · Sliding Window {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-sw]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**1. State the fixed-size window invariant and the one-line update. Why is it $O(n)$ and not $O(nk)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`cur` always equals the fold over the current length-$k$ window; the update is `cur += a[l+k-1] - a[l-1]` (add the enterer, drop the leaver). Consecutive windows share $k - 1$ cells, so each slide is two operations instead of a re-sum of $k$: $O(1)$ per step for $n - k + 1$ steps, plus $O(k)$ for the first window (@sec-sw-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**2. What is the grow–shrink loop's invariant, and what property of the rule makes `l` a forward-only finger?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After the repair `while`, `a[l..r]` is valid and `l` is the least valid left end for `r`, so the window is the longest valid one ending at `r`. The property is **shrink-safety**: every sub-window of a valid window is valid. It gives two facts — the valid left ends for `r` form a suffix, and the least one never decreases as `r` grows — so `l` never needs to move back. Negatives or equality predicates destroy it (@sec-sw-a2, @sec-sw-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**3. Longest versus shortest window: where does the answer update in each, and why does it move?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Longest: **after** the `while`, because the rule is shrink-safe and the window is valid, and widest, exactly when the repair stops. Shortest: **inside** the `while`, because the rule is grow-safe — the window becomes valid by growing — and you must log each valid window before shrinking past it. The window is valid at a different instant in the two loops (@sec-sw-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**4. Count subarrays with product less than $k$ (positive numbers). Give the loop and the count update, and justify it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Multiply in `a[r]`; `while prod >= k and l <= r: prod //= a[l]; l += 1`; then `count += r - l + 1`. After the shrink `a[l..r]` is the longest window ending at `r` with product $< k$, and positivity makes every shorter window ending at `r` smaller still, so all $r - l + 1$ of them qualify and none starting before `l` does (@sec-sw-p4-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**5. Why can't a single batch count subarrays with exactly $k$ distinct values? What do you compute instead?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For a fixed right end, starting too far left gives more than $k$ distinct values and too far right gives fewer, so the valid starts are a band in the middle, not a suffix, and `r - l + 1` cannot count them. "At most $K$" is shrink-safe, so compute $f(K)$ = number of subarrays with at most $K$ distinct by the batch window, and answer $f(k) - f(k - 1)$ (@sec-sw-a4, @fig-sw-band).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**6. LC 209 (shortest sum $\ge$ target) needs positive entries. Concretely, what fails with a negative number?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The loop only shrinks while the window is valid, assuming that an invalid window cannot become valid by dropping its front. A negative front breaks that: on $[5, -10, 6]$ with target $6$, the window $[5, -10, 6]$ sums to $1$, so the loop never shrinks it and never finds $[6]$; it answers "none" while the truth is $1$. The fix is prefix sums plus a monotone deque (LC 862) (@sec-sw-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**7. LC 1658 (reduce $x$ to $0$): explain the complement inversion and why the answer is $n$ minus the longest middle.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Removing elements from the ends leaves one contiguous middle; the removed ends sum to $x$ exactly when the middle sums to `need = total - x`. Fewest removals means longest middle, so find the longest subarray with sum `need` — a window, because entries are positive — and return $n - \mathit{len}$, or $-1$ if none exists. `need < 0` must be rejected before the loop (@sec-sw-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**8. A window must answer "are all elements distinct?" in $O(1)$ per slide. What state do you keep and how do you update both ends?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A frequency table `freq`: on enter `freq[v] += 1`; on leave `freq[v] -= 1` and **erase** $v$ if its count reaches $0$. All distinct iff `len(freq)` equals the window size — an $O(1)$ read. A `dups` counter (values with count $> 1$) is an alternative that needs no erase (@sec-sw-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**9. When is the sliding window the wrong tool? Give three triggers and the replacement for each.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) Negatives where a sum rule should be shrink-safe → prefix sums + hash map (@sec-pref-hash), or prefix sums + monotone deque for "shortest sum $\ge T$". (2) An exact-equality rule on sums ("sum $= s$" with negatives or zeros) → the prefix map; for exact integer counts of a shrink-safe attribute, the at-most difference (@sec-sw-a4). (3) A window aggregate that cannot be undone — min or max of each window → the monotone deque (LC 239). In one sentence: the window needs a rule whose valid starts form a suffix (or prefix) that moves forward; when that fails, another structure does the job (@sec-sw-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**10. LC 2962 (count where the max appears at least $k$ times): why `ans += n - r` and not `+= r - l + 1`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both batch a count, but on different ends. "Contains at least $k$ maxima" is preserved by **growing** the window, so once `nums[l..r]` is good, every extension to the right is good — $n - r$ right ends for start `l` — and then `l` moves on. `r - l + 1` counts left ends and needs a rule preserved by **shrinking** (LC 713's product $< k$). Choose the batch by which extension keeps validity (@sec-sw-p5-b, @sec-sw-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**11. Contrast "longest window with sum $\le T$" with "maximum subarray sum (any length)". Why is the second not a sliding window?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The first has a budget, which makes validity shrink-safe (for non-negative numbers) and the answer a length. The second has no rule to repair against: with negatives the best subarray is found by Kadane's running maximum of "best sum ending here" (@sec-cx-p1-max-subarray), a one-pass DP, not by chasing a boundary. Windows answer "contiguous under a constraint"; unconstrained best sums are a different tool (@sec-sw-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**12. Give the amortised-$O(n)$ argument for the variable window in two sentences.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`r` advances once per outer iteration, $n$ moves in total, and each pass of the `while` body advances `l` once, never backwards, so it too makes at most $n$ moves over the whole run. All work is $O(1)$ per pointer move, so the total is $O(2n) = O(n)$ even though one `r` may trigger many `l` steps (@sec-sw-a2, @sec-cx-loops).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**13. In Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, why is `left = last[c] + 1` wrong and `left = max(left, last[c] + 1)` right? Give a failing input.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The last copy of `c` may already lie to the left of the window; jumping to it moves `left` backwards and lets an old repeat back in. On `"abba"`, at the final `a`, `last['a'] = 0` and the plain version sets `left = 1`, counting `"bba"` (length 3) as repeat-free; the true answer is 2. The `max` enforces "the left end never moves back", the fact the whole method rests on. `"tmmzuxt"` hides the same bug from random tests unless the generator repeats letters (@sec-test-p2-substring, @sec-sw-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="9"}
**14. How would you test a sliding-window solution before submitting it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write the $O(n^2)$ brute force that checks every subarray, and compare on thousands of random small arrays (@sec-testing). Make the values collide often (a tiny alphabet, values in $1..5$, budgets near the typical sum) so repairs, multi-step repairs and empty windows all happen, and add the edge cases by hand: $n = 1$, nothing valid, everything valid, $k = n$, the largest values for overflow. Every solved problem in this chapter is checked this way.
:::
:::

## 10 · Sorting as a Tool {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-srt]{.cs-link}

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. -->


::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**1. Why does sorting find the closest pair of values in $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort ($O(n\log n)$), then scan adjacent pairs ($O(n)$). For $i<j$, $b[j]-b[i]$ is a sum of adjacent gaps, so the minimum over all pairs equals the minimum over neighbours; no non-adjacent pair can win (@sec-srt-p1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**2. When do you need a comparator instead of a key, and what contract must it satisfy in C++?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When "who goes first" seems to depend on the *pair*, not on a score of each element — e.g. Largest Number's $a{+}b$ against $b{+}a$. In C++ the comparator must be a **strict weak ordering**: irreflexive, transitive, with transitive ties. Use `<`, never `<=`; a `<=` comparator is undefined behaviour and can make `std::sort` read out of bounds. Prefer a key when one exists: comparing numbers is always consistent (@sec-srt-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**3. What does a stable sort buy you, and where does C++ `std::sort` bite?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stability keeps equal-key items in input order, so you can sort by several fields with several passes (least significant first), and ties come out in a deterministic order. Python's sort is guaranteed stable; `std::sort` is not, so use `std::stable_sort` or put every criterion into one comparator (@sec-srt-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**4. How does Maximum Gap (LC 164) find the largest successive difference in $O(n)$ without sorting?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The $n-1$ sorted gaps add up to $\max-\min$, so the largest is at least the average. Use buckets of width $\lfloor(\max-\min)/(n-1)\rfloor$ (at least $1$): two values in one bucket are closer than that, so the answer joins the max of one non-empty bucket to the min of the next. Keep only per-bucket min and max; one scatter pass, one seam pass (@sec-srt-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**5. Values reach $10^9$ and you need an array indexed by value. What is the fix and what does it cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Coordinate compression: `rank = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}`, then index by `rank[x]`. Sparse magnitudes become dense indices $1\dots n$; $O(n\log n)$ for the sort, $O(n)$ space, $O(1)$ per lookup. In C++, `sort` + `unique` + `lower_bound` does the same without a hash map (@sec-srt-a4, @sec-srt-p4-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**6. Why does the median minimise the total distance to a set of points?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Slide the target one step right: it gets closer to every point on the right and farther from every point at or on the left, so the cost changes by (count at or left) $-$ (count right). While most points lie to the right, moving right helps; once at least half lie at or left, it does not. That turn is the median; for even $n$ the whole middle interval ties (@sec-srt-a5, @sec-srt-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**7. In Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal, what changes when each value has its own price per unit, and how do you find the target?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
