Count becomes weight: the slide argument stops where the cumulative weight first reaches half the total, the **weighted median**. Sort the (value, cost) pairs, walk accumulating cost, stop at the first `2*cum >= total`, and sum $c_i|\mathit{nums}_i - t|$ in 64-bit; $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-srt-p5-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**8. When should you sort indices rather than values?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When records live in parallel arrays, when the original positions are part of the answer (write a rank back to position $i$), or when the values must not move. `order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])` is a permutation to read through; `a` and its partner arrays stay untouched. Zipping (value, payload) pairs is the alternative when you do not need the positions (@sec-srt-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**9. How do you choose between a comparison sort, counting sort, buckets and compression?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nothing known about the values: comparison sort, $O(n\log n)$, the safe default. A small fixed value range $V$: counting sort, $O(n+V)$. A huge range but a proof that only bucket extremes matter: buckets, $O(n)$. A huge, sparse range where only relative order matters: compression, then index by rank (@sec-srt-a3, @sec-srt-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**10. Why can't "sort by frequency, ties by value" be done by a comparator that looks only at the two values?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The frequency is not a property of a value's magnitude: it depends on the whole array. You must count first (`Counter`, or a sort and run lengths), then sort with a key that reads that table. It is a derived-key sort; the comparator or key may *use* the table, but the table must be built before sorting (@sec-srt-p4, @sec-lang-p3-frequency).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**11. How do you turn an exchange argument into a sort order, as in Robot Vacuum Cleaner?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Look at two adjacent items and ask what swapping them changes; everything else is unaffected. In Robot Vacuum Cleaner only the crossing pairs change: $s(a)h(b)$ against $s(b)h(a)$. "Put $a$ first when that is larger" is the comparator. Then check it is a strict weak ordering, ideally by showing it compares one number per item (here the ratio $s/h$), and compare by cross-multiplication to stay exact (@sec-srt-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**12. How can sorting replace a hash map, and when would you prefer it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After sorting, equal values are contiguous, so counting, grouping and de-duplicating are one pass over runs, and "is $x$ present" is a binary search. It costs $O(n\log n)$ instead of expected $O(n)$, but it needs no hash function, has no worst case on adversarial inputs (a real concern for `unordered_map` on Codeforces, @sec-lang-p7), and gives the values in order for free (@sec-srt-p4-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="10"}
**13. When is sorting first a waste?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When one pass over the unsorted array answers the question (maximum, sum, a count), when a hash set does the job in expected $O(n)$ and order is never used, when only one order statistic is needed (selection is expected $O(n)$), or when the positions themselves are the answer and sorting would destroy them without an index sort (@sec-srt-a1).
:::
:::

## 11 · Binary Search as a Tool {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-bst]{.cs-link}

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. -->


::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**1. How do you find the first position where a sorted array is $\ge x$ in $O(\log n)$, and what is the loop invariant?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`lo, hi = 0, n; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if a[mid] >= x: hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1; return lo`. Invariant: the first index with $a[i] \ge x$ (or $n$ if none) lies in $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$. Each branch keeps it and shrinks the window, because $\mathit{lo} \le \mathit{mid} < \mathit{hi}$; at `lo == hi` that index is the answer. This is `bisect_left` / `lower_bound` (@sec-bst-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**2. How do you count the elements of a sorted array in a closed value range $[L, R]$ with two calls?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`bisect_right(a, R) - bisect_left(a, L)`. The first term counts the elements $\le R$, the second those $< L$; the difference is the number with $L \le x \le R$. Both calls are $O(\log n)$, and an empty range correctly gives $0$ (@sec-bst-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**3. With $q$ queries on $n$ fixed items, when is sorting and binary searching worth it compared with scanning?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Scanning costs about $qn$; sorting first costs about $n\log n + q\log n$. Sorting wins once $q$ exceeds roughly $\log_2 n$ queries, ignoring constants; for one query, scanning is cheaper. If the data changes between queries, a sorted list costs $O(n)$ per insertion, so use an ordered container such as C++ `std::set`. If all queries are known in advance, you can also sort the queries and sweep (@sec-bst-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**4. Many queries ask how many items, taken in order, fit in a budget, and you may not reorder them. What do you search?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The prefix-sum array, if the values are non-negative: it is non-decreasing, and the answer is `bisect_right(pref, budget)`. If values can be negative, prefix sums are not monotone and the search is wrong. If the question is about a maximum ("every item $\le k$") rather than a sum, search the prefix maxima, which are monotone for any input (@sec-bst-a4, @sec-bst-p3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**5. What is "binary search on the answer", and what two things must you prove before using it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The unknown is a value in a range $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$ with a check "is $v$ good enough?"; you binary search the range of values, running the check at each probe. You must prove the check is **monotone** (if $v$ passes, so does every larger $v$, or every smaller one) and that the range **brackets** the answer (`hi` passes, nothing below `lo` can be the answer). Example: the smallest ship capacity that delivers packages within $D$ days, searched over $[\max w, \sum w]$ with a greedy day count as the check (@sec-bst-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**6. In a "closest to a target" search on the answer, why is the value returned by the search not enough, and what do you compare?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The search returns the first value whose objective reaches the target. The objective jumps over the target between that value and the one just below it, so the closest value is one of these two; every value further left is further below the target and every value further right further above. Compare both distances and, on a tie, return the smaller value (LC 1300's rule) (@sec-bst-p4-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**7. Your binary search sometimes loops forever or returns the wrong index. What are the two standard contracts, and which mixtures break?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Half-open: `while lo < hi`, `hi = mid`, `lo = mid + 1`, answer `lo`. Closed: `while lo <= hi`, `hi = mid - 1`, `lo = mid + 1`, answer `lo` (the first true is $\mathit{hi} + 1$ at the end). Mixing them breaks: `while lo <= hi` with `hi = mid` never terminates once `lo == hi`; `while lo < hi` with `hi = mid - 1` can discard the answer; `lo = mid` with a rounding-down `mid` stalls when `hi = lo + 1` (@sec-bst-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**8. How do you binary search a non-increasing array, for example to find the first index with `b[j] < v`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"`b[j] >= v`" holds on a prefix of a non-increasing array, so the answer is the first index where it fails. Either search a negated copy, `bisect_right([-x for x in b], -v)`, or pass a comparator in C++: `lower_bound(b.begin(), b.end(), v, [](int e, int v) { return e >= v; })`, or `upper_bound(b.begin(), b.end(), v, greater<int>())`. What these functions really require is that the comparator be true on a prefix of the range and false after it (@sec-bst-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**9. Why do C++ binary searches write `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`lo + hi` can exceed the largest `int` (about $2.1 \cdot 10^9$) when the search range is large, for example a search on the answer over $[0, 2 \cdot 10^9]$ or indices of a very large array; signed overflow is undefined behaviour. `hi - lo` never overflows when both are in range, so `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is safe. Joshua Bloch's well-known 2006 note describes exactly this bug in widely used library code. In Python, integers do not overflow (@sec-arr-cost).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**10. Does binary search require a sorted array?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. It requires a predicate that is false…false true…true over an ordered set of candidates. A sorted array supplies one ("$a[i] \ge x$"), but so do prefix maxima of an unsorted array (Scuza), prefix sums of non-negative values, and ranges of answers with a monotone check (ship capacity, Special Array). Conversely, a sorted array with the wrong predicate (one that flips twice) cannot be binary searched (@sec-bst-a1, @sec-bst-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**11. How do you find the largest element $\le x$ in a sorted array, and how do you report that none exists?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`i = bisect_right(a, x)` counts the elements $\le x$; if `i == 0` there is none, otherwise the answer is `a[i - 1]`. In C++: `auto it = upper_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), x);` then `it == a.begin()` means none, else the answer is `*prev(it)`. The smallest element $\ge x$ is the mirror: `a[bisect_left(a, x)]` if that index is $< n$ (@sec-bst-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**12. What is the complexity of `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` on a `std::set`, and what should you call instead?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It performs $O(\log n)$ comparisons, but set iterators are not random-access, so each jump to the middle walks the tree step by step and the total is $O(n)$. Call the member function `s.lower_bound(x)`, which descends the tree in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-lang-p4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**13. Why can no comparison-based search of a sorted array beat about $\log_2 n$ comparisons in the worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A search must distinguish $n + 1$ possible outcomes (the insertion point can be any of $0..n$). Each comparison has two outcomes, so after $t$ comparisons at most $2^t$ cases can be told apart; we need $2^t \ge n + 1$, so $t \ge \lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil$. Binary search meets this bound, so it is optimal among comparison-based methods (the decision-tree argument of @sec-pf-lower-bounds).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="11"}
**14. Is binary search always faster than a linear scan in practice?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not always. For very small arrays a linear scan is often as fast or faster, because it reads memory sequentially and its branches are predictable, while binary search jumps around the array. For a single query on unsorted data, scanning ($O(n)$) beats sorting first ($O(n\log n)$). Binary search wins clearly when $n$ is large and the data is already sorted, or when many queries share one sort (@sec-bst-a3).
:::
:::

## 12 · Sorting Algorithms {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-salgo]{.cs-link}

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. Answers may cite @sec-… -->


::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**1. Name five comparison sorts and give each one's time, extra space and stability.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Insertion: $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(n)$ best, $O(1)$ space, stable. Selection: $\Theta(n^2)$ always, $O(1)$, not stable. Merge sort: $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, $O(n)$, stable. Quicksort: $O(n\log n)$ expected, $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(\log n)$ stack, not stable. Heapsort: $O(n\log n)$ worst, $O(1)$, not stable (@sec-salgo-a9).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**2. Why is quicksort $O(n^2)$ on sorted input with a last-element pivot, and what are the standard fixes?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The last element of a sorted range is its maximum, so every partition splits $n-1 \mid 0$ and the costs add up to $\binom n2$. Fixes: a random pivot (expected $O(n\log n)$ on every input), median-of-three, and introsort's heapsort fallback after a depth limit (a guarantee). Separately, a three-way or Hoare partition fixes the all-equal-keys blow-up (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a7).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**3. What makes merge sort $\Theta(n\log n)$ in the worst case while quicksort is only $O(n\log n)$ on average?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge sort's split is input-independent (always the middle), so its recursion tree always has $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ levels of $O(n)$ work. Quicksort's split depends on the pivot's rank, which can be extreme again and again, giving $n$ levels. Balanced by construction versus balanced by luck (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**4. Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort and heapsort in practice, even though all three are $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its inner loop is a sequential scan that compares with one pivot held in a register and moves few elements; it works in place, so it touches less memory and uses the cache well. Merge sort moves every element at every level and needs a buffer; heapsort jumps between $i$ and $2i+1$, which is cache-unfriendly, and makes about twice as many comparisons. The expected $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons of random-pivot quicksort are a small price for that (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**5. How do you keep quicksort's stack depth $O(\log n)$ even in its worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Recurse into the smaller side and loop (tail-iterate) on the larger side. The smaller side has at most half the elements, so each nested call at least halves the size and the depth is at most $\log_2 n$; time can still be quadratic, but the stack cannot overflow (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**6. State the $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound and its hypothesis. How do counting and radix sort escape it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Any comparison sort makes at least $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil = \Theta(n\log n)$ comparisons in the worst case (and on average): its decision tree needs $n!$ leaves and a binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$. The hypothesis is that the algorithm learns about keys only through pairwise comparisons. Counting and radix sort use key values as array indices, which is not a comparison, so they can run in $O(n + k)$ (@sec-salgo-a6-bound, @sec-lts).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**7. Why is building a heap $O(n)$ and not $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Bottom-up building sifts each node down at most its height, and most nodes are near the bottom: about $n/2$ leaves cost nothing, $n/4$ nodes cost one level, $n/8$ cost two, and so on. The sum $\sum_h \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} h$ is less than $n$. Only repeated pushes (sift-up from the bottom for each new element) cost $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**8. What is a stable sort, why does it matter, and which standard sorts are stable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stability keeps equal-key items in input order. It matters for multi-key sorting by successive passes, for keeping a group in its original order (LC 937's digit-logs), and for predictable output. Python's `sorted` and `list.sort` (Timsort) and C++ `std::stable_sort` are stable; C++ `std::sort` is not. Any sort becomes stable if it sorts `(key, index)` pairs (@sec-salgo-a6-stable, @sec-salgo-p5-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**9. What do `std::sort` and Python's `sorted` actually run?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`std::sort` (in GCC's libstdc++) is introsort: median-of-three quicksort with a recursion depth limit of $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, a heapsort fallback when the limit is hit, and a final insertion sort over blocks of at most 16; worst case $O(n\log n)$, not stable. `sorted` is Timsort: natural runs (strictly descending ones reversed), short runs extended to `minrun` by binary insertion sort, a stack of runs merged with a balance rule, galloping merges; stable, $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted input, $O(n\log n)$ worst case (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**10. How do you count inversions in $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge sort with a counter. Pairs within a half are counted recursively; for the pairs across the halves, when a right-half element is output before the left-half elements still waiting, it forms an inversion with each of them, so add their number. Both halves are sorted, so this is linear per merge. Sort indices instead of values to get per-element counts (@sec-salgo-p2-a, @sec-salgo-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**11. Find the $k$-th largest element without sorting. Give the algorithm, its cost and the alternative for a stream.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Quickselect: partition around a random pivot and continue only into the side that contains index $n - k$; expected $O(n)$, in place, worst case $O(n^2)$ (median of medians or introselect make it linear in the worst case). For a stream, keep a min-heap of the $k$ largest: $O(\log k)$ per element, the root is the answer (@sec-salgo-a4-select, @sec-salgo-p3-a, @sec-salgo-p4-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**12. Why is merge sort, not quicksort or heapsort, the sort for a linked list?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A list has no random access: heapsort's children $2i+1, 2i+2$ cannot be reached cheaply, and quicksort's partition swaps elements at arbitrary positions. Merge sort splits with a slow/fast walk and merges by relinking `next` pointers, with no copying; done bottom-up it needs only $O(1)$ extra memory (@sec-salgo-p1-c).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**13. When do you keep a heap instead of sorting?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When you need the extreme, or the $k$ extremes, repeatedly but never the full order: top-$k$ ($O(n\log k)$ instead of $O(n\log n)$), running medians, priority scheduling, $k$-way merging, and anything streaming. Extracting *all* $n$ elements from a heap is heapsort, $O(n\log n)$, so the win comes only from extracting or keeping far fewer than $n$ (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**14. How would you sort 100 GB of records on a machine with 8 GB of memory?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
External merge sort. Pass 1: read the file in chunks that fit in memory, sort each chunk (any in-memory sort), write it out as a sorted run: about 13 runs. Pass 2: merge all runs at once with a min-heap holding the current head of each run, reading and writing sequentially with large buffers. If there are too many runs for one pass, merge them in groups. Merge sort fits because the merge reads its inputs strictly in order (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**15. Insertion sort is $O(n^2)$. Why do production sorts still use it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its cost is $O(n + \text{inversions})$ with a tiny constant: for blocks of a few dozen elements, or data that is nearly sorted, it beats the $n\log n$ sorts and their overhead. Introsort finishes blocks of at most 16 with one insertion pass, and Timsort extends short runs with binary insertion sort, which needs only $O(\log n)$ comparisons per element (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**16. How does selection sort differ from insertion sort in what it minimises?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Insertion sort minimises work on nearly sorted input: $O(n + \text{inversions})$ comparisons and moves. Selection sort always makes $\binom n2$ comparisons but at most $n - 1$ swaps, so it minimises writes, which matters when moving an element is expensive (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**17. For "count pairs with $a_i > 2a_j$, $i < j$", give the brute force, the faster method and the subtle bug.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Brute force: test all pairs, $O(n^2)$. Faster: merge sort with a separate cross-count pass before each merge; both halves are sorted, so one forward pointer counts the pairs in $O(n)$ per level, $O(n\log n)$ in total. Bug: `2 * a[j]` overflows 32-bit integers for values near $2^{31}$; use 64-bit (@sec-salgo-p2-c).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="12"}
**18. Why does Timsort make only $n - 1$ comparisons on an already sorted list, and does that contradict the lower bound?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Run detection compares each element with its predecessor once; on sorted input that finds a single run of length $n$ with $n - 1$ comparisons, and there is nothing to merge. It does not contradict the lower bound, which is about the *worst* (or average) input: an adaptive sort may be fast on easy inputs as long as some inputs still cost $\Omega(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a8, @sec-salgo-a6-bound).
:::
:::

## 13 · Linear-Time Sorting {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-lts]{.cs-link}

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. Answers may cite @sec-… -->


::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**1. What does the $\Omega(n\log n)$ sorting lower bound assume, and how does counting sort get around it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It assumes the algorithm learns about the order **only by comparing pairs of keys**; then a decision tree with $n!$ leaves has height at least $\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$. Counting sort never compares: it uses each key as an array index, a step with $k$ outcomes, so the argument does not apply. It runs in $O(n + k)$, linear when the key range $k$ is $O(n)$ (@sec-lts-a1-wall).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**2. When is counting sort a bad idea even though it is "linear"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the key range $k$ is much larger than $n$: keys up to $10^9$ need a $10^9$-cell array, worse than $O(n\log n)$ in time and memory. Also when the keys are not integers (or cannot be mapped to small integers). Check the value range in the constraints first; consider clamping, coordinate compression or radix sort (@sec-lts-a1, @sec-lts-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**3. What does "stable" mean, and how does counting sort achieve it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A stable sort keeps records with equal keys in their input order. Counting sort turns counts into end positions with a prefix sum and then places records scanning **backward**, decrementing the position; equal keys fill their block from the right in reverse input order, so they end up in input order. (Equivalently: start positions with a forward scan.) (@sec-lts-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**4. Walk through LSD radix sort and explain why the per-digit sort must be stable.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort by the units digit, then the tens, then the hundreds, each time with a stable counting sort. After $j$ passes the array is sorted by the lowest $j$ digits. When the next pass meets two keys with the same digit, only stability keeps them in the order the lower digits established; an unstable pass could swap them and break the result (@sec-lts-a3-proof).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**5. Counting sort or radix sort for $n$ integers in $[0, n^2)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Radix sort. Counting sort would be $\Theta(n + n^2)$. Each key has two base-$n$ digits, so two stable counting-sort passes with $b = n$ cost $\Theta(2(n + n)) = \Theta(n)$ (@sec-lts-a3-base).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**6. How do you pick the digit size for radix sort?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For $\beta$-bit keys and $r$-bit digits the cost is $\Theta((\beta/r)(n + 2^r))$. Choosing $2^r \approx n$ balances the two terms and gives $\Theta(\beta n/\log n)$. For a million 32-bit keys that is $r = 16$ (two passes); in practice 8-bit digits are common because the 256-entry count array is cache friendly (@sec-lts-a3-base).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**7. How does radix sort handle negative integers?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Either add $-\min$ to every key and subtract it afterwards, or (for fixed-width integers) flip the sign bit, which maps the signed range onto the unsigned range in the same order; sort as unsigned, then flip back. Plain digit extraction on negatives gives the wrong order (@sec-lts-a3-neg).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**8. LSD or MSD radix sort for strings?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
LSD for fixed-length strings (IDs, codes, equal-length keys): simple, stable, $\Theta(w(n + R))$. MSD for variable-length strings: it recurses into groups sharing a prefix, needs an "ended" bucket below every character, and reads only the distinguishing prefixes; it needs a cutoff to insertion sort because each call pays for an $R$-entry count array (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**9. Give the expected-time argument for bucket sort and an input that defeats it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $n$ uniform keys in $n$ buckets, each bucket size $n_i$ is binomial with $p = 1/n$, so $\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$. Insertion sort on bucket $i$ costs $O(n_i^2)$, so the expected total is $\Theta(n) + n \cdot O(1) = \Theta(n)$. If all keys fall into one bucket (say all in $[0, 1/n)$), the insertion sort there costs $\Theta(n^2)$ (@sec-lts-a4-proof).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**10. Find all missing numbers in an array with $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le n$, in $O(1)$ extra space.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sign marking: for each value $x$, negate slot `abs(x) - 1` if it is positive; afterwards every still-positive slot $i$ means value $i + 1$ never appeared. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space. Use `abs` because a slot may already have been negated when you read it (@sec-lts-a5, @sec-lts-p2-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**11. "First missing positive" in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The answer is in $[1, n+1]$, so only values in $[1, n]$ matter. Cyclic placement: while `a[i]` is in range and its home slot does not already hold it, swap it home. Then the first $i$ with `a[i] != i + 1` gives $i + 1$, else $n + 1$. At most $n$ swaps in total (@sec-lts-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**12. Top $k$ frequent elements in linear time?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Count with a hash map, then bucket the values by frequency (`buckets[f]`, $f \in [1, n]$) and scan from $f = n$ down, stopping after $k$ values. $O(n)$ time and space. A size-$k$ heap gives $O(n + A\log k)$, quickselect expected $O(n + A)$ (@sec-lts-p3-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**13. "Two indices within $k$ whose values are within $t$": a linear-time solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Buckets of width $t + 1$ keyed by $\lfloor x/(t+1) \rfloor$, holding only the last $k$ elements. A value already in the same bucket is a match; a value in a neighbouring bucket is a match if within $t$; otherwise insert and evict the element that left the window. $O(n)$ expected time, $O(k)$ space. Use a real floor for negative values (@sec-lts-p5-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**14. For each, choose counting, radix, bucket or comparison sort: (a) $10^7$ ages in $[0, 120]$; (b) $10^6$ floats uniform in $[0, 1)$; (c) $10^6$ arbitrary 64-bit integers; (d) dates as (year, month, day).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Counting sort: $k = 121$, $O(n)$. (b) Bucket sort: expected $O(n)$. (c) Either a comparison sort or LSD radix with 8- or 16-bit digits; radix is linear but with 4 to 8 passes over the data, and a good library sort is often competitive, so measure. (d) LSD radix: stable counting sort by day ($k = 31$), then month ($k = 12$), then year (offset by the earliest year) (@sec-lts-a3, @sec-lts-a4, @sec-lts-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**15. Is counting sort in place? Can it be made in place?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The stable version is not: it writes into a separate output array of size $n$, plus the $k$-cell count array. An in-place version exists (the "American flag sort" style of cycling each element to its bucket's next free slot), but it is not stable, so it cannot serve as the inner sort of LSD radix. When the keys are bare numbers, the histogram form can overwrite the input in place from the counts, using only the $O(k)$ count array (@sec-lts-a1, @sec-lts-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="13"}
**16. Why do standard libraries use comparison sorts if radix sort is linear?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A library sort must work for any type with a comparator, where radix sort does not apply. Radix sort also needs $O(n + b)$ extra memory, several passes over the data, and per-type digit extraction (signs, floats, strings), and its advantage appears mainly for large arrays of short fixed-width keys. A comparison sort like introsort or Timsort is general, in place or nearly so, and adaptive to presorted input (@sec-lts-a6).
:::
:::

## 14 · Intervals & Sweep Line {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-int]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**1. Given $n$ intervals on $[0, 10^9]$, how do you answer $q$ queries "how many intervals contain point $t$?" in $O((n + q)\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort the starts into $S$ and the ends into $E$. For closed intervals, the count is the number of starts $\le t$ minus the number of ends $< t$: `bisect_right(S, t) - bisect_left(E, t)`. For half-open $[a, b)$, subtract the ends $\le t$: `bisect_right(S, t) - bisect_right(E, t)`. Preprocessing $O(n\log n)$, each query $O(\log n)$. If the queries are known in advance, sorting them and sweeping once also works (@sec-int-events, @sec-bst-p1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**2. How do you merge $k$ lists of intervals, each already sorted and merged, into one merged list?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $N$ intervals in total, either concatenate, sort by start and run the merge walk ($O(N\log N)$), or do a $k$-way merge with a min-heap keyed by the next start of each list, feeding intervals into the same running-block walk in start order ($O(N\log k)$). Overlaps inside one list are already resolved, but overlaps across lists are not, so the walk is still needed (@sec-int-merge).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**3. Given half-open intervals, how do you check in $O(n\log n)$ whether they cover $[L, R)$ completely?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort by start and keep `reach = L`. For each interval, if its start is greater than `reach` there is a gap at $[\text{reach}, \text{start})$ and the answer is no (as long as `reach < R`); otherwise set `reach = max(reach, end)`. Answer yes once `reach >= R`. The invariant: $[L, \text{reach})$ is covered by the intervals processed so far (@sec-int-merge, @sec-int-p5-c).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**4. Why is "sort by end, take what fits" optimal for the number of non-overlapping intervals, and why does it fail when intervals have weights?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unweighted: by induction, the greedy's $i$-th interval ends no later than the $i$-th interval of any valid set, so the greedy is never behind and cannot stop early. Weighted: $[0,2)$ worth $1$ ends first and blocks $[1,10)$ worth $100$. The weighted problem is DP over intervals sorted by end, with `bisect` to find the last compatible interval (@sec-int-sched, @sec-int-circle).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**5. Two merged lists $A$ and $B$. How do you compute their union in $O(|A| + |B|)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge the two lists by start with two pointers, as in merging sorted arrays, and feed each interval into the running-block walk of @sec-int-merge. Each list is sorted, so the combined stream is in start order without a sort. The intersection walk of @sec-int-p5-a is the same two pointers with a different action.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**6. In Car Pooling, why must a drop-off be processed before a pick-up at the same kilometre?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The statement says so: passengers are dropped off before new passengers are picked up at the same location, which is the half-open reading $[\text{from}, \text{to})$. If pick-ups came first, the load would briefly include passengers who have already left, and touching trips such as $[3,1,5],[4,5,9]$ with capacity $4$ would be wrongly rejected. Sorting `(position, delta)` pairs does it automatically, since negative deltas sort first (@sec-int-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**7. Design a structure that supports `add_interval(a, b)` and `max_overlap()`, each in $O(\log n)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Store the $+1$ and $-1$ events in a balanced search tree keyed by coordinate (or a segment tree over compressed coordinates if they are known in advance). Each node keeps the sum of its subtree's deltas and the maximum prefix sum inside the subtree; a parent combines its children as `sum = L.sum + R.sum` and `maxpre = max(L.maxpre, L.sum + R.maxpre)`. An insertion adds two events and updates two root paths; `max_overlap` is the root's `maxpre`. With range-add updates instead of point events, a segment tree with lazy propagation does the same (later volumes); @sec-int-p2 is the offline version.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**8. Merging sorts by start, packing sorts by end. Why the difference?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merging must *see* every interval that touches the current block before the block is closed, and sorting by start guarantees that everything still to come starts later, so a block that is passed is final. Packing must *decide* which intervals to keep, and the right decision depends on when the resource is released, which is the end. Packing by start lets a long early interval block many short ones; merging by end would close a block before a long interval that starts earlier arrives (@sec-int-merge, @sec-int-sched).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**9. How do you compute the minimum number of meeting rooms, and why are the two standard methods equivalent?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Method 1: the peak overlap from the event sweep. Method 2: sort by start and keep a min-heap of room end times; reuse the room at the top if it is free by the next start, otherwise open a room; the answer is the heap size. They agree because rooms needed $\ge$ peak (the meetings at the peak moment need different rooms) and the heap never opens a room unless all rooms are busy at that start, which is a moment with as many overlapping meetings as rooms (@sec-int-events).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**10. Your merge works for closed intervals. What changes for half-open intervals, and how do you test it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Decide first whether touching half-open intervals ($[1,3)$ and $[3,5)$) should merge. As *sets* they are disjoint, so a strict merge uses `start < out[-1].end`; but if the goal is maximal *contiguous* stretches (busy periods), they should merge, and the test stays `<=`. State the choice, and put a touching pair in the tests together with a nested interval and a duplicate (@sec-int-repr).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**11. Intervals arrive one by one as a stream (for example, LC 352 adds single numbers). How do you keep the merged list up to date?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep the disjoint blocks in a sorted map keyed by start. For a new interval, find the block just before its start (floor lookup) and the blocks that start inside it; absorb them all into one block, delete the absorbed keys and insert the merged one. Each insertion is $O(\log n)$ plus $O(\log n)$ per absorbed block, and each block is absorbed at most once, so the total is $O(n\log n)$ amortised. Python's standard library has no sorted map; `bisect` on a list gives the same lookups with $O(n)$ shifts (@sec-int-p1-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**12. You sort intervals in C++ with the comparator `return a[0] <= b[0];`. What can go wrong?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`std::sort` requires a strict weak ordering, and `<=` is not irreflexive (an element compares less than itself), so the behaviour is undefined: in practice wrong orders, or reads past the end of the array on some inputs. Use `<`, or for several keys compare the first key and fall back to the second, as in `a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] < b[0] : a[1] > b[1]` (@sec-srt-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="14"}
**13. Can the maximum overlap of $n$ intervals be computed faster than $O(n\log n)$ in the comparison model?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not in general. Deciding whether some two numbers among $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are equal (element distinctness) needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons in the algebraic decision-tree model, and it reduces to the overlap question: the closed point-intervals $[x_i, x_i]$ have peak overlap $\ge 2$ exactly when two numbers are equal. With small integer coordinates the difference array beats the bound, because it uses the values as addresses, not comparisons (@sec-pref-diff).
:::
:::

## 15 · Partitioning & In-Place Rearrangement {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-part]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**1. Sort an array of $0$s, $1$s and $2$s in one pass with $O(1)$ extra memory. What is the invariant, and why does the cursor `mid` not move after a swap with `hi`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Dutch national flag (@sec-part-dnf): regions $[0..\text{lo})$ all $0$, $[\text{lo}..\text{mid})$ all $1$, $[\text{mid}..\text{hi}]$ unknown, $(\text{hi}..n)$ all $2$. Each step shrinks the unknown region by one, so $n$ steps. After `swap(a[mid], a[hi])` the value at `mid` came from the unknown region and has not been classified, so `mid` must look at it again.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**2. Lomuto or Hoare? Name one input where the choice matters.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Hoare does about a third of Lomuto's swaps and splits an all-equal array in the middle, because both fingers stop on keys equal to the pivot; Lomuto sends all equal keys to one side, so quicksort with Lomuto is $\Theta(n^2)$ on all-equal input (@sec-part-a1-compare). Lomuto is simpler and leaves the pivot at its final index, which quickselect likes. With many duplicates, use the three-way partition.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**3. Can you partition stably in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not with the simple walks: Lomuto, Hoare and the Dutch flag all lose the order inside groups. The practical options are an $O(n)$ buffer (append each element to its group) or divide and conquer with rotations, $O(n\log n)$ time in place (@sec-part-stable-rot). Linear-time constant-space stable partitioning exists in the research literature but is far too intricate to write in an interview; naming the trade-off is the expected answer.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**4. Rearrange an array with equal numbers of positives and negatives so that signs alternate, keeping the order inside each sign. What is the simplest $O(n)$ solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One read pass with two write cursors: a positive goes to `res[pw]`, `pw += 2`, starting at $0$; a negative to `res[nw]`, `nw += 2`, starting at $1$ (@sec-part-p2-a). Each class's slots receive its elements in input order, so it is stable. An in-place swap partition would lose that order.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**5. In Sort Array by Parity II, why does one cursor running off the end mean nothing is left to fix?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The array has as many even values as even slots, so the number of even slots holding an odd value equals the number of odd slots holding an even value. Each swap removes one of each, so the two counts stay equal; when one cursor finds no more misplaced cells, the other has none either (@sec-part-p2-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**6. Find the next permutation in place. Why is reversing the suffix enough, and what goes wrong with duplicates?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pivot: rightmost $i$ with $a_i < a_{i+1}$; successor: rightmost $j > i$ with $a_j > a_i$; swap; reverse $a[i+1..n)$ (@sec-part-perm). The suffix is non-increasing before the swap, and the value placed at $j$ is below its left neighbour and at least its right neighbour, so it stays non-increasing and the reversal sorts it. With duplicates both scans must be non-strict; otherwise $[1, 5, 1]$ swaps two equal values and the result is smaller than the input.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**7. Given an integer, find the smallest larger integer with the same digits. What are the traps?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Next permutation on the digit string, $O(d)$ for $d$ digits (@sec-part-p3-b). The traps: no pivot means "no answer" (no wrap-around), and the result can overflow 32 bits (parse into 64 bits, then compare with $2^{31} - 1$). Leading zeros cannot appear, because the result is larger and has as many digits.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**8. How do you get the $k$-th permutation of $1..n$ without stepping $k$ times?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unrank with factorials (@eq-rank): the first value is the $\lfloor k / (n-1)! \rfloor$-th smallest unused one, then continue with $k \bmod (n-1)!$. $O(n^2)$ with a list, $O(n\log n)$ with a Fenwick tree over the unused values (@sec-part-rank).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**9. Wiggle Sort II: why does "sort and interleave" sometimes fail, and how do you fix it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Interleaving the sorted halves in increasing order puts copies of the middle value side by side in the middle of the array: $[1, 2, 2, 3] \to [1, 2, 2, 3]$. Dealing both halves in decreasing order sends those copies to opposite ends, and they can then meet only if the value occurs more than $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ times, in which case no answer exists (@sec-part-p4-a). For $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space: quickselect the median and run a three-way partition through the virtual index $(1 + 2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**10. Why is the virtual-index modulus $n \mid 1$ rather than $n$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$t \mapsto 1 + 2t$ must hit every cell once, which needs an odd modulus ($\gcd(2, w) = 1$). For even $n$, the modulus $n$ would visit only odd cells, each twice. $n \mid 1$ is $n + 1$ for even $n$ and $n$ for odd $n$; with $n + 1$, the one extra residue, $n$, is never reached for $t < n$ (@sec-part-virtual).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**11. Compare the three ways to rotate in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Which do you write in an interview?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three reversals: about $2n$ writes, sequential, almost impossible to get wrong; the default. Juggling: exactly $n$ writes, but jumps by $k$ and needs the $\gcd(n, k)$ cycle count. Block swap: $2(n - \gcd(n, k))$ writes in sequential runs, Euclid-shaped (@sec-part-rotate-costs). Write the reversals; mention juggling if the interviewer asks for the fewest writes.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**12. A split by threshold $x$ (all values $< x$ first, both sides keeping their order) is the only operation allowed. How many are needed to sort a permutation?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number of values $v$ with $\text{pos}[v+1] < \text{pos}[v]$. A split changes the relative order of $v$ and $v+1$ only when $x = v + 1$, so each backwards pair needs its own split, and splitting at each of them once sorts the array (@sec-part-p1-b). $O(n)$ with the inverse permutation.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**13. You may cyclically shift either of two permutations. Why is it enough to try rotations of one of them, and how do you avoid trying all $n$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Shifting $a$ by $s_1$ and $b$ by $s_2$ aligns the same pairs as shifting only $b$ by $s_2 - s_1$, so only the relative offset matters. Each value $v$ matches under exactly one offset, $(\text{pos}_a(v) - \text{pos}_b(v)) \bmod n$; count the votes and take the maximum, $O(n)$ (@sec-part-p5-b).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="15"}
**14. Make a stable partition with no buffer. What does rotation have to do with it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Divide and conquer: partition both halves stably, giving $T_1 F_1 T_2 F_2$, then rotate the middle $F_1 T_2$ into $T_2 F_1$. Rotations move blocks without changing the order inside them, so the result is stable; the total is $O(n\log n)$ time (@sec-part-stable-rot). This is what `std::stable_partition` does when it cannot allocate memory.
:::
:::

## 16 · Index Tricks: Cyclic Sort, Marking & Permutation Cycles {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-idx]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**1. Why is cyclic sort $O(n)$ when it has a `while` loop that does not always advance?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Count events, not loop shapes. Each iteration either advances the cursor (at most $n$ times) or swaps, and every swap writes a value into its home slot, after which that slot is never swapped again. So there are at most $n$ swaps and at most $2n$ iterations in total (@sec-idx-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**2. When would you use cyclic sort rather than a hash set or a counting array on $1..n$ data?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When $O(1)$ extra space is required and the array may be rearranged. A counting array is simpler when $O(n)$ memory is fine; a hash set when values are not in a small known range; marking (@sec-idx-a3) when the input order must survive; arithmetic (@sec-idx-a5) when the array is read-only.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**3. Find all duplicates in an array of $n$ values from $1..n$ in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. What precondition does your method need, and how do you undo the damage?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Negation marking: for each $x$, look at cell $|x| - 1$; if it is negative, $|x|$ is a duplicate, else negate it. It needs values in $1..n$ and all positive (zero has no sign to flip). Read every value through `abs`, and restore with a final `abs` pass. Cyclic sort also works and reports the values left in misfit slots, but it rearranges the array (@sec-idx-p1-dups).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**4. State and prove the minimum number of swaps to sort a permutation.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$n - c$, with $c$ the number of cycles including fixed points. A swap rewires two arrows, so it splits one cycle or merges two: $c$ changes by exactly one. Sorted means $n$ cycles, so at least $n - c$ swaps; cyclic sort uses $L - 1$ swaps per cycle of length $L$, which is $n - c$ in total (@sec-idx-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**5. What is the minimum number of *adjacent* swaps to sort a permutation, and why is it different?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number of inversions. An adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly one, and while the array is unsorted some adjacent pair is inverted, so swapping it reduces the count by one (bubble sort). Arbitrary swaps can fix far-apart elements at once, which is why $n - c$ can be much smaller. Both counts have the same parity (@sec-idx-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**6. Given a permutation and $K$ up to $10^{18}$, output the permutation applied $K$ times.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Decompose into cycles once, $O(n)$. On a cycle $c_0 \ldots c_{L-1}$, the element at offset $t$ goes to offset $(t + K) \bmod L$. Each position costs $O(1)$, so $O(n)$ in total, with no dependence on $K$. Repeated squaring of the permutation would cost $O(n \log K)$; simulation is hopeless (@sec-idx-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**7. When does a permutation first return to the identity under repeated application, and why can the answer be huge?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At the lcm of its cycle lengths: each cycle of length $L$ is home exactly at multiples of $L$. Cycle lengths can be pairwise coprime ($2 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 11 = 28$ elements give order $2310$), so the order grows much faster than $n$; compute it with 64-bit lcm, never by simulation (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5-shift).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**8. One number is missing and one is doubled in $1..n$. Compare sum, XOR and marking when the array is read-only and $n$ is large.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read-only rules out marking. A single sum gives $m - d$ and a single XOR gives $m \oplus d$: one equation each, two unknowns. Add the sum of squares ($m^2 - d^2$, so $m + d = S_2 / S_1$), watching for overflow of $\sum a_i^2$; or split the XOR by a set bit of $m \oplus d$, which never overflows, and use one more pass to tell $m$ from $d$ (@sec-idx-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**9. Define the MEX. How do you compute the MEX of $n$ integers in $O(n)$, and why is it at most $n$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The smallest non-negative integer not present. Among the $n + 1$ candidates $0..n$, at most $n$ can be present, so some value $\le n$ is missing. Mark the values in $0..n$ in a boolean table (ignore larger ones) and scan for the first unmarked entry; with a writable array of non-negative values, the marking can be done in place (@sec-idx-a3, @sec-idx-p2-mex).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**10. Find a duplicate among $n + 1$ integers from $1..n$ without modifying the array and in $O(1)$ extra space.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read the array as the function $i \mapsto a_i$ on indices $0..n$. There are $n + 1$ indices and only $n$ values, so some value has two preimages (pigeonhole), and the walk from index $0$ ends in a cycle whose entry point is that value. Floyd's tortoise and hare finds the entry in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Solved in @sec-gr-p5-duplicate.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**11. What exactly does add-$n$ marking store, and why can you recover both the count and the original value?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After shifting to $0..n-1$, cell $j$ ends as $\text{orig}_j + n \cdot \text{count}_j$ with $0 \le \text{orig}_j < n$. Division by $n$ with remainder is unique, so `a[j] // n` is the count and `a[j] % n` is the original. During the pass, every index must be computed as `a[i] % n`, because the cell being read may already carry counts (@sec-idx-a3, @eq-arr-encode).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**12. How do you apply a permutation to an array in place?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Follow each cycle once, carrying one value: pick up $a_s$, drop it at $p_s$ while picking up what was there, and continue until you are back at $s$. To skip finished cycles without a visited array, mark $p_j$ when visiting $j$ (by complementing it, which works even for the value $0$) and restore $p$ at the end. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra (@sec-idx-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**13. Can every permutation be sorted with exactly $m$ swaps for any large $m$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: only for $m \ge n - c$ with $m \equiv n - c \pmod 2$ (and $n \ge 2$). Each swap changes the number of cycles by exactly one, so the parity of the swap count is fixed by the permutation. Extra swaps can only be wasted in pairs (@sec-idx-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**14. Your function marks the input in place and restores it before returning. Is it really "read-only"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only from the caller's sequential view. During the call the array is visibly modified, so another thread or an alias holding a reference sees negative values; and an exception mid-pass leaves it corrupted. Say so in an interview: in-place marking trades memory for atomicity, and a truly read-only input calls for the arithmetic of @sec-idx-a5 or Floyd's walk (@sec-idx-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**15. For CF 864D, why is the number of changes fixed before you decide which copies to overwrite?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each value that occurs $c > 1$ times has $c - 1$ spare copies, and each missing value is one gap. Both totals equal $n$ minus the number of distinct values, so $q = $ number of gaps is forced by the frequency table alone. What depends on the order is *which* copies to overwrite, and that only decides the lexicographic order of the result (@sec-idx-p1-makeperm).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="16"}
**16. Why is the inverse of a permutation a scatter and composition a gather?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Composition $r_i = p[q_i]$ *reads* from the position named by the data, which is a gather. The inverse needs, for each value $v$, the position holding it; knowing only $p$, the natural loop visits each position $i$ and *writes* $i$ to the position $p_i$, which is a scatter. Writing the inverse as a gather would need a search per value, $O(n^2)$ (@sec-idx-a6, @sec-idx-p5-presents).
:::
:::

## 17 · Matrices & 2D Arrays {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-mat]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**1. What is row-major flattening, and why is `for i: for j:` faster than `for j: for i:` on the same grid?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Row-major stores row 0, then row 1, …, so $(i,j)$ is at $i\cdot C + j$. With `j` in the inner loop consecutive reads are adjacent in memory and one cache line serves several of them; with `i` inner each read jumps $C$ cells and usually needs a new line. Same $\Theta(RC)$ operations, very different constants (@sec-mat-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**2. What is the difference between a transpose and a $90^\circ$ rotation, and which shapes allow each in place?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Transpose: $A[i][j] = M[j][i]$, a reflection across the main diagonal. Clockwise rotation: $\text{rot}[i][j] = M[n-1-j][i]$, a transpose followed by reversing each row. On a square both are done in place with swaps and reversals. On a rectangle both change the shape to $C\times R$; use a new grid, or the cycle-following transpose of a flat buffer (@sec-mat-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**3. Write the shrinking-wall spiral. Which two checks stop a leftover row or column from being emitted twice?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After the top row (`top += 1`) and the right column (`right -= 1`), re-test `top <= bottom` before the bottom row and `left <= right` before the left column. These make $1\times n$, $n\times 1$ and centre cells work without special cases (@sec-mat-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**4. How do you group cells by diagonal and by anti-diagonal, and how many groups are there?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Key by $i - j$ for diagonals (top-left to bottom-right) and by $i + j$ for anti-diagonals. Each key takes $R + C - 1$ values. One $O(RC)$ pass fills the buckets; or loop over the key and compute each line's row range directly (@sec-mat-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**5. Set every row and column containing a zero to zero with $O(1)$ extra space. Why does the corner need special care?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Use row 0 as column flags and column 0 as row flags. `M[0][0]` would have to mean both "row 0 has a zero" and "column 0 has a zero", so save two booleans before marking, mark and wipe the interior, then wipe row 0 and column 0 last. (One boolean also works if you wipe bottom-up, @sec-mat-a4.)
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**6. Reduce "maximum-sum sub-rectangle" to 1-D. What is fixed, what is collapsed, and what does it cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix the top and bottom rows; collapse the band into column sums `col[j]`, grown one row at a time; run Kadane on `col`. $O(R^2)$ bands times $O(C)$ is $O(R^2C)$ time, $O(C)$ space; fix pairs along the shorter side (@sec-mat-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**7. Rotate an $n\times n$ matrix clockwise in place without the transpose. What is the basic move?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A four-cycle: $(i,j) \to (j,n-1-i) \to (n-1-i,n-1-j) \to (n-1-j,i) \to (i,j)$. For each ring $i < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and each $j$ from $i$ to $n-2-i$, move those four values one step with one temporary. Each cell is written once; the odd centre never moves (@eq-mat-orbit).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**8. Sum both diagonals of an $n\times n$ matrix in one pass. What is the trap?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Add `M[i][i] + M[i][n-1-i]` for each row $i$. When $n$ is odd the centre is on both diagonals ($i = n-1-i$ at $i = (n-1)/2$) and is added twice; subtract it once, or skip the second term when $n-1-i = i$. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space (@sec-mat-p5-diagsum).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**9. A matrix is sorted non-increasingly along every row and every column. Count its negative numbers faster than $O(RC)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Staircase walk from the top-right corner. At $(i,j)$: if $M[i][j] < 0$, every cell below it in column $j$ is also negative, so add $R - i$ and move left; otherwise move down. Each step leaves a row or a column for good, so $O(R + C)$ time and $O(1)$ space. It uses the sortedness that a plain traversal ignores (LeetCode 1351).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**10. Rotate only the border of a matrix by one position clockwise. Which tools combine?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read the outer ring into a list with the first lap of the spiral (@sec-mat-a2), rotate that list by one (move the last element to the front), and write it back along the same coordinates. Rotating every ring by $k$ (LeetCode 1914) is the same per ring, with $k$ reduced modulo the ring size.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**11. You must transpose an $R\times C$ matrix but may use only $O(1)$ extra memory. Possible? At what cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: on a flat buffer the transpose is the permutation $p \mapsto pR \bmod (RC-1)$, and you rotate each of its cycles in place, starting each cycle only from its smallest index so no visited array is needed. The code is harder than the square's swaps and can take more than linear time to find cycle leaders; it pays off only when memory truly cannot grow (exercise 13).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**12. How does the fix-two-rows reduction change for "count sub-matrices with sum = target" and for "largest sum $\le k$"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The band loop is unchanged; only the 1-D kernel changes. Counting: prefix sums with a hash map, adding `cnt[S - target]` per column ($O(R^2C)$, @sec-mat-p4-submatrix). Bounded maximum: prefix sums in a sorted set, looking up the smallest earlier prefix $\ge S - k$ ($O(R^2C\log C)$, @sec-mat-p4-nolarger).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**13. How do you find the $k$-th element of a spiral without building the whole order?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Subtract ring sizes ($2h + 2w - 4$, or $h$ or $w$ for a one-thick ring) until $k$ falls inside ring $t$, then decide by arithmetic which side of that ring holds it. $O(\min(R,C))$ per query (exercise 16).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**14. Design an iterator that flattens a 2-D vector, with `next()` and `hasNext()`. What state do you keep?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A row index $r$ and a column index $c$. Keep the invariant "if any element remains, $(r, c)$ points at it": after each `next()` advance $c$, and while $c$ is past the end of row $r$ move to the next row and reset $c = 0$ (this also skips empty rows). `hasNext()` is then $r <$ number of rows. Nothing is copied (LeetCode 251, a premium problem).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**15. Why can't a mutilated chessboard (two opposite corners removed) be tiled with dominoes? What general tool does the proof use?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Opposite corners have the same colour in the checkerboard colouring $(i+j) \bmod 2$, so the board has $30$ cells of one colour and $32$ of the other, while every domino covers one cell of each. The tool is an **invariant**: find a quantity every piece or move preserves, and compare it with the target (@sec-mat-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="17"}
**16. Many problems ask for the largest Manhattan distance between points. What transformation makes it easy?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rotate the coordinates: $u = x + y$, $v = x - y$. Then $|\Delta x| + |\Delta y| = \max(|\Delta u|, |\Delta v|)$, so the largest distance is $\max(u_{\max} - u_{\min},\, v_{\max} - v_{\min})$, two linear scans (@eq-mat-uv).
:::
:::

## 18 · Designing Array-Based Data Structures {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-ds]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**1. Design a set with `insert`, `remove` and `getRandom`, all $O(1)$. Why does neither a plain hash set nor a plain list do it, and what does the `value -> index` map buy?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A list gives $O(1)$ sampling and append but $O(n)$ removal from the middle (the shift of @sec-arr-vec) and $O(n)$ membership. A hash set gives $O(1)$ insert and remove but no index to sample uniformly from. Combine them: a *packed* array (so `a[randrange(len(a))]` is uniform) plus `pos` (so "find the doomed slot" is a lookup); removal is one copy from the tail, one map repair and one pop (@sec-ds-a1, @sec-ds-p1-randset). State the invariant: the live elements are exactly `a[0..n-1]`, and `pos` records each one's slot.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**2. Now duplicates are allowed. What changes in the map, and what does "remove any occurrence" let you keep?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`pos` becomes `value -> set of slots`; `insert` adds the new last slot, `remove` takes an arbitrary member of the set, moves the tail into it, re-points the tail value's set, and deletes the key when the set empties. Because the array stays dense, sampling probabilities are automatically the multiplicities. "Any occurrence" is the licence that keeps it $O(1)$; "remove the oldest copy" would need an ordered structure per value (@sec-ds-p1-randcol).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**3. How would you add `deleteRandom()` in $O(1)$ to the same structure?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`i = randrange(len(a)); v = a[i]; remove(v)`. Do not `del a[i]`: that is the $O(n)$ shift and it breaks `pos` for the whole tail. Reusing `remove` costs nothing extra, and every element is deleted with probability $1/n$ (@sec-ds-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**4. Snapshot array: what are three designs, and what does each cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(i) Copy on every `snap()`: $O(n)$ per snapshot and $O(ns)$ memory, up to $2.5\cdot10^9$ integers at LC 1146's limits. (ii) Per-cell `(version, value)` lists with a linear walk: $O(1)$ `snap` and `set`, $O(k_i)$ `get`, $O(n + w)$ memory. (iii) The same lists with `bisect_right`: $O(\log k_i)$ `get`. Two details decide correctness: `snap()` returns the version before the increment, and a second write under the same version overwrites rather than appends (@sec-ds-a2, @sec-ds-p2-snapshot).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**5. Browser history: one array and a cursor, or two stacks? Why does `visit` destroy the forward branch?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The array version makes `back`/`forward` $O(1)$ clamps, `max(0, i - k)` and `min(end - 1, i + k)`, and `visit` writes at `i + 1` and moves the end marker. Two stacks avoid index arithmetic but move one page per step, $O(\text{steps})$. `visit` discards the forward pages because the history is one line: a new page cannot coexist with the future you abandoned. Keeping branches turns the line into a tree with a parent pointer per page (@sec-ds-p2-history).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**6. FreqStack: why does "a stack per frequency" break ties by recency for free? How far can `top` move on a pop?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A value is pushed onto `levels[f]` exactly when it *reaches* count $f$, so within a level the order is the order in which values reached it: the top is the most recent. On a pop only the returned value's count changes, so either its level still has members (the cursor stays) or it emptied and the answer is $\text{top}-1$, which is non-empty because the popped value is on it. One step, never a search (@sec-ds-a3, @sec-ds-p3-freqstack, exercise 14).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**7. AllOne needs `getMinKey`/`getMaxKey` without removing anything. Why linked buckets rather than a sorted container, and what are the sentinels for?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Counts change by $\pm 1$, so a key's new bucket is always adjacent to its old one: a doubly linked list of buckets ordered by count turns `inc`/`dec` into "move the key to the neighbouring node, creating it if the neighbour has another count, unlink the old node if it emptied". `getMin`/`getMax` read `head.next`/`tail.prev`. The sentinels remove every special case for the first and last node. A sorted map is correct but $O(\log L)$ per call (@sec-ds-p3-allone, exercise 19).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**8. How do you design a hash map from scratch, covering buckets, load factor, resizing and adversarial input?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`table[h(k)]` holds a chain; `get` walks it, `put` updates or appends, `remove` unlinks. The expected chain length is $\alpha = n/m$, so keep $\alpha \le 0.75$ by doubling $m$ and **re-inserting every key**, since $k \bmod m$ changes; the doubling makes the resizes $O(1)$ amortised. With a predictable hash, an attacker sends keys with one residue and makes one chain of length $n$; defend with a seeded mixing hash or tree-shaped chains (@sec-ds-a4, @sec-ds-p4-hashmap, @sec-hash-anti).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**9. LRU cache, AllOne, FreqStack: is this one pattern three times?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Largely, yes: each keeps a `key -> position` map into an *ordered* collection whose order changes by one step per operation. LRU orders keys by recency (a doubly linked list, evict the tail; @sec-lang-p1-lru); AllOne orders buckets by count; FreqStack orders values within each frequency level by push time and tracks the top level with a scalar. The LFU cache (LC 460) combines two of them: frequency levels whose members are kept in LRU order.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**10. Ten thousand slots are cleared thousands of times, with one write between clears. How do you design it, and what is the design bad at?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`val[]` and `stamp[]` plus a global clock: a write sets `stamp[i] = clock`, a clear is `clock += 1`, a read is `stamp[i] == clock ? val[i] : default`. Bad at: (a) listing the live cells, which still needs a pass over all stamps (a dirty list or a sparse set fixes that); (b) memory, since stale values are never freed; (c) a clock that wraps around, which a 64-bit counter makes impossible in practice (@sec-ds-a5, @sec-ds-a5-sparse).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**11. Underground system answers averages in $O(1)$. Now the interviewer asks for the median, then for the average of only the last $k$ trips. What changes?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`(sum, count)` is exactly enough for a mean and not enough for anything order-based. Median of all trips: keep a per-route pair of heaps (or a sorted multiset), $O(\log t)$ per check-out. Average of the last $k$: the structure must *forget*, so keep a per-route queue of the last $k$ durations and a running sum that adds the new duration and subtracts the one that leaves. A fold works only for statistics that can be updated from the summary plus one new item (@sec-ds-p5-underground).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**12. Recent Actions: why is the arrival-rank rule correct, and which constraint makes it true?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every action's post id is $> n$, so a new post is always placed above the surviving initial posts, and the bottom of the field is always the highest-numbered initial post still present. Hence the $k$-th distinct arrival evicts initial post $n-k+1$, and a repeat evicts nobody. Post $i$'s answer is `firsts[n-i]` if at least $n-i+1$ distinct ids arrived, else $-1$: $O(n + m)$. Drop the constraint $p_t > n$ and an initial post can be moved back to the top, so the rule breaks (@sec-ds-p5-recent).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**13. Your `getRandom` uses `random.randrange(len(a))`. Why is the density of `a` essential?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Uniform over slots is uniform over elements only when every slot holds a live element: no gaps, one slot per copy, so $\Pr[v] = \text{count}(v)/n$. The same invariant makes `len(a)` the size and makes swap-with-last legal. A design with holes (tombstones) must either reject and redraw, which is cheap only while few slots are dead, or use a counting structure to find the $r$-th live slot, $O(\log n)$ (@sec-ds-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**14. Which guarantees in this chapter are worst-case and which are expected or amortised?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Worst-case $O(1)$: array reads and writes, `snap()` as a counter bump, the frequency cursor, linked-bucket hops once the node is found, bit arrays and direct addressing, a clock or flag update. Expected: anything that goes through a hash map (`pos`, `at`, buckets, probes), which depends on the hash spreading the keys (@sec-hash-anti). Amortised: appends to a dynamic array, rehashing, rollback, the dirty-list reset. Two honest caveats: a single resize is $\Theta(n)$, and the hotel's bounds are not $O(1)$ amortised at all when checkouts happen deep inside an occupied block (@sec-ds-p4-hotel).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**15. Chaining or open addressing: which would you pick, and why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Chaining is simpler, degrades gracefully at high load factors and makes deletion trivial; it pays a pointer per entry and a cache miss per chain step. Open addressing stores keys in the array itself, so probes walk adjacent memory and there are no pointers; it needs a lower load factor (about $1/2$ for linear probing), tombstones for deletion, and a good hash, because linear probing amplifies clustering. For small integer keys, neither: use direct addressing (@sec-ds-a4, @sec-ds-p4-hashset).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**16. How do you support `setAll(x)`, `set(i, v)` and `get(i)` in $O(1)$ each?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep `base`, a clock `epoch`, and per cell `val[i]`, `stamp[i]`. `setAll(x)`: `base = x; epoch += 1`. `set(i, v)`: `val[i] = v; stamp[i] = epoch`. `get(i)`: `val[i] if stamp[i] == epoch else base`. The invariant is "a cell whose stamp is current holds its own value; any other cell holds `base`". For "add to one cell" the cell must first be refreshed to `base` (@sec-ds-a5, @sec-ds-p5-assign).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="18"}
**17. How can you clear a set of integers in $O(1)$ without initialising any memory, and still list its members in $O(\text{size})$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The sparse set: `dense[0..n-1]` holds the members, `sparse[k]` is the position of $k$ in `dense`, and membership requires both `sparse[k] < n` and `dense[sparse[k]] == k`, so garbage in either array cannot produce a false positive. `clear()` sets `n = 0`; deletion is swap-with-last on `dense`; iteration walks `dense[0..n-1]` (@sec-ds-a5-sparse, exercise 21).
:::
:::

## 19 · Counting Subarrays, Pairs and Triples: The Contribution Technique {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-cnt]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**1. How do you compute the sum of the sums of every subarray in one pass, and why is the formula right?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Do not enumerate windows; ask how many of them contain slot $i$. A window is a pair of cut points with the left one in $\{0..i\}$ and the right one in $\{i..n-1\}$, so $i$ is covered $(i+1)(n-i)$ times and the answer is $\sum_i a_i (i+1)(n-i)$. Sanity-check by putting $a_i = 1$: the cover sum must be $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, the *sum of window lengths* — $20$ at $n = 4$, against $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ windows. Both numbers come out of the same formula, and naming the difference is what separates a derivation from a recitation (@sec-cnt-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**2. How does that answer change if only odd-length subarrays count?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nothing about the swap changes; only the cover count does. Of the $(i+1)(n-i)$ windows covering slot $i$, half have odd length, and when that product is odd the odd class is the larger one, so it is $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$. At $n = 5$ the odd covers are $[3, 4, 5, 4, 3]$ and the answer for `[1,4,2,5,3]` is $3 + 16 + 10 + 20 + 9 = 58$. Watch for the trap in the follow-up: "and how many odd-length windows are there?" is *not* $19$ — it is $(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1) \lceil n/2 \rceil$, i.e. $3 \times 3 = 9$ at $n = 5$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$ at $n = 4$, counted by choosing cut points of opposite parity (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**3. Why do cover counts fail for the sum of $\max - \min$ over all subarrays, and what replaces them?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A maximum is not additive, so the credit has to be re-derived as "the windows in which this slot is the *appointed* winner", and the appointment has to be unique. Each slot's span is a product $L_i R_i$ of two distances found by a monotonic stack, and the tie-break must be strict on one side and non-strict on the other — pop `<=` going left, `<` going right (or the mirror). Then $\sum \max - \min = \sum_i a_i (L_i R_i - L'_i R'_i)$ in $O(n)$. Prove you know the failure mode: on `[3, 3]` with the same predicate on both passes the credits are $[2,2]$ — four claims for three windows — and the sum of maxima comes out $12$ instead of $9$. The cheap invariant is that each credit row must sum to $\binom{n+1}{2}$ (@sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**4. Can a sliding window count the subarrays that sum to $K$ when the array has negatives?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A shrink loop is a monotonicity argument — "if `a[left..right]` is legal, every shorter suffix is too" — and a negative entry breaks it. On `[1,-1,1,-1,1]` with $K = 0$ the window rung answers $10$, the honest at-most-$0$ count is $9$, and the true exactly-$0$ count is $6$. Use prefix equality: $P[r] - P[l] = K$, so sweep the right end and add `cnt[p - K]` before inserting `cnt[p]`, seeded with `cnt[0] = 1`. $O(n)$ on any integers, and the seed is what lets a window start at index $0$ (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-a).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**5. How do you count subarrays whose sum is divisible by $k$, and why might a C++ version disagree with Python?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same sweep, keyed on the *residue*: $P[r] \equiv P[l] \pmod k$, so add `cnt[p]` then `cnt[p] += 1` with `p = ((s % k) + k) % k`. In C++ and Java `(-2) % 5` is $-2$, not $3$, so unnormalised keys split each bucket into two mirror images and the count comes out low; Python's `%` is already non-negative, which is why the bug is invisible there. Equivalent offline statement: bucket the $n+1$ prefix residues and add $\binom{c}{2}$ per bucket — that form works even with negatives because "same residue" is an equivalence relation (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-b, cross-checked on `[4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1]` with $k = 5$, which gives $7$ both ways).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**6. When do you reach for $\text{atMost}(k) - \text{atMost}(k-1)$ to count windows with exactly $k$ of something?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the window statistic is monotone under shrinking, which for sums means non-negative entries — binary arrays, counts of odds, lengths.
