Then two calls to one shrinking loop give $O(n)$, with $\text{atMost}(-1) = 0$ as the base case. On `[1,1,1,1]` with $k = 2$ that is $7 - 4 = 3$; on `[1,0,1,0,1]` with $k = 1$, $10 - 2 = 8$. With negatives the identity is false (@sec-cnt-a4). The other reflex to state: $\text{exactly}$ of a *shape* property (all `1`s) is a run decomposition, not a difference of two rungs (@sec-cnt-p3-ones).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**7. What are the two ways to count equal-value pairs, and which one generalises to inversions?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix the right end and add `seen[v]`, or build the histogram once and add $\binom{c}{2}$ — on `[1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3]` both give $4$ (charges $[0,0,0,1,2,1]$, and $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{2}{2}$). Only the first generalises, because $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ presumes the relation is an equivalence: for inversions on `[3, 1, 2, 1]` the histogram answers $1$ where there are $4$ inversions. When $i < j$ and $a_i > a_j$ matter, "how many earlier values are bigger?" is a prefix query over *values* — a table if the range is small, otherwise merge sort or a Fenwick tree (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-lts-a5, @sec-salgo-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**8. How do you count triples $(i, j, k)$ with three pairwise value conditions when $n \le 100$ and $arr[i] \le 1000$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Start with the triple loop ($\binom{100}{3} = 161{,}700$ steps — say out loud that it is affordable), then improve it by pivoting on $j$: with $j$ fixed, the condition on $i$ and the condition on $k$ are independent, and "$|a_i - a_j| \le a$ and $|a_i - a_k| \le c$" is one interval $[\max(a_j - a, a_k - c), \min(a_j + a, a_k + c)]$ clamped to $[0, V]$, answered by a subtraction on a cumulative histogram. $O(nV + n^2)$. Two traps to volunteer: clamping (an unclamped negative index reads the wrong end of the table in Python and is undefined behaviour in C++), and not multiplying the two pair counts — on `[3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7]`, $a = 7, b = 2, c = 3$ the product method gives $5$ because $(0,4,5) = (3,9,7)$ passes the two chain conditions and fails $|3 - 7| \le 3$ (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**9. When counting triplets whose left-part XOR equals their right-part XOR, why does the middle index disappear?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Because $x \oplus x = 0$: writing $a = P[j] \oplus P[i]$ and $b = P[k+1] \oplus P[j]$ (with $P$ the prefix XOR), $a = b$ iff $P[i] = P[k+1]$, and $P[j]$ cancels. So count equal-prefix cut pairs — windows $(i, k)$ with $P[i] = P[k+1]$ — and then remember that every $j \in \{i+1..k\}$ is a legal split, which is $k - i$ triplets, not $k - i - 1$. On `[2, 3, 1, 6, 7]`: $P = [0, 2, 1, 0, 6, 1]$, windows $(0,2)$ and $(2,4)$, each worth $2$, total $4$. Dropping the $j = k$ case (a single-element right array) gives $2$ (@sec-cnt-p4-xortri).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**10. Before writing an $O(n)$ counting solution, how do you choose the accumulator type and decide whether the answer needs a modulus?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Estimate the answer first. $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ fits a signed 32-bit int with $347{,}513{,}647$ left over; $\binom{10^5}{2} = 4{,}999{,}950{,}000$ does not, and LC 1513's answer $5{,}000{,}050{,}000$ (all-`1` string at $n = 10^5$) is why that statement hands you $10^9 + 7$. Mixed products are worse: LC 2104 at $n = 1000$ with $|v| \le 10^9$ reaches about $5 \cdot 10^{14}$ for the maxima alone, so the *credit* must be 64-bit even though $n$ is small. Accumulate in `long long`, reduce only at the end (or after each addition, never before) (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-arr-size-trap).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**11. What does a constraint like $1 \le arr[i] \le 500$ buy you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An array indexed by *value*: $501$ cells, $O(1)$ lookups, no hashing, no sorting. Conditions like $\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$ (@sec-cnt-p5-lucky) or "$|a_i - a_j| \le a$" (@sec-cnt-a5) become table reads, and the same trick gives a bound for free: a lucky $v$ occupies $v$ slots, so lucky values cost $\sum v^2 \le n$ — at $n = 500$ at most $10$ of them, since $1^2 + \cdots + 10^2 = 385 \le 500 < 506$. Alphabet-size constraints ($26$ letters, $\le 100$ values) are the same gift. The failure mode is solving it with maps and sorts when the statement offered an address (@sec-lts-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**12. For the sum of beauty (max frequency minus min frequency) over all substrings, how do you improve an $O(n^2 \cdot 26)$ solution's inner step?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The outer $O(n^2)$ is the enumeration; the win is making each extension $O(1)$. Keep `cnt[letter]` *and* `how[f]` — a counter of counters — so the extremes are cursors over frequency buckets instead of a scan of $26$ cells. The hard part is the discipline: $\min_f$ is over letters *present* in the window, so a bucket only becomes meaningful once a letter's first arrival has been recorded, and a cursor may move only while the bucket it is leaving is provably empty. Two sample values to keep: `"aabcb"` $= 5$ over $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ windows, `"aaabbb"` $= 8$. And the trap: using $\max_f - 1$ gives $6$ instead of $5$ on `"aabcb"` and no error at all on `"abc"`, so a sample can hide it completely (@sec-cnt-p5-beauty, @sec-ds).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**13. Rabbits report how many others share their colour; what is the smallest population consistent with the reports?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Group by the answer: $n_x$ rabbits reporting $x$ must be split into groups of size $x+1$, so they imply $\lceil n_x / (x+1) \rceil \cdot (x+1)$ rabbits. On `[1,1,2]` that is $2 + 3 = 5$; `[1,1,1]` is $4$ (one group of two, one rabbit short of a third pair), `[2,2,2,2,2]` is $6$, `[10]` is $11$, `[0,0,0]` is $3$. Pedagogically it is the same move as this chapter's count tables: the quantity you read is not the value but the *count of a count*, rounded up to a capacity (@sec-cnt-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**14. How do you test a counting solution whose answer you cannot verify by hand?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three things, all cheap. (1) A brute force at $n \le 9$ with values in a tiny range, fuzzed over hundreds of cases — every pattern in this chapter is locked that way (120 trials for the span credits, 80 for the at-most/exactly pair, 40 for the triplets). (2) A second independent framing, since rungs 2 and 3 disagree informatively: sweep vs $\sum \binom{c}{2}$, prefix-hash vs at-most difference, and they must agree exactly. (3) Structural invariants that fail loudly: credit rows sum to $\binom{n+1}{2}$, cover counts sum to $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, answers are monotone in $K$, and $\text{exactly}(K) \le \text{atMost}(K)$ (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-a4; the harness is @sec-cnt-why's bookkeeping).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**15. How do you sum $|a_i - a_j|$ over all pairs when $n = 10^5$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort; the set of pairs does not change. In sorted order $|b_m - b_k| = b_m - b_k$ for $k < m$, so the element of rank $k$ is added $k$ times (as the larger member) and subtracted $n - 1 - k$ times, weight $2k - n + 1$. $O(n \log n)$ for the sort and one pass. The running form `total += k * x - prefix` is the same sum and generalises to any charge linear in the earlier member. Use 64 bits: with $n = 10^5$, half the values at $0$ and half at $10^9$, the answer is $(n/2)^2 \cdot 10^9 = 2.5 \cdot 10^{18}$, which still fits a signed 64-bit integer (@sec-cnt-pairsum, @sec-cnt-psum-weird).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**16. Why is a single histogram wrong for counting pairs with $j - i = a_i + a_j$, and what works instead?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rewrite as $i + a_i = j - a_j$. The two sides are different functions of the index, so the relation is not "same key" and $\binom{c}{2}$ over one key counts something else. Sweep $j$ left to right: add the number of earlier indices whose left key equals $j - a_j$, then file $j + a_j$. Keys above $n$ can be dropped, so an array of size $n + 1$ replaces the hash map (@sec-cnt-idxval, @sec-cnt-pidx-message).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**17. When does complementary counting need inclusion–exclusion, and how do you get the intersection term?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Whenever the bad set is a union of events that can happen together. Each object in $A \cap B$ is subtracted once for $A$ and once for $B$, so it is added back once: $|U| - |A| - |B| + |A \cap B|$. The intersection is usually either provably empty (distinct couples cannot share both a boy and a girl) or another quantity of the same shape (windows containing neither $x$ nor $y$ are again runs). Say which one it is out loud — that is the step interviewers check (@sec-cnt-comp, @sec-cnt-pcomp-ball).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="19"}
**18. How do you count increasing triples $i < j < k$, which index do you fix, and can you beat $O(n^2)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix the middle: $\sum_j (\#\text{smaller on the left}) \cdot (\#\text{larger on the right})$, exact because nothing relates $a_i$ to $a_k$ directly. Counting both sides by scanning is $O(n^2)$. Both counts are prefix counts over values, so a Fenwick tree over (compressed) values gives each in $O(\log n)$ and the whole answer in $O(n \log n)$; when the values are small, a cumulative table does the same job (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-teams).
:::
:::

## 20 · GCD, Divisibility and Number-Theoretic Arrays {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-gcd]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**1. Why does Euclid's algorithm run in $O(\log \min(a, b))$ steps, and what inputs produce the worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each step replaces $(a, b)$ with $(b, a \bmod b)$, and after two steps the larger entry has at least halved, because $a \bmod b < b$ and the chain of remainders is strictly decreasing. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case: $\gcd(F(n{+}1), F(n))$ takes exactly $n - 1$ reductions. At $10^9$ the largest Fibonacci not exceeding it is $F(44)$, so the bound is around $44$ reductions (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**2. How do you compute "the gcd of the array except position $i$" in $O(n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Build `pref[i]` left to right and `suf[i]` right to left. Then the answer is $\gcd(\mathit{pref}[i-1],\; \mathit{suf}[i+1])$, with $\gcd(0, x) = x$ handling the boundary cases. The key is that gcd is associative but has **no inverse**, so you cannot subtract the contribution of position $i$ from a single fold — you need a second table (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**3. Why is the gcd of all subarrays ending at position $i$ at most $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ distinct values, and what algorithm does that enable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each strict drop in the gcd chain lands on a proper divisor, which is at most half. Starting at $V$, at most $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ halvings reach $1$. So you can fold the gcd set over positions in $O(n \log V)$ total, rather than enumerating $\binom{n+1}{2}$ subarrays. This is the technique behind LC 1819 and the $O(n \log V)$ complexity class of all "distinct subarray gcd" problems (@sec-gcd-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**4. Given an array of rectangles $(w_i, h_i)$, how do you count pairs with $w_i / h_i = w_j / h_j$ without floating point?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reduce each pair by its gcd: $\mathit{key}(w, h) = (w / g,\; h / g)$. Two ratios are equal exactly when their reduced forms are identical, so you build a histogram of canonical keys and compute $\sum_{\mathit{key}} \binom{c}{2}$. On `[(4,8),(3,6),(10,20),(15,30)]` all four reduce to $(1,2)$, giving $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ (@sec-gcd-p2-rects, @sec-gcd-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**5. Explain the greedy for splitting an array into the fewest contiguous segments with gcd $> 1$, and why it is provably minimal.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Maintain a running gcd $g$; extend the current segment while $\gcd(g, a_i) > 1$; the instant $\gcd(g, a_i) = 1$, cut and restart at $a_i$. The proof is that gcd only shrinks — once it reaches $1$ no future element can raise it, so any segment containing that pair is doomed. The cut is *forced*, and the greedy is minimal by exchange: any valid partition must have at least as many segments as the greedy creates (@sec-gcd-p2-split, @sec-gcd-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**6. How do you count how many elements in an array are divisible by each $d \le V$, and what is the total work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Build a frequency table `freq[v]`, then for each $d = 1, 2, \ldots, V$, sum `freq[m]` over multiples $m = d, 2d, 3d, \ldots \le V$. Total reads: $\sum_{d \le V} V / d \approx V \ln V$. At $V = 10^5$ this is $1{,}166{,}750$; at $V = 10^6$ it is $13{,}970{,}034$. The cost is independent of $n$ (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**7. How do you go from "$\binom{c_d}{2}$ pairs have gcd a multiple of $d$" to "$\mathit{exact}[d]$ pairs have gcd exactly $d$"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Process $d$ from $V$ down to $1$. Initialize $\mathit{exact}[d] = \binom{c_d}{2}$, then subtract $\mathit{exact}[m]$ for every multiple $m = 2d, 3d, \ldots$. The top-down order ensures all higher multiples are already finalized. The total inversion cost is the same $V \ln V$ harmonic sum. This is the Möbius principle in its simplest form (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**8. What is the $3$-cycle balance problem (CF 1490B), and why does only a forward sweep work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
You have $n$ integers, $3 \mid n$, and an operation adds $1$ to one element. Adding $1$ walks it from bucket $r$ to $(r+1) \bmod 3$; there is no backward move. So surplus can only flow in one direction around the cycle. The optimal plan is a single forward sweep: for each bucket, hand its excess to the next bucket. The answer for `[0, 2, 5, 5, 4, 8]` is $3$ moves (@sec-gcd-p4-balance, @sec-gcd-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**9. In CF 1374D, why is the answer $\max_d (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1) \cdot k + d + 1$ and not a sum?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each move picks one element and adds the current counter value $x$ to it, then $x$ advances. Elements in bucket $d$ are served at $x = d, d + k, d + 2k, \ldots$, and each $x$ serves exactly one element. So the *last* move happens at $x = (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1) \cdot k + d$ for whichever bucket has the highest such $x$ (the $\max$), and reaching that $x$ takes one more increment (the $+1$). Summing would double-count: the counter is shared across all buckets (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod, @sec-gcd-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**10. In LC 2197, why is one stack pass sufficient to simulate the repeated-merge process?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A shared factor is *transitive along a contiguous run*: if $\gcd(a_i, a_{i+1}) > 1$ and $\gcd(a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}) > 1$, the entire run folds into one lcm. A stack processes left to right, popping and folding whenever the top shares a factor with the new element. This is equivalent to merging all pairs and re-scanning, because the fold is associative ($\text{lcm}(\text{lcm}(a,b),c) = \text{lcm}(a,\text{lcm}(b,c))$). `[6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]` gives `[12, 7, 6]` in one pass (@sec-gcd-p5-merge, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**11. CF 1629B: how do you decide the answer without touching the array?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\gcd(x, x+1) = 1$ always, so any range $[l..r]$ with $r - l \ge 1$ has array gcd $1$. A product-move absorbs one odd element (pairing it with an even). The odd count in $[l..r]$ is $(r+1)//2 - l//2$. The answer is YES iff that count $\le k$. One-element ranges are exceptions: $[x..x]$ has gcd $x$, so $[13..13]$ with $k=0$ is YES. At $r - l = 10^9$ this is the only feasible approach (@sec-gcd-p5-parity, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**12. What is Euler's totient function, and how does it count coprime pairs in $[1..n]^2$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\varphi(k)$ counts $1 \le j \le k$ with $\gcd(j, k) = 1$, computed as $k \prod_{p \mid k} (1 - 1/p)$ from prime factors. In the grid $[1..n]^2$, the diagonal $i = j$ is coprime only at $(1,1)$, and the upper triangle contributes $\sum_{k=2}^n \varphi(k)$ while the lower triangle mirrors it. Total: $1 + 2\sum_{k=2}^n \varphi(k)$. At $n = 5$: $1 + 2(1+2+2+4) = 19$ (@sec-gcd-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**13. You need to answer "how many elements are divisible by $d$?" for every $d \le V$. Give three rungs of a ladder and the crossover.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rung 1: for each query $d$, scan all $n$ elements — $O(n)$ per query. Rung 2: for each $d$, walk multiples in a frequency table — $O(V \ln V)$ precompute, $O(1)$ per query. Rung 3: if queries arrive online with varying $d$ and updates change the array, use a Fenwick tree over multiples or a divisor lattice. The crossover is when the number of queries $Q$ satisfies $Q \cdot n > V \ln V$: at $V = 10^5$ that's $Q > n / 12$ roughly. The harmonic sieve (rung 2) is always the right answer for offline batches when $V \le 10^6$ (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**14. What is the pigeonhole argument that $n + 1$ integers from $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$ always contain a divisor pair?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write each integer as $x = 2^a \cdot o$ (odd part $o$). In $[1..2n]$ there are exactly $n$ distinct odd parts ($1, 3, 5, \ldots, 2n-1$). By the pigeonhole principle, choosing $n + 1$ integers forces two to share the same odd part $o$. Those two are $2^a \cdot o$ and $2^b \cdot o$ with (WLOG) $a < b$, so the first divides the second. The proof is the bucket structure of odd parts, not any search (@sec-gcd-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**15. A statement says $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $a_i \le 10^5$, and asks a question about divisibility of pairs. What is your first move?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Check whether the value bound ($10^5$) is small enough to own a table. $\sum_{d \le V} V/d = 1.17 \cdot 10^6$ steps precompute the multiple counts $c[d]$ for every divisor simultaneously. Then $\binom{c_d}{2}$ gives the "at most" count, and the top-down inversion gives "exactly $d$" in the same harmonic total. The pair loop is $\binom{2 \cdot 10^5}{2} \approx 2 \cdot 10^{10}$, which is clearly too slow; the sieve is $\sim 10^6$, which is comfortable. This is Pattern 3 (@sec-gcd-p3, @sec-gcd-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="20"}
**16. How do you stress-test the harmonic sieve and the top-down inversion?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three checks. (1) `sum(exact[d] for d in 1..V)` must equal $\binom{n}{2}$ — every pair has some gcd. (2) Fuzz over small arrays (values $\le 25$, $n \le 7$) comparing `exact[d]` against a brute-force Counter of all pair gcds, for $\sim 60$ random cases. (3) Invert the test: compute $\sum_{m: d \mid m} \mathit{exact}[m]$ and check it equals $\binom{c_d}{2}$ — the original at-most count. The inversion is the most error-prone step, and a wrong loop order (bottom-up) passes test (1) but fails test (2) informatively (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::
:::

## 21 · MEX, Distinctness and Value-Domain Problems {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-mex]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**1. Define MEX. Compute it in `O(n)` time and `O(n)` extra space; then argue why `O(n)` extra space is required in the comparison model.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
MEX of a set `S ⊆ Z≥0` is `min Z≥0 \ S`. `O(n)` time: presence table + walk-up. Extra space is required because the answer depends on the pattern of values seen; sorting takes `O(n log n)` and can be walked with `O(1)` extra, but a linear-time solution needs random access into a bucket per value (@sec-mex-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**2. Give a one-line Python expression for the prefix-MEX list; then convert it to `O(n)` time.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One-liner (slow): `[mex(a[:i+1]) for i in range(len(a))]` — `O(n^2)`. `O(n)`: maintain a set and a pointer `m`; after each insert, `while m in seen: m += 1`; append `m`. The pointer is monotone so total work across all `while` steps is `O(n)` (@sec-mex-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**3. Design `insert(v)`, `erase(v)`, `mex()` on a dynamic multiset in `O(log n)` amortised.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Track `cnt[v]` and an ordered set `missing`. On insert, if `cnt[v]` goes 0→1, remove `v` from missing; on erase, if `cnt[v]` goes 1→0, add `v`. `mex()` returns `min(missing)`. With `std::set`, Python `sortedcontainers.SortedSet`, or a Fenwick over `present` with binary lifting for the first zero, every op is `O(log n)` (@sec-mex-pit, exercise 14).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**4. Given `n` integers up to `10^9` and `q` offline "distinct in `[l, r]`?" queries, answer in `O((n + q) log n)` total.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort queries by `r`. Sweep `r` left-to-right, maintaining a BIT over positions with `+1` at the last occurrence of each value and `-1` at the previous position. For query `[l, r]`, the sum on `[l, r]` is the number of distinct values. Per-value sorted lists (as in @sec-mex-p4-dcq) work online at `O(Σ log n)` per query but need a small alphabet (@sec-mex-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**5. How do you check "is `a` a permutation of `1..n`?" in `O(1)` extra space?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Negation trick: walk `a`; for each `|a_i|`, negate `a[|a_i| - 1]`. If already negative, duplicate found. After the pass, every entry must be negative. Restores the array on exit. `O(1)` extra, `O(n)` time. XOR-check also works but does not detect duplicates alone (@sec-mex-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**6. Explain the difference between "frequency of values" and "frequency of frequencies". Give a problem that requires the latter.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`cnt[v]` = number of occurrences of `v`. `fc[c]` = number of values with count `c`. The second is a histogram of the first. CF 1490F (Equalize the Array) needs `fc`: given counts per value, compute the cheapest deletions to make every remaining count equal; iterate targets `c` and use `fc` to sum the values to trim (@sec-mex-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**7. Why does "sum + distinct" fail as a permutation test without a range check? Give a counterexample.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`[0, 2, 4]` for `n = 3`: sum `6 = n(n+1)/2` and all three entries are distinct, but `{0, 2, 4} ≠ {1, 2, 3}`. The test only proves "sum matches target", not "membership in the target range". Add `all(1 <= x <= n)` or use MEX `= n + 1` (@sec-mex-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**8. CF 1406A: derive the closed form `mex(>=1) + mex(>=2)` and justify the two-subset assignment.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every value with count `>= 1` can be placed into `A` to grow `mex(A)` up to the first gap; every value with count `>= 2` can additionally be placed into `B`. Once a value with count `= 1` goes into `A`, `B` never sees it, so `mex(B)` stops there. Assignment: `A` takes one copy of every present value (`mex = ` first gap of `cnt >= 1`); `B` takes one copy of every doubly-present value (`mex = ` first gap of `cnt >= 2`) (@sec-mex-p1-subset-mex).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**9. CF 1294D: state the amortised-`O(1)`-per-query argument and the invariant the pointer preserves.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Invariant: values `0..(ans-1)` are covered and `ans` is the smallest uncovered value. Each query contributes exactly one token to `cnt`. The while-loop consumes one token per advance, and total advances across all queries cannot exceed total tokens, which is `q`. So the while-loop's combined cost is `O(q)` amortised (@sec-mex-p2-mex-max).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**10. For LC 1695, argue that the sliding window is amortised `O(n)` even though the inner while-loop can run multiple times per iteration.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each index `l` advances monotonically from 0 to `n` over the run. Total `set.discard` operations across every iteration of the outer `for` is at most `n`. Combined with `n` insertions on the right, the set is touched `O(n)` times. Sum operations and best updates are `O(1)` each (@sec-mex-p4-erasure).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**11. CF 1234D: generalise the per-character set solution to alphabet size `Σ`. What changes when `Σ = 26` vs `Σ = n`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Per-character set is `O(Σ log n)` per query. With `Σ = 26` that is a small constant factor; with `Σ = n` it degenerates to `O(n log n)` per query, which loses to a segment-tree bitmask (only fits when `Σ <= 64` per machine word) or a Wavelet tree / BIT of last-occurrences (@sec-mex-p4-dcq).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="21"}
**12. CF 1364C: argue that the greedy walk either produces a valid `a` or correctly returns `-1`. Where is the completeness argument?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On growth (`m[i] > m[i-1]`), `a[i] = m[i-1]` is forced — the only placement that fills the previous hole without disturbing earlier prefix MEXes. On same (`m[i] = m[i-1]`), `a[i] ≠ m[i]` and must not consume a value needed later: the spare pool (values never appearing in `m`) is exactly the safe set. If a growth step is rejected because values in `(m[i-1], m[i])` were not pre-placed, no alternative assignment could have placed them: earlier same-steps drew from the spare pool and earlier growth-steps were forced (@sec-mex-p3-prefix-mex).
:::
:::

## 22 · Coordinate Compression and Offline Processing {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-coord]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**1. What is coordinate compression, and what two guarantees does the rank map keep?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A translation of arbitrary comparable values to dense indices $1 \ldots |\text{distinct}|$ via `sorted(set(a))` + dict (or bisect). It keeps exactly: (i) $x < y \iff \mathit{rank}(x) < \mathit{rank}(y)$; (ii) $x = y \iff \mathit{rank}(x) = \mathit{rank}(y)$. It drops arithmetic — gaps, sums, mod — hence it's valid only when the algorithm's comparisons never see raw values (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-srt-a4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**2. Count "how many earlier elements are smaller than me" for every position. Give two $O(n \log n)$ answers and their trade-offs.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge-sort counting across the merge (@sec-salgo-p2 — LC 315's home method) and BIT over compressed ranks (@sec-coord-a2). The divide version is static, batch, recursion-heavy; the BIT version handles *interleaved* "how many smaller seen so far" online and generalises to sums (`range_sum`) and order statistics (`kth`).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**3. Why can't a hash-map prefix count solve "number of subarrays with sum in $[lo, hi]$" when values can be negative, and what does?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The hash form answers exact-key equality $P_j - P_i = s$; a *range* $[lo, hi]$ needs order statistics — "count earlier $P_i \in [P_j - hi, P_j - lo]$" — which is a BIT over compressed prefix values ($O(\log n)$ per step) or merge-count; that's LC 327, the promise @sec-pref-hash left open (@sec-coord-p1-rangesum).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**4. You're given a static array and $10^5$ queries "how many elements $\le t$". Then a variant with point updates interleaved. Solve both.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Static: sort once; either offline sweep ($O(n\log n + q)$, @sec-coord-a3) or `bisect_right` per query ($O(\log n)$ each, online). With interleaved updates: neither works — a value-indexed structure is mandatory: BIT over compressed positions/values (the Fenwick "later volume" promise; LC 307 is its textbook drill) (@sec-coord-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**5. A stream deletes elements from an array; after each deletion report the largest contiguous-block sum. Sketch the solution and state why forward is hopeless.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reverse time: replay deletions as insertions; an inserted cell activates, unions with live neighbours, component sums grow monotonically; track the running best. Forward is hopeless because *splitting* a block needs re-searching inside it; merging is $O(\alpha)$ (@sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3-destroy).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**6. Explain the Fenwick `kth` descent: why is walking the tree by powers of two a binary search?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From $i = 0$, try $j = i + 2^b$ downward in bits: if $t[j] < k$, then all of $j$'s covered range lies inside the answer's prefix, so commit $i = j$, $k -= t[j]$. It mirrors finding the largest prefix with sum $< k_{\text{target}}$ by binary representation instead of midpoints; each step halves the remaining candidates. Costs $O(\log n)$ and requires non-negative entries (@sec-coord-a2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**7. Segments over $[0, 10^{18}]$, count integer points covered exactly $k$ times, for every $k$. Give the algorithm and the two implementation traps.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Events $(l, +1), (r+1, -1)$, sort, sweep; charge `cur` coverage to stretches `x - prev` between grouped events. Traps: (1) apply deltas at a shared coordinate *after* charging; (2) $r + 1$ overflows 32-bit and needs care at $10^{18}$ boundaries (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**8. Sum the union area of $n \le 200$ axis-aligned rectangles with integer coordinates up to $10^9$ (LC 850). Two approaches and their complexities.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Compress both axes: unique x- and y-coordinates ($\le 2n$ each), mark the $\le 4n^2$ uniform cells against each rectangle — $O(n^3)$, trivially correct (mod $10^9+7$ at the end). Sweep one axis with an interval-coverage counter on the other — $O(n^2 \log n)$ — heavier to code. At $n = 200$ the cubic cell loop is the intended path (@sec-coord-p5-area, @sec-coord-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**9. Given a permutation encoded by $s_i$ = "sum of earlier elements smaller than $p_i$", restore it. Why process right-to-left and what structure?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Right-to-left, every not-yet-used value sits at earlier positions, so $s_i$ = sum of unused values $< p_i$: a prefix-sum lookup over a live-values BIT, then *find the largest prefix whose sum is $\le s_i$* and take the next survivor — `kth`-style descent, $O(\log n)$ per position, $O(n \log n)$ total, with the sum-BIT alongside the count-BIT to remove (@sec-coord-p3-restore).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**10. Points on a line with velocities; sum of minimum pair distances. Reduce to a sweep + compressed BIT in one minute.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Two points meet iff the left one's velocity is greater; otherwise $\min$ distance $=$ initial gap. Sort by coordinate; sweep left-to-right; at $j$ the contributing earlier points are those with $v_i \le v_j$ — count and coordinate-sum among them via two BITs over compressed velocities, answer $+ = x_j \cdot \mathit{cnt} - \mathit{sum}$ (@sec-coord-p4-moving).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**11. When must you *refuse* to sort the queries? Two statement features to spot.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) Updates interleaved with queries (the data moves while you plan to batch-read it). (2) Adaptive queries — the statement says the next query depends on your previous answer (interactive or XOR-encrypted input like several CF problems). Both make any "sort the queries" order illegal; the online structures (bisect on rebuilt pieces, BIT, segment tree) are the fallback (@sec-coord-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**12. $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ vertices, $m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ edges, $k \le 400$; find the $k$-th smallest pairwise shortest distance. What is the compression argument?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep the $k$ lightest edges; call their endpoints relevant ($\le 2k$). Any pair with both vertices irrelevant has distance $\ge w_k$, while the kept edges alone already witness $\ge k$ pairs at distance $\le w_k$ — so the answer sits between relevant vertices. Run Dijkstra from each relevant vertex (early exit when all relevant settled), collect relevant-relevant distances, take the $k$-th smallest of deduped unordered pairs (@sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="22"}
**13. "Compress the tree" (virtual trees) is a phrase you'll meet in the trees volume. In one paragraph: what does the same habit look like there?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a tree, a batch of $k$ *marked* vertices induces a minimal Steiner-like subtree; the "space you touch" is the union of root-paths through LCAs, so compress $n$ tree vertices to the $O(k)$ marked ones + their $O(k)$ LCAs, sorted by Euler order. Identical logic: bound the answer's witnesses, keep only those coordinates, rebuild adjacency by parent jumps (ch. 185 "virtual trees" in the roadmap; cf. @sec-coord-p5-kthpath's endpoint-pool argument).
:::
:::

## 23 · Square Root Decomposition {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-sqrt]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**1. In your own words: what is square-root decomposition, and what is the core tradeoff it makes?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Split the array into $\approx \sqrt n$ contiguous blocks of $\approx \sqrt n$ cells, keep a cheap summary per block, and answer a range query as (two partial edge blocks scanned cell-by-cell) plus (whole middle blocks read from their summaries). One point update rebuilds a single block in $O(\sqrt n)$; one query is $O(\sqrt n)$. It trades a $O(\log n)$ tree's asymptotics for far simpler code and arbitrary per-block summaries (@sec-sqrt-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**2. When would you reach for blocks over a segment tree, and when is the tree strictly better?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Blocks win when the combine is not associative or hard to define (count of a value, mode, a modulo, per-value histograms), when insertions change the structure's size, or when you just need code you can trust. The tree wins when the op is a clean $O(\log n)$ monoid (sum/min/gcd) *and* the time limit is tight, or when lazy range-add/assign must propagate over arbitrary $O(\log n)$-many nodes (@sec-sqrt-a6, @sec-seg).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**3. Explain a lazy block tag and the push/pull discipline it forces.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A tag stores a *pending* whole-block operation (add, assign, XOR) instead of applying it to cells, making range updates $O(\sqrt n)$ (one tag per covered block). Any partial touch must first `push` the tag into the cells (so you act on true values) and later `pull`/`redo` the summary so the block's cached aggregate matches the edits (@sec-sqrt-a2, @sec-sqrt-p2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**4. Name three rebuild strategies and when each is right.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) Partial: rebuild only the block(s) a change touches — point updates (@sec-sqrt-p1). (2) Buffer-then-flush: log $O(\sqrt n)$ updates, answer queries by combining base + buffer, rebuild the whole array when the buffer is too long — many interleaved updates you cannot fold into a tag (@sec-sqrt-a3). (3) Periodic/split-rebuild: keep a self-adjusting structure (unrolled list) and rebuild/split a block only when it exceeds a size bound — inserts and deletes (@sec-sqrt-p3-serega).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**5. Some problems put blocks on the *value* axis, not positions. Give two and the tell.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
CF 220B ("$x$ occurs exactly $x$ times") and CF 1638E ("add to every element of colour $c$"). The tell: the question or update names a *value/colour*, not an index range, so a table keyed by value ($\mathit{add}[c]$, per-value position lists) is the primary structure; you then split that table by magnitude or frequency at $\sqrt n$ (@sec-sqrt-a4, @sec-sqrt-p4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**6. Heavy-light by a threshold is the pattern behind P5. Walk CF 797E through it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The cost depends on the query parameter $k$: small $k$ is expensive to simulate but there are only $\sqrt n$ distinct small values, so precompute a table $f[k][\cdot]$ for them ($O(n\sqrt n)$); large $k$ is rare-cheap because each hop advances $> \sqrt n$, so just simulate ($O(\sqrt n)$). Precompute exactly the side that is expensive to answer and cheap to batch (@sec-sqrt-p5-arrq, @sec-sqrt-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**7. Why does an unrolled linked list beat a balanced BST for CF 455D's cyclic shifts?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The operations are pop-one-cell and insert-one-cell at arbitrary ranks, plus "count $k$ in a range" — order-statistics and histograms you want *per block*, and a rebuild flush is a few lines. A BST would need a subtree Counter maintained on every rotation/rebalance; blocks give $O(\sqrt n)$ rank-walk and $O(\sqrt n)$ count via per-block histograms with far less machinery (@sec-sqrt-p3-serega).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**8. A range-modulo has no lazy tag. Why, and what saves CF 438D?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Modulo is not distributive over the sum/min you would tag, and applying it changes each cell individually, so there is nothing to defer. What saves it: skip a whole block when its `max < x` (no cell changes under $\bmod\, x$), and note every *effective* modulo at least halves the touched value, so each cell rebuilds $\le \log A$ times — amortised $O(\sqrt n)$ (@sec-sqrt-p3-childseq, @sec-sqrt-a3).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**9. How do you tell a Mo's-algorithm problem from a sqrt-decomposition problem when neither has updates?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Check for an associative, query-independent block summary. If the aggregate needs to *know the current window* and only updates in $O(1)$ as the window slides ($\sum \text{freq}^2$, mode, #distinct), that is Mo's (ch. 24). If you can combine whole-block summaries into an answer for any range without reordering queries — per-value position lists, a block-pair precompute — blocks are genuine (@sec-sqrt-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**10. Your $O(\sqrt n)$ is too slow. What knobs, other than swapping in a segment tree, can you turn?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Retune $B$ to the real update/query ratio (heavy queries: bigger $B$; heavy updates: smaller), or use $n^{2/3}$ when a rebuild dominates. Split the query into a precomputed interior ($O(1)$) plus a $O(B)$ fringe (P5's block-pair table). Cache per-block data you recompute too eagerly (bit-counts, histograms). Often these turn $\sqrt n$ into $1$ per query at the cost of an $O(n\sqrt n)$ build (@sec-sqrt-a5, @sec-sqrt-p5-closeq).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**11. Design question: range add and, per query, count elements equal to $v$ in $[\ell,r]$. Sketch blocks.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Per block store a frequency map of *base* values and a lazy `add` tag. Range add: whole blocks `tag += x` ($O(\sqrt n)$), partial blocks push+edit+rebuild the map ($O(B)$). Count-$v$: whole block answer is `freq[v - tag]`; partial blocks scan cells adding `tag`. $O(\sqrt n)$ per op — the tag turns "count $v$" into "count the shifted key" (@sec-sqrt-a2, @sec-sqrt-p4-colorops).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**12. What is the complexity of CF 220B's value-split answer and where does the $\log n$ come from?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(n)$ to build per-value position lists and find heavy values; each query $O(T)$ small-value checks plus $O(n/T)$ heavy checks, each an $O(\log n)$ count by two binary searches into a position list — so $O(\sqrt n \log n)$ per query. The $\log n$ is purely the binary search; replacing position lists with per-block histograms (as in CF 455D) trades it for a different $\sqrt n$ scan (@sec-sqrt-p4-learray).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="23"}
**13. Give a concrete bug that appears only when the lazy tag and the block summary disagree, and how to catch it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In CF 242E, computing a whole-block sum as $\sum_k \mathit{bit}[b][k]\cdot 2^k$ while `tag[b] != 0` ignores that the live value is $a_i \oplus \mathit{tag}$ — you must complement the bit count where the tag's bit is set. The catch is a stress test: keep a plain-array brute force and, after every random operation, assert the structure's query equals the brute's, so any tag/summary desync fires immediately (@sec-sqrt-p2-xorseg, @sec-sqrt-p1's oracle discipline).
:::
:::

## 24 · Mo's Algorithm {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-mo]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**1. State Mo's algorithm in one sentence and name the single property of the input it exploits.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Mo answers a *batch* of offline range queries by sorting them so consecutive windows overlap heavily, then sliding one $[\ell,r]$ pointer pair with $O(1)$ add/remove. The exploited property is **reorderability**: because no query depends on another's answer, you may permute them and merely remember the original indices (@sec-mo-a1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**2. Why $B = n/\sqrt q$ and not $\sqrt n$? Give the movement formula you are minimising.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Total pointer travel is $qB$ ($\ell$-jitter) $+\ n^2/B$ ($r$-sweeps across the $n/B$ blocks). AM–GM / calculus minimises it at $B = n/\sqrt q$, yielding $O(n\sqrt q)$. $\sqrt n$ is only optimal when $q\sim n$; for sparse queries it is off by a real, measurable factor (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-pit).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**3. What makes a problem Mo-*legal* versus merely Mo-*fast*? Give a counterexample where Mo is illegal.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Legal = offline (queries known up front, no answer-chaining) plus an $O(1)$ slide. Illegal = adaptive queries: e.g. CF 455D-style inputs where $\ell,r$ are XOR-ed with `lastans`, so you cannot know query $i$ until you answered query $i-1$ — reordering is void and you need an online structure (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-sqrt-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**4. Explain rollback Mo and the situation that forces it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When you can extend the window in $O(1)$ but cannot cheaply *un*-extend it, sort by $\ell$-block and keep $r$ monotone-forward within the group; per query snapshot the aggregate, `add` the $\le B$ left fringe, read, restore. Amortised $O(n\sqrt n)$ with zero deletes. The canonical forcing problem is CF 868F (cost of a window depends on equal-pairs, no clean remove) (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**5. Mo-with-updates: what is the third pointer, and what discipline does moving it impose?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`t` = how many of the updates have been applied; a query is $(\ell,r,t)$ and you sort by $(\ell/B, r/B, t)$ with $B=n^{2/3}$. Advancing $t$ applies one update and **must stash the cell's old value before overwriting** so retreating $t$ can revert it; if the changed position is inside the window you also remove-old/add-new in the aggregates (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**6. What does the Hilbert curve buy over block order, and what does it cost you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A shorter practical two-pointer walk: space-filling-curve ordering keeps spatially-near queries near in sort order, so pointers travel fewer steps (better constant, same $O(n\sqrt q)$ family). The cost is losing the clean textbook bound and a uglier key — a recursive `hilbertOrder(x,y,pow,rot)` whose `pow` must cover the grid and whose result must be 64-bit (@sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**7. A query answer is not one number but a *function of the frequency multiset* (mode, exact-$k$, MEX-of-frequencies). How do you keep it $O(1)$ per slide?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Maintain `freq[v]` *and* `ftf[c]` = how many values currently have count $c$, updated together on every add/remove. exact-$k$ is `ftf[k]`; the mode is the top index with `ftf>0` (a running pointer that only drops when `ftf[mode]==0`); MEX-of-frequencies is the smallest $c\ge1$ with `ftf[c]==0`. One leaner trick handles a yes/no shape: a single `off` counter for "all present values at count 3" (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-mode, @sec-mo-p5-threeocc).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**8. When you would reach for Mo, when for a segment tree, when for sqrt blocks?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Mo: many offline queries, no/few updates, $O(1)$ slide of a non-associative aggregate. Segment tree / Fenwick: online or heavily-updated ranges with an associative $O(\log n)$ combine. Sqrt blocks: online middle ground, $O(\sqrt n)$ per op, no reordering, arbitrary per-block summaries. The gate is reordering freedom — no it means not-Mo (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-sqrt-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**9. Why is tree-path Mo out of scope in a flat-array chapter, and how would you adapt the window to a tree?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The core method is identical but the array is a stand-in for an Euler/first-occurrence tour; path queries become range queries over that tour with a *toggle* (an in/out-of-path flag) so a node counts only while on the current path. That extra machinery (Euler tour + Mo on a subtree vs a path) belongs with tree data structures, so this chapter cites CF 375D / 246E / 600E as the deferred variant rather than solving them (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-mo-pit).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**10. Walk CF 617E: what is the window actually over, and why does the $O(1)$ update count pairs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The window is over prefix-xor indices $[\ell-1, r]$. A subarray in the original range has xor $k$ iff two prefix values differ by $k$. Adding prefix index $j$ to the window pairs it with every present prefix equal to $p_j\oplus k$, which is `freq[p[j]^k]` — so the pair count rises by that and `freq[p[j]]` is bumped. Removing mirrors it (@sec-mo-p1-xorfav).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**11. What is the single most common Mo bug and how do you catch it in development?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An `add`/`remove` that is not the exact inverse of the other — usually a value structure (`ftf`, a witness set, `off`) updated on add but not symmetrically on remove. The catch is the same as always in this book: keep a raw brute-force oracle (a `Counter`/slice scan) and, after every random query on random data, assert the window answer equals it (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-pit).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**12. Design: $n\le 10^5$ static array, $q\le 10^5$ queries, each asks "is there a value appearing exactly once in $[\ell,r]$ and print one". Give complexity and the structures.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Classic Mo with a `freq` table and a `ones` set maintained across the $1\rightleftarrows2$ crossings; answers are offline so print in input order. $O(n\sqrt q)$ (or Hilbert for the same order with a smaller constant), space $O(n)$. This is CF 1000F; its sibling "*how many* appear once" is `ftf[1]` (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc, @sec-mo-a5).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="24"}
**13. A colleague set the Mo block size to $\sqrt n$ "because Mo is a sqrt-decomposition algorithm". Correct them precisely.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Classic Mo minimises $qB + n^2/B$, whose optimum is $n/\sqrt q$, not $\sqrt n$; $\sqrt n$ is only right when $q\sim n$. Rollback Mo genuinely uses $\sqrt n$ (its cost is $n^2/B + qB$ with a different balance), and Mo-with-updates uses $n^{2/3}$. Each variant has its own $B$ — copying one across the others is the classic slow-Mo bug (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-pit).
:::
:::

## 25 · Multidimensional & Higher-Order Prefix Sums {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-nd]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**1. Build a 2D prefix sum in one pass and answer a sub-rectangle. Give both recurrences and the query, and the cost of each.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Build $P[i{+}1][j{+}1] = P[i][j{+}1] + \text{rowsum}$ (or $P[i{+}1][j{+}1] = a[i][j] + P[i][j{+}1] + P[i{+}1][j] - P[i][j]$), $O(nm)$. Query $[r_0,r_1)\times[c_0,c_1)$ as $P[r_1][c_1]-P[r_0][c_1]-P[r_1][c_0]+P[r_0][c_0]$, $O(1)$. Space $O(nm)$; keep it 64-bit (@sec-nd-a1, @sec-nd-p1-rectsum).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**2. Explain the prefix↔difference duality. You have many rectangle-adds and read the grid once at the end — what do you do and why is it fast?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A difference array is the prefix run backwards: to *add* rather than *read*. Each rectangle-add writes $+v/-v$ at the four corners of a padded $(n{+}1)\times(m{+}1)$ grid in $O(1)$; one 2D prefix at the end materialises every cell. Total $O(k + nm)$, versus $O(\sum\text{area})$ to paint cells (@sec-nd-a2, @sec-nd-p2-rectadd).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**3. Generalise a rectangle sum to a box in a 3D array. How many terms, and how do you not screw up the signs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2^3 = 8$ terms; a query takes the two opposite corners and the sign of each partial sum is $(-1)^{\text{# of lowered indices}}$ — one lowered subtracted, two added, three subtracted. Build $P[i][j][t]$ with the same 8-term recurrence. $O(nmk)$ build, $O(1)$ per box (@sec-nd-a3, @sec-nd-p2-3dbox).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**4. The update is "add $1,2,3,\dots$ to a range" instead of a constant. What structure absorbs that in $O(1)$ and why two arrays?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A second-order (two first-order) difference. The added value at cell $i$ is $d\cdot i + (t-\ell d)$ — a line in $i$. Keep one difference array for the slope $d$ and one for the intercept, four boundary writes per update, then one scan that accumulates both running sums and emits `cb*i + cc`. $O(1)$ per update, $O(n)$ to materialise (@sec-nd-a4, @sec-nd-p3-aprange).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**5. You must answer range-sum *queries* after those linear updates. How do the two halves of the chapter compose, and what is the total cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Difference for the writes, prefix for the reads. Rebuild `a` with the two-array difference in $O(n+k)$, then `prefix1d` over `a` so every query is `P[r+1]-P[l]` in $O(1)$. Overall $O(n + k + q)$ — the inverse pair used in one pipeline (@sec-nd-p3-linear).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**6. A grid query asks for the sum along a diagonal, not a rectangle. What changes in the preprocessing?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The axis you prefix *along*. Bucket cells by $d = i-j$ (or $s=i+j$) in increasing $i$, run an ordinary 1D prefix inside each bucket once ($O(nm)$), and a diagonal run is two reads of that bucket's prefix — the 1D trick on a slanted slice (@sec-nd-a5, @sec-nd-p4-diag).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**7. What is a contribution / multiplicity argument, and give the 1D formula for "sum of every subarray"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Instead of iterating the containers (subarrays/pairs), iterate the elements and multiply each by how many containers it appears in, weighted. A 1D element at index $i$ lies in $(i+1)(n-i)$ subarrays, so the total is $\sum_i a[i](i+1)(n-i)$ — one weighted pass instead of $O(n^2)$. The 2D version separates to $\sum_{i,j} a[i][j](i{+}1)(n{-}i)(j{+}1)(m{-}j)$ (@sec-nd-a6, @sec-nd-p4-rybinsk).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**8. CF 1195D2 sums an interleaving of all ordered pairs. Why is it a weighted prefix and how do you handle the $n^2$ pairs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Never build the pairs. Each digit's *place value* depends only on the two numbers' lengths and the digit's index from the right, so group by length ($\le 10$ classes), precompute per-length digit sums, and sum the $\le 10\times 10$ length-pairs with each digit charged its power-of-ten weight. That is exactly the multiplicity idea with $10^{\text{power}}$ as the weight, done mod $998244353$ (@sec-nd-p4-rybinsk, @sec-nd-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**9. Given a static grid and $2\cdot10^{5}$ rectangle-sum queries with $n,m\le10^{3}$, choose prefix vs per-query scan and justify by numbers.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Prefix. Scanning is $q\cdot nm$ up to $2\cdot10^{11}$ — too slow; a $O(nm)$ build ($10^{6}$) plus $O(1)$ per query is $O(nm + q)\approx10^{6}$. The table costs $10^{6}$ cells of memory, comfortably fine; a value up to $10^{15}$ demands 64-bit (@sec-nd-p1-rectsum).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**10. When does this whole family stop working — i.e. updates and queries arrive interleaved, online? What do you switch to?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Prefix and difference tables are *offline/static* (a difference needs a final scan; a prefix rebuild is $O(nm)$ per point change). Interleaved online point/rectangle updates with rectangle sums need a Fenwick / 2D BIT in $O(\log^2 n)$, or a lazy segment tree; a large offline batch with a hard-to-decompose answer may instead go to Mo. That is a different data structure, @sec-ds / @sec-mo (@sec-nd-a6).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**11. Walk us through the overflow discipline for weighted sums. When can a $10^{5}$-element, $10^{9}$-value problem still blow a `long long`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A single product $a[i](i{+}1)(n{-}i)$ with those bounds is $10^{9}\cdot(10^{5})^{2} = 10^{19}$, already past the $9.22\cdot10^{18}$ `long long` ceiling before you even sum. Mitigate by taking a given modulus after every multiply/add, by factoring the sum so no intermediate exceeds $\sim10^{14}$, or by `__int128` accumulation (@sec-nd-pit, @sec-nd-p3-linear, @sec-nd-p4-rybinsk).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**12. A problem is tagged `matrices` and asks for rectangle sums, but a plain 2D prefix TLEs. Give three reasons that happen and how you'd diagnose which.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) Updates interleave with queries → it is a 2D BIT (SPOJ MATSUM, CF 1252K). (2) The update applies a transform/matrix to a range → lazy segtree with matrix exponentiation (CF 718C). (3) The query answer is a DP over toggled cells, not a static sum (CF 1598E). Diagnosis: read whether the grid *changes* between questions and whether "sum" is literally additive — the tag is not the technique (@sec-nd-pit, @sec-nd-p1).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="25"}
**13. Prove your difference-and-prefix duality claim: for the same rectangle-add workload, show that prefixing the difference array yields exactly the painted grid.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each add writes $D[r_0][c_0]{+}=v$, $D[r_1][c_0]{-}=v$, $D[r_0][c_1]{-}=v$, $D[r_1][c_1]{+}=v$. The 2D prefix at cell $(i,j)$ sums $D$ over $[0,i]\times[0,j]$; the $+v$ at $(r_0,c_0)$ enters that window for every $(i,j)$ with $i\ge r_0, j\ge c_0$, and the three cancelling marks subtract it again exactly once $i$ or $j$ pass $r_1/c_1$. Net $v$ iff $(i,j)\in[r_0,r_1)\times[c_0,c_1)$ — the painted cell. Linearity over operations gives the full grid (@sec-nd-a2, @sec-nd-p2-rectadd).
:::
:::

## 163 · Introduction to Trees {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-tr]{.cs-link}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does a tree on n vertices have n − 1 edges?"}
An acyclic graph with an edge has a leaf. Delete the leaf and its edge. Repeat until one vertex remains. You deleted $n - 1$ edges. A program that checks "connected and $n - 1$ edges" does not also need a cycle detector.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="n − 1 edges were given. Is it a tree?"}
Not yet. The edges can form a cycle in one component and leave another vertex out. One BFS must visit every vertex.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is the height of a single node?"}
This book: $0$ edges. LeetCode maximum depth: $1$ node. Empty: $-1$ edges, or $0$ in the LeetCode function. Returning $1$ for null makes every leaf report $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Full, complete, perfect, balanced — which implies which?"}
Perfect implies complete and full. Complete implies balanced. A full tree need not be complete. A complete tree need not be full. The formula $2^k - 1$ needs the perfect case of a complete tree.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the complete-tree node count O(log² n)?"}
A complete tree of unequal left and right path lengths has exactly one child that is not perfect. The recursion follows that child, $O(\log n)$ nodes, and each of them walks $O(\log n)$ edges. The perfect child returns $2^k - 1$ and stops.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where does the minimum-depth recursion go wrong?"}
When a missing child is treated as depth $0$. A node with only a right child then reports $1$. Recurse only into children that exist.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Same tree versus symmetric tree?"}
Same tree pairs left with left. Symmetric pairs left with right. Both null is a success in both.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is a fresh string on the way down quadratic?"}
A left spine of $n$ nodes copies $1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ characters. One shared list, pushed before the children and popped after, copies a path only when a leaf emits it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The parent array is a path of 10⁵ vertices. What breaks?"}
The call stack. A BFS from the root is an array in top-down order, and its reverse is bottom-up. Subtree sizes add along that reverse. The arithmetic is still $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How do you test whether the tree is a star without rooting it?"}
Degree $n - 1$. A tree has no parallel edges, so that vertex touches every other vertex. A path of three is a star. A path of four is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why do three labels at one vertex cap the path MEX at 2?"}
A path uses at most two edges at any vertex. If $0, 1, 2$ meet at one vertex, every path misses at least one of them. A path-shaped tree has no such vertex, and the pair of endpoints sees every label, so the MEX is $n - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The infection only walked down and returned 1. What was missing?"}
The parent. Build the parent map, then BFS over left, right and parent, and mark a node seen when it is enqueued.
:::

## 164 · Tree Traversals {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-tv]{.cs-link}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where does the root sit in each order?"}
First in preorder, last in postorder, and between its two subtrees in inorder. Level order meets it in round $0$, alone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why push the right child first in iterative preorder?"}
A stack pops the most recently pushed child. The left child must be visited next, so it is pushed last.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What does the postorder pointer last mean?"}
It is the node just emitted. A node still on the stack is emitted when its right child is missing or is exactly `last`. Comparing values instead of pointers fires early when two nodes share a value.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why capture the queue length?"}
Children pushed during a round belong to the next level. If the loop condition re-reads the live size, those children are popped in the same round and the level average mixes two rows.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What does Morris change, and what must it undo?"}
It points the inorder predecessor's null right child at the current node, walks the left subtree, then clears that pointer and emits. Leaving the pointer in place is a cycle. The tree's shape at the end matches the tree's shape at the start.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="When is a permutation a DFS order of the heap?"}
It starts at $1$, and for every adjacent pair the parent of the next vertex is an ancestor of the current vertex or the current vertex itself. On this perfect heap that ancestor test is a bit shift. The BFS order $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ fails it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the optimal interval maximum the number of leaves?"}
Two leaves are disjoint non-empty subtrees, so they need two different positive numbers. Numbering the leaves in DFS finish order, and giving each vertex the block of leaves in its subtree, uses nothing larger.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does zigzag not alternate a queue's push order?"}
A queue preserves order. Pushing right then left still pops the earlier child first after the previous level's own reversal has been lost. Reverse the stored row, or use a stack, whose pop reverses.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is a cousin sum, and what does the root become?"}
The sum of the nodes at the same depth with a different parent. That is the level sum minus the sibling group. The root has no cousins, so it becomes $0$. Read the old group sum before writing either child.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the flatten splice three assignments in that order?"}
The rightmost node of the left subtree is the last preorder node before the right subtree. Point it at the old right subtree first. Then move the left subtree onto `right` and clear `left`. Swapping the first two assignments drops the right subtree.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How do two swapped BST values show up in the inorder?"}
As one descent if they were adjacent in the inorder, and as two descents otherwise. The larger node of the first descent and the smaller node of the last descent are the swapped pair.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does a serialisation need null markers?"}
Preorder `1, 2` is both a left child and a right child. A `#` for every missing child makes the left subtree a well-defined prefix of the remaining tokens, so decode can be a single left-to-right scan.
:::

## 199 · Introduction to Graphs {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-gr]{.cs-link}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the sum of degrees even?"}
Each edge has two ends, so the sum is $2|E|$. A self-loop contributes both ends at one vertex. An even sum forces an even number of odd degrees.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="When do you allocate a matrix?"}
When the algorithm looks at pairs and $n \lesssim 5000$. At $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$ the matrix does not fit. The default store is an adjacency list, $1$-indexed in contests ($n + 1$ slots) and $0$-indexed on the LeetCode problems of this chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What do you set before the BFS loop?"}
$\mathrm{dist}[s] = 0$, and $s$ is already in the queue, marked. A source left at the sentinel $-1$ makes its own neighbours look undiscovered.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why mark on the way in?"}
A vertex then enters the queue once. Marking on the way out allows two neighbours to push the same cell. The $2 \times 2$ island measures $5$ under that bug and $4$ under the push-time mark.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Connected, acyclic, n − 1 edges: how many do you test?"}
Any two imply the third, for $n \ge 1$. The practical test is "$n - 1$ edges, and one search from vertex $1$ visits everyone." @sec-tr records the same fact for rooted trees.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What does a functional graph look like?"}
$n$ vertices, $n$ arcs, out-degree $1$ everywhere. Every component is a cycle with trees directed into it. It contains a cycle, so it is not a DAG.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the Two Buttons window twice the larger endpoint?"}
$3 \to 5$ is the walk $3 \to 6 \to 5$. The state $6$ is larger than both endpoints. The window $\max(n, m)$ leaves the distance at $-1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How do you roll a lock wheel down from 0?"}
The next digit is $(g + 9) \bmod 10$. At $g = 0$ that is $9$. The C++ expression `(g - 1) % 10` is negative at $0$, and the place-value update writes a different code.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Badge: why does a cycle vertex answer itself?"}
The walk from that vertex repeats when it returns to the start. The first repeated student on the walk from $3$ in $2 \to 3 \to 2$ is $3$. Copying the entrance of the cycle onto every cycle vertex answers $2$ for all three, and the sample wants $2, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does a boolean visited array invent a cycle?"}
It cannot tell "repeated on this walk" from "visited in a previous component." On `[1, 0, 3, 1]` the cycle $\{0, 1\}$ is stamped first. The tail $2 \to 3 \to 1$ then hits an old stamp. Subtracting that old stamp reports length $3$. The start-time test rejects it and leaves the answer at $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Four neighbours or eight?"}
Four: shared sides only. The diagonal plan `.#` / `#.` is two rooms. Eight: the same plan is one room, because the floors touch at a corner. A $1000 \times 1000$ checkerboard is $500000$ rooms under the four-neighbour rule.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does the duplicate equal the cycle entrance?"}
Index $i$ points at `nums[i]`, and every value is in $1..n$, so nothing points at $0$. The walk from $0$ therefore has a tail. The entrance is reached from the last tail vertex and from the last cycle vertex: two indices hold that value. Phase 1 meets on the cycle after a multiple of the cycle length. Phase 2 restarts at $0$, and the two pointers meet at that entrance after exactly the tail length. Restarting at `nums[0]` keeps a constant gap, so the loop does not finish.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What do you write down before coding?"}
The vertex, the edge and its direction, whether it is weighted, the question in those words, $|V|$ and $|E|$ from the constraints, and the shape: tree, grid, DAG, or one successor per vertex. The pattern is usually the shape.
:::

## 200 · Depth-First Search {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-df]{.cs-link}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What are the gray vertices?"}
The root path of the current call. A directed edge into a gray vertex closes a cycle. A vertex turns black when its call returns, and an edge into a black vertex does not close a cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="State the parenthesis theorem."}
$u$ is an ancestor of $v$ in this search when $\mathrm{tin}(u) \le \mathrm{tin}(v)$ and $\mathrm{tout}(v) \le \mathrm{tout}(u)$. The interval of $u$ contains the intervals of its descendants and of nobody else.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Name the four directed edges."}
Tree: the head was white. Back: the head is gray. Forward: the head is black and was entered after the tail. Cross: the head is black and was entered before the tail.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does the undirected search skip the parent?"}
The road back to the vertex that discovered $u$ is the tree edge, looked at from the child. Counting it produces a cycle of length $2$ on every tree edge. Any other visited neighbour is a real back edge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="When is the index loop a post-order?"}
When every parent has a smaller index than its child. Scanning from $n$ down to $1$ then meets the children first. Scanning upward hands a vertex to its parent before those children have been added.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where does a subtree value get added?"}
On the way out, after the recursive calls. A size, a colour balance, a product of component sizes: each of them exists once the children have returned.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where does a pushed value get added?"}
On the way in, before the children run, or in a separate parent-before-child order such as a BFS from the root. Ki records the operation at $p$ and lets one such pass carry it through the subtree.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is the k-th soldier one array lookup?"}
The command is a DFS that always takes the smallest child index, so the receivers under $u$ are a contiguous block of one global preorder, of length $\mathrm{sz}[u]$, starting at $u$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why does a DAG need no visited array for path listing?"}
A walk cannot return to an ancestor, so the path stack cannot repeat a vertex. The same program on a grid must clear the mark on the way out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Who are the ancestors of v?"}
The vertices that reach $v$. Reverse the arcs and search from $v$. Leave $v$ itself out of the list, and emit the marks in index order.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="When is walling the exit allowed?"}
When there is no good person. A bad neighbour of the exit is sealed by walling the exit. A good person next to a bad person cannot be sealed at all, because neither of those two cells may become a wall.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recursive or explicit stack?"}
Recursion while the depth fits. A path of $10^5$ vertices can overflow a call stack of a few megabytes. A cursor on an explicit stack, or a parent-before-child array, computes the same sums.
:::

## 229 · Introduction to Dynamic Programming {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-dpi]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**1. What is dynamic programming, and how does it differ from divide and conquer and from greedy?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
DP solves a problem from answers to smaller subproblems and stores each answer once, because the subproblems **overlap**. Divide and conquer also recurses on smaller instances, but they do not overlap (merge sort's halves), so there is nothing to store. Greedy commits to one choice per step without comparing alternatives; DP compares all choices at each step, which is why it is correct where greedy fails.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**2. Memoisation or tabulation: which do you choose?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Memoisation when the recursion is natural, the reachable states are sparse, or the order is awkward; it only computes states that are needed. Tabulation when the states are dense and the order is obvious; it has no recursion overhead, no stack-depth risk, and allows rolling arrays for $O(1)$ space. In Python, large inputs push you to tabulation because of the recursion limit.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**3. How do you choose the state?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Imagine stopping halfway through building a solution and ask what you need to know to finish it optimally — nothing about how you got there unless it restricts the future. That information is the state: the position, plus anything that restricts the next choice (the last activity, holding or not, transactions used). Then write the state as a sentence and check that the transition only needs smaller states.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**4. How do you know a problem has overlapping subproblems?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write the brute-force recursion and look at its arguments: if the number of distinct argument tuples is polynomial while the recursion tree is exponential, the same arguments must repeat. Counting the distinct states (e.g. $n$ positions × 3 activities) is the quickest check.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**5. How do you reduce the space of a DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If row $i$ only reads rows $i-1$ (and $i-2$), keep just those rows (rolling arrays). In 0/1-style updates, iterate in the direction that does not overwrite values you still need. The price is reconstruction: you lose the table, so keep parent pointers or recompute.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**6. How do you return the actual solution, not just its value?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Either store, for each state, which transition gave its best value (parent pointers), or keep the table and walk back from the answer, at each step choosing a transition whose value explains the current state. Then verify by recomputing the value of the reconstructed solution.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**7. You count the ways to make change and get too large an answer. What happened?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
You probably counted ordered sequences (compositions) when combinations were asked: with the loop over the amount outside and the coins inside, $1+2$ and $2+1$ are counted separately. Putting the coin loop outside fixes the order in which coins are added, so each multiset is counted once.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**8. Why does greedy fail for House Robber, and why does DP work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Taking the richest house can block two neighbours worth more together (e.g. $[2, 3, 2]$). DP never commits early: for each prefix it keeps the best value both with and without the last house, which captures every possibility.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**9. When is a recursion not a valid DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the subproblem graph has a **cycle**: a state depends, directly or indirectly, on itself (e.g. shortest paths in a graph with cycles, or a grid where you can move in all four directions). Then there is no order in which to fill the table; you need a graph algorithm (Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford) or to solve equations.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**10. What is the time complexity of a DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The sum over states of the work per state — usually (number of states) × (number of transitions per state). Climbing stairs: $n \times 2$. A grid: $nm \times 2$. Stock with $k$ transactions: $n \times k \times 2$. This is what to compare with the operation budget.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**11. Explain Kadane's algorithm as a DP.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
State: $e_i$ = best sum of a subarray **ending at** $i$. Transition: extend the best one ending at $i-1$ or start fresh, $e_i = a_i + \max(e_{i-1}, 0)$. Answer: $\max_i e_i$. The "ending at $i$" state is the key trick: it makes the subarray contiguous by construction, and variants add phases (deleted or not, inside or outside a segment).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**12. Your DP passes small tests but fails on large ones. What do you check?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Overflow (32-bit sums, $-\infty$ plus a cost), a missing modulus, the recursion limit or stack size, and time (states × transitions too large). Then stress test against a brute force on random small inputs to rule out a logic bug that only shows on rarer cases.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="229"}
**13. How would you handle "at most $k$ operations" in a DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Add the number of operations used as a state dimension: $dp[i][j]$, $0 \le j \le k$. The table grows by a factor $k$; if $k$ is large, look for a shortcut (as in the stock problem, where $k \ge n/2$ means no limit) or for convexity in $k$ (the Aliens trick, a later chapter).
:::
:::

## 230 · One-Dimensional DP {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-od]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**1. What are the six look-back shapes, and why do you name the shape before you code?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$W(i)$ is the set of earlier positions that $dp[i]$ reads (@sec-od-look). The six shapes are a fixed handful of neighbours, a set the input chooses, a sliding range, every earlier index, the one latest compatible predecessor, and a cell keyed by a value rather than by an index. The shape is the complexity: a window of width $k$ is $O(nk)$ until a deque or a prefix sum removes the inner loop, and "all earlier indices" is a partition. Naming it also picks the tool in @sec-od-fast instead of reaching for a deque on a sum.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**2. When do you pull, when do you push, and when do you write a suffix?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pull when the statement describes the last piece or the predecessors of $i$: $dp[i]$ reads cells that are already final (@sec-od-dir). Push when the statement lists the moves out of $i$: standing at $i$, write into each successor. A suffix, $f(i)$ = best from $i$ to the end, is the natural question when the move is "from here, jump forward", and it is filled from the right. The three are the same DAG. Push wins when the out-degree is tiny (Frog Jump's three lengths). Pull wins when a monotone test can stop the scan (a shelf that has grown too wide).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**3. When is a monotonic deque the legal speed-up?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When $dp[i]$ needs the minimum or the maximum of a contiguous window that slides one step at a time, and the value stored in the deque is exactly the value being optimised (@sec-od-p1-jump6). Indices enter from the left, the front falls out when it leaves the window, and the back drops any index that the new index dominates. A range sum is prefix sums.
