A set of divisors is a loop over the set. A window whose cost is $dp[j]$ plus something that depends on both ends is not this deque.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**4. When does BFS replace the DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When a move can point backward, the dependency graph can contain a cycle and no index order is safe (@sec-od-wrong). Jump Game III is that case: visit each index once. BFS also replaces a shortest-path DP when every edge has cost 1. Jump Game II's layer scan is that BFS, collapsed to two integers because the reachable set of each layer is a prefix. The collapse uses the range lemma. An exact jump length keeps the queue.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**5. Why is the min-jump table of Jump Game II non-decreasing, and what does that buy?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From a reachable index $j$ you can land on every index in $(j, j + a_j]$. So if $j$ is reachable and $i < j$, then $i$ is reachable, and a shortest route to $j$ has already passed some cell of the prefix, which means $dp[i] \le dp[j]$. The cells with $dp \le t$ are therefore a prefix, and the frontier of layer $t$ is a single farthest index. The scan in @sec-od-p4-jump2 maintains that frontier in $O(n)$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**6. Where does a partition go off by one?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The last block of a solution for the first $i$ items is a half-open segment $[j, i)$, and the prefix in front of it is $dp[j]$, including $j = 0$ (@sec-od-part). The inner index runs from $i - 1$ downward so the block's max, sum, or width grows by one element. The first failing monotone test ends the loop. Scoring the block before the test records an infeasible shelf. In the suffix form, solving $i$ and skipping the next $b_i$ items lands on $i + b_i + 1$, and that index is clamped at $n$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**7. How do you keep an impossible state from overflowing?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pick a sentinel you are allowed to add a real cost to. Daily difficulties sum to at most $n \cdot 1000$, so $10^9$ is above every real answer and $10^9 + 1000$ still fits in a signed 32-bit integer (@sec-od-p5-diff). `INT_MAX` plus a positive cost overflows and becomes negative, and the minimum then prefers the impossible cell. The transition adds only when the previous cell is strictly below the sentinel. Initialising impossible cells to 0 schedules empty days: $[1,1,1]$ with three days returns 1.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**8. Why is the state of Frog Jump the pair $(i, k)$, and why is the first jump 1?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Two routes can stand on the same stone with different last jumps, and the next jump is chosen from $\{k-1, k, k+1\}$. Position alone throws away the only fact the future needs. The start is a virtual jump of length 0, so the first real jump is exactly 1. A jump of length 0 is rejected: it would land on the same stone. Because each jump grows by at most 1 and lands on a later stone, a reachable $k$ on stone $i$ satisfies $k \le i$, and the table is $n$ by $n+1$ (@sec-od-p4-frog).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**9. Why can house robber use two variables, while brainpower cannot?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
House robber reads $f(i+1)$ and $f(i+2)$, a window of length 2. Brainpower's take branch reads $f(i + b_i + 1)$, and $b_i$ is data (@sec-od-p5-brain). While the fill walks left, a question still to the left may land on any cell to the right of $i$. A ring of width $\max b_i + 2$ is legal. Two variables are not. The answer is also up to $10^{10}$, so it is a 64-bit integer.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**10. What is the difference between a prefix formulation and a suffix formulation on the same choices?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A prefix $dp[i]$ answers "best for the first $i$ items, the past is finished". A suffix $f(i)$ answers "best from $i$ to the end, $i$ is free to decide". They match when every jump has the same length. They stop matching when an earlier take can still be blocking $i$ through a data-dependent window: the prefix then has to remember how long the block lasts, which is a second index, while the suffix already stores that fact by where the jump landed (@sec-od-dir).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**11. Decode Ways II gives 9 for `"*"`, 18 for `"1*"`, and 15 for `"2*"`. Where do those numbers come from?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A single `*` is the nine digits 1 through 9. `"1*"` is a one-digit letter followed by another (9 ways) or one of the two-digit codes 11 through 19 (9 ways), total 18. `"2*"` is nine one-digit pairs plus the six codes 21 through 26, total 15. `"**"` is $9 \cdot 9$ one-digit pairs plus the fifteen two-digit codes, total 96. Forgetting the multiplicity and treating `*` as one character is the bug (@sec-od-p3-decode).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**12. The knight dialer at $n = 3131$ is too big for a recursion. What do you actually run?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The phone graph has ten vertices and the walks are counted modulo $10^9+7$. Symmetry leaves four classes: the corners 1, 3, 7, 9; the key 5 (only at $n = 1$); the side keys 2, 4, 6, 8; and the pair 0 and 8's partner structure used in @sec-od-p3-knight. One step updates the four class totals, in $O(n)$, and the answer for $n = 3131$ is $136006598$. The recursion and the memo are for the samples $n = 1$ and $n = 2$. A matrix power is the same recurrence written for a huge $n$ that is not this constraint.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**13. You rolled a layered partition into one array and the answers became too small. What did the loop do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Layer $k$ may read only layer $k-1$, and only at indices $j < i$. Filling $i$ downward leaves every $j < i$ on the old layer. Filling $i$ upward reads the value just written, so two days collapse into one (@sec-od-p5-diff). After the downward pass, index $k-1$ goes back to the sentinel: that cell is $dp[k][k-1]$, which cannot exist, and the next layer's lower bound never reads it.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="230"}
**14. A counting DP matches the samples and is too big on a long string. What do you check?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The product of multiplicities, not a missing transition, is the usual cause: the answer is taken modulo $10^9+7$ at every addition, in a 64-bit integer, because two partial counts already overflow a 32-bit `int`. Then check that a leading zero, a `*`, and a two-digit code each contribute the weight from the rule table rather than 1. A brute force that expands wildcards on strings of length at most 6 is the check that catches a wrong weight.
:::
:::

## 231 · Two-Dimensional Grid DP {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-gd]{.cs-link}

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**1. Why does a forward DP fail on Dungeon Game, and why is the backward value clamped at $1$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A prefix has two numbers that do not dominate: the lowest health so far, and the health you hold now. "Most health left" on sample 1 follows down, down, right, right, gains $28$, and needs $8$. The answer is $7$. A suffix has one number, the least health on entering it. After the room you must cover the cheaper successor, and you must be alive on entry, so $need = \max(1, \min(\text{next}) - \text{cell})$. Without the floor, `[[0, 30, -5]]` returns a negative (@sec-gd-p3-dung).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**2. What is wrong with a pad of $0$, and with seeding the princess's own cell with $1$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Zero is smaller than every real need, so the minimum walks off the board and skips the rest of the dungeon. Sample 1 returns $6$. The princess's room has a value too: seeding her cell with $1$ ignores the $-5$, and sample 1 again returns $6$. Outside cells are $+\infty$, except the single seed past her room.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**3. Why does the rolling dungeon row run right to left?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`row[c]` still holds the value from the row below, and `row[c + 1]` must already hold the new value to the right. A left-to-right sweep reads the old right neighbour. The square's rolling row is the mirror image of the same idea: you overwrite left to right, and one variable remembers the diagonal you just destroyed (@sec-gd-p5-square).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**4. When do you add a layer instead of reversing the fill?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reverse the fill when the suffix has a one-number summary and the moves still go only right and down. Add a layer when the moves can go backward, so the cells have a cycle, but some counter — moves, time, fuel, a strictly larger value — increases on every step. The counter, not the cell, is the fill order. If nothing increases, the search is BFS or Dijkstra (@sec-gd-p3-out).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**5. Why is a memo on $(r, c)$ wrong for out-of-boundary paths?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"Ways to leave $(0, 0)$" is $2$ with one move left and $6$ with two, on the $2\times 2$ sample. A key without the budget returns whichever value was stored first. On a cyclic grid that key also fails to terminate, because a cell calls its neighbour and the neighbour calls it back.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**6. Why are two arrays required for one layer of a four-direction walk?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cells in the same layer do not depend on each other. Every arrow goes to the next value of the counter. Writing the push into the array you are reading lets one ball take several steps in a single round. Sample 2 of out-of-boundary paths stops being $12$.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**7. Why is a round trip two forward walkers, and why is $t = r + c$ enough?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read the return trip backwards and it is a right/down walk on the same cells. The score is the set of cells, so the direction of the second walk does not matter. Every right or down step increases $r + c$ by one, so after $t$ steps both walkers are on that anti-diagonal and the column is $t - r$. The state is $(t, r_1, r_2)$, not four coordinates (@sec-gd-p4-cherry).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**8. When do two walkers share a cell, and what goes wrong if you add it twice?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A cell $(r, c)$ is visited only at tick $r + c$. Both walkers are there at that tick exactly when their rows match. The gain adds the second cell only when $r_1 \ne r_2$. Adding it always makes sample 1 return $8$: both walkers take the same route and its cherries are paid twice. A $1\times 1$ grid must score its only cell once.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**9. Why is $-\infty$ not $0$, and why does the public answer clamp at $0$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A thorn is unreachable. If that state holds $0$ and is extended like any other state, sample 2 of cherry pickup returns $3$: the walkers cross the thorn diagonal. Keep $-\infty$, and apply $\max(0, \cdot)$ once at the corner, because "no route" is reported as $0$. Do not clamp the intermediate cells: a later cherry cannot rescue a walk that already hit a thorn, and a zero cherry is a real total.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**10. Why is cherry pickup II's answer one entry, not the max of the first row?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The suffix $dp[r][c_1][c_2]$ is "best from here downward", and "here" for the problem is the two starting corners. $dp[0][0][\mathrm{cols}-1]$ is that state. The maximum over row $0$ lets the robots start in any columns. Both official samples still return $24$ and $28$. The grid with a single $9$ that neither robot can reach returns $9$ instead of $0$ (@sec-gd-p4-cherry2).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**11. What does $sq[r][c]$ mean, and why the minimum of three neighbours?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is $(r, c)$. A square of side $k$ leaves three squares of side $k - 1$ when you delete its last row, its last column, or both, so the side is one more than the shortest of those three, and only if $(r, c)$ is a one. Up and left are the edges. The diagonal is the interior. The problem asks for the area, $(\max sq)^2$ (@sec-gd-p5-square).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**12. Why does the histogram need a bar of height $0$ at the end?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Bars still on the stack have not been measured. Row 2 of the sample is $3, 1, 3, 2, 2$. Without the sentinel the stack still holds the bar of height $1$ and the bar of height $2$, and the area $6$ is never written; the routine returns $4$. The sentinel pops every remaining bar. The width is $i - left - 1$, with $left = -1$ when the stack becomes empty (@sec-gd-p5-rect).
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**13. Why is the largest rectangle not the square recurrence?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One number at a corner cannot name every rectangle that uses that corner: the rectangle's height and width are independent. The square on the sample matrix is $4$. The rectangle is $6$, a $2\times 3$ whose floor is row 2. Fix the bottom row, turn the columns into histogram bars, and solve the histogram.
:::
:::

::: {.qb-item data-chapter="231"}
**14. When is a grid problem not a DP?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When no quantity strictly increases along a move, the cells can contain a cycle and no fill order exists. Path With Minimum Effort is a shortest path. Unique Paths III visits every free cell exactly once, so the state would be the set of visited cells; with at most $20$ cells the intended search is backtracking. A closed walk of odd length on a grid is impossible for a cheaper reason: every edge flips the colour of $r + c$.
:::
:::

## 232 · Subsequence DP (the LIS Family) {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-lis]{.cs-link}

**1.** What is the difference between a subarray and a subsequence?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A subarray is a contiguous block, so the previous chosen index is the neighbour. A subsequence keeps the array order and may skip, so the previous chosen index is any earlier compatible index. There are $O(n^2)$ subarrays and $2^n$ subsequences. The DP stores one answer per ending, not the list.
:::

**2.** Why is the LIS answer $\max_i end[i]$ and not $end[n - 1]$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The definition of $end[i]$ forces the subsequence to include $i$ as its last element. The longest one in the whole array may end earlier. On a decreasing array every $end[i]$ is 1. On the envelope sample the last sorted envelope does not extend the chain of three.
:::

**3.** Why is the tails array not a subsequence you can print?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$tails[k]$ is the smallest value that currently ends some increasing subsequence of length $k + 1$. A later, smaller value overwrites that slot and throws away the previous end. The length of the array is the LIS. One actual subsequence is the parent walk stored at insertion time.
:::

**4.** When do you use the first tail $\ge x$, and when the first tail $> x$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Strictly increasing uses $\ge$, so an equal value replaces a slot and does not extend. Non-decreasing uses $>$, so an equal value extends. Seven equal values have strict LIS 1 and non-decreasing LIS 7. A $k$-increasing chain is non-decreasing.
:::

**5.** Why do Russian-doll heights go descending when the widths tie?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Equal widths do not nest. If the heights also increase, a strict LIS on the heights reports a chain. Descending heights inside the tie make the later height smaller, and the strict test refuses it. $[[1, 1], [1, 2]]$ answers 1 only with that tie-break.
:::

**6.** Why does sorting a cuboid's three sides not lose the optimum?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
You may rotate. If one box fits under another in some orientation, it fits after both triples are sorted, smallest side against smallest. The height you add is the largest side. The comparison is $\le$, so equal boxes stack.
:::

**7.** A mountain subsequence uses two LIS tables. What do you subtract, and what do you reject?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The peak is in both the rising length and the falling length, so the mountain length is $left + right - 1$. An arm of length 1 means that side is empty, and that index is not a peak. The removals are $n$ minus the longest accepted mountain.
:::

**8.** Why is the state of an arithmetic subsequence not just the index?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Several differences can end at the same index. Keeping only the longest throws away a shorter difference that a later element extends. The state is $(index, difference)$. A difference that is given in the input collapses back to one map from value to length.
:::

**9.** Why is LIS II a segment tree rather than the tails array?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Tails answers "any smaller value". LIS II allows only values in $[x - k,\ x - 1]$. That window has a left end, which a prefix structure cannot express. Query the window, then write the new length at $x$.
:::

**10.** Why does $k$-increasing split into $k$ independent chains?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The only comparisons are $a[i] \le a[i + k]$. Index $i$ never constrains $i + 1$ unless $k = 1$. Each residue class is its own non-decreasing problem, and the changes add. The kept length is an LNDS, not a strict LIS.
:::

**11.** What goes wrong if the three mod-3 totals are updated in place?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Taking $x$ writes a new remainder, and a later iteration of the same element reads that new remainder and takes $x$ again. Copy the row first. Also leave remainders 1 and 2 at $-\infty$ until a real sum reaches them. Remainder 0 starts at 0 because the empty sum is legal.
:::

**12.** `"aaa"` has seven non-empty subsets. Why is the answer 3?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The problem counts distinct strings, not index sets. The subsets spell `a`, `aa`, and `aaa`. The update replaces the count of subsequences ending at this letter, or equivalently doubles the total and subtracts what the previous copy of the letter already produced. The empty string is not counted.
:::

**13.** How do you delete the fewest elements to leave a strictly increasing array? How do you cover the array with the fewest increasing subsequences?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Deletions: keep an LIS, so the answer is $n - \mathrm{LIS}$. A cover by increasing subsequences has size equal to the longest decreasing subsequence. Both are the complement view: the object you delete or the objects that cannot share a chain are what the LIS machinery measures.
:::

## 233 · String DP: Two Sequences at Once {.unnumbered .qb-chapter}

[Chapter: @sec-st]{.cs-link}

**1.** What does $dp[i][j]$ mean on the prefix grid, and why is the fill order safe?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the answer for $s[0..i)$ and $t[0..j)$. The three arrows come from shorter prefixes, so every dependency points up or left. Filling by increasing $i$, and increasing $j$ inside the row, meets every arrow.
:::

**2.** Why are row 0 and column 0 different problems for LCS and for edit distance?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An LCS with an empty string has length 0. An edit script that builds a string from nothing inserts every letter, so the border is the length. An ASCII delete pays the prefix sum. A zero in a cost border is a free deletion.
:::

**3.** When is one row enough, and when do you lose the answer by rolling?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number, the cost, and the boolean live in the corner and need only the previous row. The string and the script live in the arrows, which a rolling row forgets. Reconstruction keeps the table, or reruns a linear-memory divide at the optimal midpoint.
:::

**4.** How do you recover one LCS, and one shortest common supersequence, from the same table?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Walk from the corner. Equal letters that explain the cell are a match: the LCS records the letter, and the supersequence writes it once. A step up or left drops a letter from the LCS and writes that letter into the supersequence. The length of the supersequence is $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}$.
:::

**5.** What is the indel distance in terms of the LCS?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Insert and delete only, no replacement: $n + m - 2 \cdot \mathrm{LCS}$. Each unmatched letter is deleted from one string. Edit distance is smaller or equal because a replacement can fix two unmatched letters at cost 1.
:::

**6.** Why is minimum ASCII delete sum not "keep an LCS"?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The diagonal carries the letter's code, not 1. Two common subsequences of equal length can have different weights. Equivalently the cost is the sum of both strings minus twice the heaviest common subsequence.
:::

**7.** Distinct subsequences of one string versus embeddings of a target: which problem is which?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
@sec-lis-p5-dist counts distinct strings, so `aaa` is 3. This chapter's grid counts index sets of `s` that spell a fixed `t`, so `rabbbit` against `rabbit` is 3 even though the string is unique. The rolling row for the count sweeps from the right.
:::

**8.** Why does a greedy interleaving fail?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When both strings offer the next letter, the right choice depends on the future. Preferring `s1` fails `aabcc` / `dbbca` / `aadbbcbcac`. The cell ORs both attributions. The index in the third string is $i + j$, so the lengths must add before the table starts.
:::

**9.** What is the difference between a wildcard `*` and a regex `x*`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A wildcard star matches any characters, including none: left for empty, up for one more. `x*` matches only copies of `x`, and zero copies jumps two pattern columns because the letter and the star are one token. The wildcard greedy is wrong for regex; `aab` against `a*b*ab` is the counterexample.
:::

**10.** Why is the KMP state absorbing when you count strings that contain a pattern?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A string may contain the pattern many times. Summing over start positions counts it many times. Once the automaton reaches the end of the pattern, further letters stay there, and the string is counted once, at the end, if the other constraints (balance, bounds) also hold.
:::

**11.** How do you forbid a word instead?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Do not take the transition into the matched state. Good strings do this, and they also keep two flags: still equal to the lower bound, still equal to the upper bound. After a flag drops, that side of the next letter is the whole alphabet, not the bound's letter.
:::

**12.** A checker accepts any shortest common supersequence. What do you test?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both input strings are subsequences of the output, and the length equals $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}$. Equality with one sample string rejects another correct walk.
:::
